title: Falcons vs. Ravens recap: Ghosts converge on Atlanta in an overtime loss
summary: We knew that even a banged-up Ravens team would be a tough out for the surging Falcons, but that Atlanta could increase their chances of a win by playing a clean game that played to their considerable strengths. That’s not what we got. Instead, the offense looked shaky throughout the first quarter and into the […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons looks to pass against the Baltimore Ravens in the second quarter of a game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images We knew that even a banged-up Ravens team would be a tough out for the surging Falcons, but that Atlanta could increase their chances of a win by playing a clean game that played to their considerable strengths. That’s not what we got. Instead, the offense looked shaky throughout the first quarter and into the second quarter, with iffy run blocking and Michael Penix Jr. running ice cold. The Falcons defense forced a fumble that Jessie Bates took to the house to give Atlanta the lead, and Penix did get untracked in the second quarter to lead a productive drive. But the Falcons fought field position issues caused by multiple special teams penalties, struggled to consistently pick up yardage on the ground, had notable miscues in run defense, and tried to get a little too cute on key fourth down and red zone plays in ways that ended up harming the effort. The Ravens, who kept settling for field goals and sticking with what they knew they could do with Tyler Huntley under center and talented backs to bring to bear, made this a tense game as a result even as Jeff Ulbrich kept them at bay and held to 15 points through three quarters. It seemed like the Falcons would still cruise to a win when they went up eight points with not much time left in the fourth quarter, but instead Huntley found endless success on passes over the middle against a gassed defense, including a touchdown, and then Derrick Henry converted the two point try to tie things up. The Falcons, with 40 seconds left, couldn’t get close enough for a field goal try in regulation. That left overtime, and a gassed defense down CJ Henderson kept showing cracks as Huntley and Henry marched down the field. Jeff Ulbrich has had answers for just about everything this year, but as the game wore on, unproductive blitzes and iffy run defense came to doom Atlanta. That left Tua Tagovailoa, in for an injured Penix, to try to lead a heroic drive down the field to tie things up or win outright down 30-23. He connected on a nice ball over the middle to Drake London and then immediately threw an interception to end things. It felt like a game the Falcons would lose as soon as the Ravens got deep into Atlanta territory late in the fourth quarter, and one of the nastiest things I can say about this game is that it felt extremely familiar. Ghosts converged on this team from every angle. The shoddy run defense that cost them repeatedly in 2025 was especially costly against a Baltimore team that knows how to run the ball. Penix’s familiar problems with pressure and accuracy, which were largely absent the past two weeks, cost the team opportunities in a way that also proved costly. Mike Hughes’ coverage struggles and the team’s depth woes at cornerback, the former which has been consistent and the latter which we hoped was a thing of the past, hit hard, though in fairness this defense was never going to be in great shape down both A.J. Terrell and CJ Henderson. Coordinators trying things that either outright don’t work or offer quickly diminishing returns played a role in this loss, too, and you can see apparitions of Zac Robinson, Jimmy Lake, Dean Pees, Dirk Koetter, and so forth floating in the air as I type that. This team lost in large part because they were spiritually if not exactly like the Falcons team that have struggled so much in the recent past. What you make of this loss likely depends on what you made of the Falcons coming into this game, and what you thought Baltimore was capable of with Huntley at quarterback. If you thought Atlanta was showing signs of being a playoff-caliber team after their two beatdowns of Green Bay and New Orleans, this will be a bitter effort to reckon with, especially if you believed the Ravens were not going to be up to snuff with so many backups in. If you thought the Falcons hadn’t faced a true test yet and the Ravens were still one of the league’s better teams even with a backup quarterback and fourth-string center in, this one will sting, but likely only a little. Either way, the Falcons have fallen back under .500, Penix is hurt (though we don’t know how badly yet), there are fresh questions and familiar questions about everything from the run defense to Jake Matthews to the secondary, and this team is back on the roller coaster we fervently hoped they had hopped off after the past two weeks. They’re neither as bad as they looked the first two weeks nor as good as they looked the last two, but if this ends up representing what this team looks like in the middle of those two poles, it’s going to be another bumpy sort of season. On to the full recap. The Good Michael Penix Jr. is streaky. He started this game ice cold, not just missing passes but missing them badly, and the offense suffered as a result. He followed that up with a second quarter drive where he caught fire, heaving bombs to Drake London and Jahan Dotson and zipping a pass by two Ravens for a Kyle Pitts touchdown. When he’s on, he can make heroic throws downfield at a rate not many quarterbacks in this league can match, and he was on enough to give this team a fighting chance until quite late. Bijan Robinson had a run in the first quarter that left me speechless, where he seemed dead in the backfield and turned around and ripped off a 15 yard run thanks to agility, toughness, and good old-fashioned magic. On a day where Brian Robinson Jr. couldn’t get any breathing room, Bijan put up a tidy five-plus yards per carry and got 86 yards on 17 carries. He probably should have had more touches, honestly, even though there were plenty of unproductive runs along the way. I give him an enormous amount of credit for the sheer effort on a bad Penix throw on the final Falcons drive of regulation, too, even though he couldn’t quite get it. I think Penix would throw the ball to Drake London if he was deep in the Pacific Ocean and Penix was on the 35 yard line in Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The level of trust between those two is unreal, and London made huge third down grabs for first downs over and over again in this one, seemingly willing himself open just enough for Penix to laser passes in there to him. London is a great receiver who just needs competent quarterback play to produce like one, and with Penix he has a quarterback who is never going to be afraid to target him. Jahan Dotson can fly, and Michael Penix Jr. loves slinging that ball downfield. That’s looking like it’ll be a fruitful combination this year, as Penix hit him for a beautiful deep touchdown in Week 4 and got him on a 36 yard bomb that set up a Falcons score in the second quarter. Kyle Pitts was going to get involved, and after he lumbered to life a bit in Week 4, he arrived in Week 5. A nice grab and run in the second quarter was a prelude to a touchdown grab to finish off that drive. Samson Ebukam has been a really good signing, and he flashed again in this one. His play of the game was the big third down, third quarter sack of Tyler Huntley, putting a swift end to a Baltimore drive when they were down just two points. Ditto Jared Ivey, who has been in and out of the rotation at outside linebacker but had an early sack in this one where he fought through a defender around his . Cameron Thomas got a half sack and Gervon Dexter got none, but they were the team’s two most consistently impactful defenders up front from my point of view. Dexter was relentless in pursuit and caught a couple of run plays from behind, while Thomas was one of the few Falcons who consistently made Huntley uncomfortable on Sunday night. Kendal Daniels was not always stellar against the run—I saw a couple of iffy angles—but his tackling was mostly incredibly sound, he was getting his hand up constantly and managed to…
author: Dave Choate

title: Week 5 Snap Reactions: A late collapse dooms Falcons
summary: Dear Reader, I regret to inform you that the Atlanta Falcons blew a fourth-quarter lead and lost in overtime to the Baltimore Ravens. Here are the Week 5 Snap Reactions. The Defensive Dam Broke The Falcons defense came undone. After playing sound defense for roughly 3 quarters, Jeff Ulbrich’s unit couldn’t keep up with the […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA- OCTOBER 11: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta,Georgia. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dear Reader, I regret to inform you that the Atlanta Falcons blew a fourth-quarter lead and lost in overtime to the Baltimore Ravens . Here are the Week 5 Snap Reactions. The Defensive Dam Broke The Falcons defense came undone. After playing sound defense for roughly 3 quarters, Jeff Ulbrich’s unit couldn’t keep up with the Ravens adjustments in the 4th. After not blitzing much this season, Ulbrich turned up the heat, and it worked at first. However, the blitz stopped working toward the end of the game. The Falcons generated only one pressure on 12 dropbacks during the Ravens final two drives, per NFLPro . The unit looked exhausted on the overtime drive, and injuries finally caught up with them. Early Down Struggles Late-down heroics are unsustainable; the Falcons faced too many 3rd and long situations on offense. While the 9-5 connection bailed them out most of the game, it couldn’t when the Falcons needed to sustain drives late in the game. Credit to Jesse Minter; his defense had answers for Tommy Rees on early downs, and the young OC couldn’t adjust. Bijan hit over 100 scrimmage yards yet again, but Minter forcing Atlanta to win with Penix’s arm on 3rd down eventually paid off. https://t.co/cCh7kilYaM pic.twitter.com/NjEhop4puu — Tre’Shon (@tre3shon) October 12, 2026 The Devil is in the Details A Jake Matthews drop, a wide-open Bijan missed, and Zay Flowers running through Divine Deablo. It’s the little things that come back to bite you. Penix is still struggling to hit the easy passes, and unlike the previous two weeks, the run game couldn’t overcome those misses. With the season Matthews is having as a blocker and him dealing with an injury all week, I can’t imagine why they used that play now; yes, he should’ve caught the ball, but Matthews not timing a jump correctly isn’t surprising, considering he’s not a skill player. Rees got too cute, and with the options he has on offense, we haven’t seen enough opportunities for the players paid to catch the ball. The Ravens' win probability was as low as 4.6% with 3:27 left in regulation in their 30-23 comeback win over the Falcons. It was the Falcons' seventh loss since 2016 with an in-game WP greater than 95%. Only the Eagles (8) have more such losses in the NGS era. @BALvsATL pic.twitter.com/2hAGwN56gg — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) October 12, 2026 What is Michael Penix Jr.? Is he a franchise QB? Is he done after this year? Are the injuries too much to bear? The reality is, there are still a lot of games left this season before we can reach a final verdict. As it stands, his footwork is still a problem, causing him to miss too many easy opportunities; that and his inability to access multiple arm angles—he’s stiff as a board. He can make the difficult throws scouts drool over, but routinely botches the layups. These things matter more to me than the rib injury because a better throw to Bijan late in the game prevents that injury from ever happening, and these issues exist regardless of injury. His future is uncertain, and if he can’t work through these problems, the team won’t view him as the answer under center. Michael Penix passing chart pic.twitter.com/eivNOPrcuy — Tre’Shon (@tre3shon) October 12, 2026 Atlanta now sits at 2-3, back under .500 yet again. Penix’s ribs will be monitored, but the team is reeling from injuries across the board, an excuse that’s hard to swallow after losing to the Ravens sans Lamar Jackson. Kevin Stefanski and his will have their work cut out for them as they hit a tough two-game stretch against some of the NFC’s best.
author: Tre'Shon Diaz

title: Winners and losers from Ravens’ Week 5 win over the Falcons
summary: The Ravens entered Week 5 without Lamar Jackson against a red-hot Falcons team and left with their most impressive win of the Jesse Minter era. There were plenty of winners in this one, while one player stood out as the biggest loser. Winners QB Tyler Huntley: Huntley showed once again why Baltimore has complete faith […]
full_text: The Ravens entered Week 5 without Lamar Jackson against a red-hot Falcons team and left with their most impressive win of the Jesse Minter era. There were plenty of winners in this one, while one player stood out as the biggest loser. Winners QB Tyler Huntley: Huntley showed once again why Baltimore has complete faith in him as Jackson’s backup. He finished with 24 completions on 32 attempts for 201 yards and two touchdowns, with 20 yards rushing and the game-winning score on a quarterback sneak. Huntley was particularly impressive on the final drive of regulation to tie the game on a back-shoulder touchdown pass to Devontez Walker. RB Derrick Henry: Everyone knew it would be a heavy Henry game without Jackson under center, and that is exactly what transpired. Henry rushed for 102 yards on 24 carries while scoring on an 18-yard reception. He also found the end zone on the two-point conversion to tie the game. Henry did not have a run longer than 11 yards, but he was able to grind out the tough yards and wear down Atlanta’s defense in overtime. Offensive line: The Ravens’ offensive line paved the way for 208 total rushing yards, utterly bullying the Falcons’ front at times. Rookie first-rounder Vega Ioane continues to look like a budding star wherever he plays on the interior, allowing zero pressures against Atlanta, per Pro Football Focus. WR Rashod Bateman: Bateman made multiple key plays to keep the offense moving against the Falcons, including three catches for 38 yards on the final game-tying drive of regulation. His 62 receiving yards (on five receptions) led the team for the second time this year after zero instances in 2025. WR Zay Flowers: While Flowers didn’t set off the fireworks we’ve come to expect this year, he still made several important plays throughout the game, finishing with 53 receiving yards on eight catches, plus one carry for 13 yards. He also lost 26 yards from his statline when the Ravens also opted to take a defensive pass interference penalty he drew to save an extra few seconds on the clock. Declan Doyle has fully unlocked the fourth-year receiver, and his numbers should jump back up once Jackson returns to the lineup. WR Devontez Walker: Walker had just two catches against Atlanta, but his second could not have come at a better time as Huntley connected with him on a back shoulder throw in the end zone on the game-tying drive. RB Justice Hill: Hill started the game on the wrong foot with a drop on the opening drive, but followed up with a 21-yard run on the next play to convert on third down. Hill broke off another long run later in the game with a 47-yard gain on another third down. He finished the game with 73 rushing yards on just four carries. S Kyle Hamilton: Hamilton shows up every week for Baltimore’s defense, and he made the biggest play of the day on Sunday. After marching down the field and scoring a touchdown to start overtime, the Ravens’ defense needed a stop against backup quarterback Tua Tagovailoa to win the game. After a 20-yard pass to Drake London, Tagovailoa again went to his superstar wide receiver, but Hamilton was waiting underneath this time to secure the game-sealing pick near midfield. He finished the game with six total tackles as well as two pressures, according to PFF. S Malaki Starks: Starks has begun to stack strong performances after a rocky start to his sophomore season. The former first-round pick had perhaps his best game of the season against the Falcons in Week 5. Starks made several critical tackles against Bijan Robinson, including one that saved a touchdown when he was one-on-one with the ultra-elusive back. Starks led the defense with 10 total tackles, including two tackles for loss. His 70.0 coverage grade was also the second-highest the team, according to PFF. OLB Mike Green: Green is another second-year player who has hit a groove in recent weeks. Without Trey Hendrickson on the field in the last two weeks, Green has stepped up on the edge, both as a pass rusher and against the run. Green had three pressures against Atlanta, according to PFF, to go with a sack. Green’s quick third-down pressure on quarterback Michael Penix forced a throwaway on the Falcons’ final drive of the game, keeping them from winning in regulation with a field goal. OLB Tavius Robinson: Just two plays earlier on Atlanta’s final drive in regulation, it was Robinson who nailed Penix for a sack on first down, causing a fumble and injuring the third-year quarterback. This led to Tagovailoa taking over in overtime and serving up Hamilton’s game-ending pick. DT Nnamdi Madubuike: Madubuike looks more and more like his old self with every week that passes. He was effective on Sunday as a pass rusher with three pressures and against the run with two stops, according to PFF. Madubuike, Hendrickson, and Green should form a formidable trio of pass rushers once all three are on the field together again. K Tyler Loop: Loop was perfect against the Falcons, converting all three field goals including two from 51 yards. Loop kept the Ravens in the game until the offense was finally able to reach the end zone in the third quarter. Loop has now missed just two kicks through five weeks, with one being blocked. Losers: TE Mark Andrews: It’s never fun to point out the negatives during such a feel-good win, but if there was one glaring problem in this game, it was Andrews. The veteran tight end dropped a touchdown on the opening drive of the game and followed that up with a fumble on the next drive that Atlanta recovered and took the other way for a score to go up 7-3. Andrews later failed to secure the catch on a two-point attempt, leaving Baltimore down 17-15 in the third quarter. Andrews then let another pass hit the ground on third down while the Ravens trailed 20-15 with just over six minutes remaining in regulation, forcing a punt to give the Falcons the chance to put the game away. Andrews ended up making several catches on the last two drives of the game to finish with 28 yards, but his blunders were a primary reason that the Ravens were scrambling in the second half. Third-down defense : The Ravens have struggled to get off the field on third down all season, and that was once again a major issue on Sunday, allowing nine conversions on 17 third downs. London in particular gave Baltimore’s defense issues on third down and long. The inability to make third-down stops sullied what was otherwise a strong defensive outing by the Ravens.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 5: Huntley steps up in spot-start at quarterback
summary: Offense Tyler Huntley played all 76 offensive snaps at quarterback in-place of Lamar Jackson. In the backfield behind him, Derrick Henry’s 42 snaps edged out Justice Hill (35 snaps). Henry was given 24 rushing attempts and Hill had six touches for a season-high 78 scrimmage yards. Hill played a lot late in the game as […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 11: Starting quarterback Tyler Huntley (5) of the Baltimore Ravens with a big smile after winning the Sunday evening NFL game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Baltimore Ravens on October 11, 2026 at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Offense QB: Tyler Huntley 76 RB: Derrick Henry 42, Justice Hill 35 WR: Zay Flowers 62, Rashod Bateman 61, Devontez Walker 45, Chris Moore 7 TE: Mark Andrews 55, Matthew Hibner 30, Josh Cuevas 19, Nick Vannett 19 OL: Emery Jones Jr. 76, John Simpson 76, Ronnie Stanley 76, Roger Rosengarten 74, Carson Vinson 6, Chuma Edoga 1 Tyler Huntley played all 76 offensive snaps at quarterback in-place of Lamar Jackson. In the backfield behind him, Derrick Henry’s 42 snaps edged out Justice Hill (35 snaps). Henry was given 24 rushing attempts and Hill had six touches for a season-high 78 scrimmage yards. Hill played a lot late in the game as the Ravens were in hurry-up offense mode. Every Ravens’ starting offensive lineman nearly went the distance. Roger Rosengarten left the game for two plays after suffering a knee injury early in the game but fortunately returned quickly afterwards. Carson Vinson played two snaps at right tackle in relief of Rosengarten and four snaps as an additional blocker. Chuma Edoga was also used as an extra lineman on one play. Emery Jones Jr. played all 76 snaps in his first career start at right guard. Zay Flowers, who was questionable to play with a foot injury, took 62 offensive snaps with a team-high eight catches. Rashod Bateman nearly matched him with 61 snaps, leading the team in receiving yards (62). It was the biggest snap share of the season for Devontez Walker as the No. 3 wideout (45 snaps). He caught the late touchdown pass in the fourth quarter that resulted in a tied game after a successful two-point conversion. At tight end, Mark Andrews easily led the group with 55 snaps. Andrews caught four passes for 28 yards but had several notable miscues (dropped balls, fumble). Matthew Hibner exited the game early with a hand injury but returned in the second half to finish with 30 snaps. Josh Cuevas had a season-high 26 receiving yards in his 19 snaps. Nick Vannett played his first action of the year and took 19 snaps as well with Durham Smythe now out. Defense DL: Nnamdi Madubuike 53, Travis Jones 38, Calais Campbell 32, Broderick Washington Jr. 15, John Jenkins 10 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 48, Mike Green 37, Zion Young 26, Ethan Burke 17 ILB: Roquan Smith 64, Trenton Simpson 36, Teddye Buchanan 19 CB: Nate Wiggins 64, Marlon Humphrey 64, Chandler Rivers 19, Chidobe Awuzie 2 S: Malaki Starks 62, Kyle Hamilton 60, Jaylinn Hawkins 38 For the third straight game, Nnamdi Madubuike led the defensive line group in snaps played (53). Travis Jones exited the game late after getting shaken up and finished with 38 snaps. On the edge, Tavius Robinson (48 snaps) and Mike Green (367 snaps) led the way with Trey Hendrickson sidelined again. Ethan Burke received a good amount of playing time again as well as the fourth edge rusher. Teddye Buchanan saw his snap count increase slightly for a third consecutive game at linebacker since returning from injury. Buchanan is cleary still playing third banana behind Roquan Smith (64 snaps) and Trenton Simpson (36 snaps), though. Simpson stuffed the sheet again with a tackle for loss, sack and quarterback hit along with seven total tackles. Cornerbacks Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey, who was questionable to play with a calf injury, did not leave the field (64 snaps each). There was a big drop-off to the next corner, Chandler Rivers, whose playing time took a dip from the last few games. Rivers played 19 snaps and veteran Chidobe Awuzie was only on the field for two defensive plays. Kyle Hamilton exited the game briefly with an injury but returned after four plays, in time to make the game-winning interception in overtime. Malaki Starks played all but two snaps on defense (62) and had a team-high 10 tackles with two tackles for loss. Notably, No. 3 safety Jaylinn Hawkins’ snap share took a decrease, as he played just 38 snaps.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 5: Clutch performances lead to comeback road win
summary: The Baltimore Ravens earned a comeback win on the road in Week 5, defeating the Atlanta Falcons by a touchdown difference (30-23). The Ravens used a game-tying touchdown drive to force overtime and then took the lead with another score, erasing a prior eight-point deficit to come from behind. Here are report card grades for […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against the Atlanta Falcons in overtime of a game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens earned a comeback win on the road in Week 5, defeating the Atlanta Falcons by a touchdown difference (30-23). The Ravens used a game-tying touchdown drive to force overtime and then took the lead with another score, erasing a prior eight-point deficit to come from behind. Here are report card grades for each position group from the exhilarating victory. Quarterback: B+ Tyler Huntley came alive late and delivered a clutch final two drives for the Ravens. Over the final game-tying drive of the fourth quarter and overtime touchdown drive, Huntley completed 12-of-12 passes with multiple timely first-down throws. He capped both drives off with a touchdown via a back-shoulder throw and tough quarterback sneak. Huntley’s performance up to that point was not necessarily spectacular, but the way he came through when needed most. In relief of Lamar Jackson, the backup finished the game with a line of 24-of-32 completed passes for 201 yards and two touchdowns, along with 20 rushing yards and another rushing score. Most importantly, Huntley avoided committing any turnovers. Running Back: A- The Ravens ran for over 200 yards and averaged an efficient 5.9 yards per carry, led by Derrick Henry and Justice Hill. Henry was limited to a longest run of only 11 yards on the night but grinded out 102 yards in total and ran hard in the fourth quarter and overtime. He also an impressive 18-yard receiving score after a catch-and-run screen reception. Justice Hill exploded for 73 rushing yards on just four carries, ripping off a huge 47-yard run where he was lined up in the fullback spot. Wide Receiver: B + The Ravens’ downfield passing attack was limited for most of the game, but their wide receivers made big plays in the fourth quarter and overtime. Huntley connected with Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman and Devontez Walker for timely receptions that moved the chains. Walker reeled in the game-tying touchdown on a back-shoulder catch in the end zone. Flowers finished with a team-high eight catches and 66 scrimmage yards while Bateman had five catches for 62 receiving yards. The starting wide receiver duo combined for eight receptions over the final two drives of the game. Tight End: D+ It was a forgettable performance for Mark Andrews, who had a few costly miscues. He dropped a wide-open pass at the goal line in the first quarter, then fumbled on the second drive of the game and it was returned by the Falcons for a touchdown. Andrews was unable to reel in a two-point conversion catch in the third quarter that would have tied the game. He did catch a couple first down grabs late in the game to help move the chains. Josh Cuevas had a season-high two catches for 26 yards and Matthew Hibner was not targeted after exiting with a hand injury early in the contest – although he did return later in the second half. Offensive Line: B- The Ravens surrendered four sacks and eight quarterback hits on the night. Huntley was not able to get comfortable in the pocket in the first half and was flushed out into a scramble drill on several occasions. However, the Ravens’ offensive line settled down in pass protection more as the game went along. They also did a good job getting push in the run game, springing Hill free for long breakaway run and Henry for multiple positive-yardage gains. Vega Ioane struggled with some low snaps but was strong as a blocker at center again. As a unit, the offensive line did a much better job with penalties as well. Defensive Line: B Bijan Robinson finished the game with 86 rushing yards on 17 carries (5.1 yards per carry), but the Ravens were able to control him at the line of scrimmage for most the night. A good chunk of Robinson’s damage came on two long runs. Calais Campbell, Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones all made plays up front. Madubuike and Jones each had a quarterback hit on Michael Penix, while Campbell recorded a tackle for loss. Edge Rusher: A- Mike Green’s strong run of play continued in Atlanta with another impactful showing. Green had a sack, quarterback hit and two tackles for loss. He set the edge well and made strong stops against the run. Tavius Robinson similarly had a high-level performance. Robinson stuffed the stat sheet, recording six tackles along with a sack, quarterback hit, pass defense and tackle for loss. The Ravens were disciplined on the edge for most of the game against the Falcons’ rushing attack and crashed inside well to close gaps. Ethan Burke played a good amount of snaps again with Hendrickson sidelined and had three tackles. Linebacker: B + Trenton Simpson’s career-best campaign marched along on Sunday night as he posted seven tackles with a sack, tackle for loss and quarterback hit. Simpson was party to a couple passes allowed in zone coverage but otherwise had another impactful all-around game. Roquan Smith had eight tackles, which ranked second among all Baltimore defenders. Smith and Simpson are pairing well together as a tandem. Teddye Buchanan added two tackles of his own as the third banana of the group. Cornerback: B- The Ravens had some difficulties covering star wide receiver Drake London, who racked up 118 yards on seven catches. He did most of his damage against zone coverage, though, but did get behind Nate Wiggins for a long reception. Jahan Dotson also beat the Ravens’ deep for a 36-yard catch. Wiggins had a tackle for loss and Marlon Humphrey recorded a clutch quarterback hit, pressuring Penix on a play action pass to force an incompletion. Chandler Rivers had a costly missed tackle on a short third-down throw in the flat. Safety: A- Malaki Starks had a strong performance against the Falcons, racking up a team-high 10 tackles with two tackles for loss. Starks had some timely wrap-ups in the open field and was very impactful versus the run, providing a lurking presence against Robinson. Kyle Hamilton’s game-sealing interception in overtime was textbook deception and high IQ, as he read the eyes of the quarterback perfectly. Hamilton had six tackles with a pass defense and missed a few plays after suffering an injury before returning. He remains the most indispensable player on the Ravens’ defense. Special Teams: B+ Tyler Loop was a big factor in the Ravens’ win, as he accounted for all of the team’s points in the first half. Loop made two 51-yard field goals and another chip shot from 21 yards out. LaJohntay Wester’s lone punt return opportunity turned into a nice 11-yard gain. Rasheen Ali had a big tackle in the return game.
author: Frank Platko

title: Top takeaways from the Ravens’ overtime win over the Falcons
summary: The Baltimore Ravens stole a 30-23 overtime win from the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday night. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s top takeaways from the thrilling victory: Jesse Minter and his staff deserve credit for confident finish Jesse Minter landed on a favorite mantra shortly after arriving in Baltimore: “Be at your best when the best is […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 11: Head coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens reacts with Tyler Huntley #5 following the 30-23 victory in overtime against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens stole a 30-23 overtime win from the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday night. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s top takeaways from the thrilling victory: Jesse Minter and his staff deserve credit for confident finish Jesse Minter landed on a favorite mantra shortly after arriving in Baltimore: “Be at your best when the best is needed.” His team heeded his words on Sunday night, overcoming self-inflicted errors throughout the first three quarters for a masterful fourth-quarter comeback and overtime win. There were big moments when the Ravens fell short, but in the biggest ones, calm coaching and smooth execution prevailed. Minter and his staff were prepared for seemingly every scenario. Case in point: asking Tyler Huntley to drive 70-plus yards down the field for a game-tying touchdown was probably not on Baltimore’s pre-game wish list. But Declan Doyle pulled all the right levers, including targeting Falcons depth cornerback Mike Ford as soon as he entered the game for a touchdown. Doyle followed that up with a brilliant two-point conversion call, using Zay Flowers as eye candy to break Derrick Henry into open space out on a wildcat sweep. Opting to take the ball in overtime to keep a gassed Falcons defense on the field for a long, punishing drive was another smart decision that paid off with a Huntley touchdown seven minutes and 14 plays later. – Nikhil Mehta It’s time for a changing of the guard at tight end After looking fairly good through the first four weeks of the season, Mark Andrews’ performance in Week 5 was a reminder of his limitations at this stage of his career. While he did have a couple of timely first-down catches in the fourth quarter and overtime, it was a disaster class showing from Andrews up to that point. The veteran dropped a would-be touchdown on the opening drive of the game, failed to reel in a two-point conversion catch that would have tied the score, and lost a fumble that was then returned for a touchdown. He also failed to reel in a couple other passes that were knocked out of his hands by a defender. Andrews can still have value to the offense, but the Ravens need to begin featuring their rookie tight ends more and lessen his role. Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas have both shown some pass-catching juice in their limited opportunities thus far. They both bring more to the table athletically than Andrews does right now, and Andrews’ hands unfortunately continue to prove themselves as unreliable in big spots. – Frank Pla tko The Ravens badly needed a real center First-round rookie Vega Ioane deserves praise for stepping in as the Ravens’ emergency center over the past few weeks, but his inconsistent snapping would have cost the team eventually. Huntley did an excellent job of handling Ioane’s snaps on Sunday night, but last week’s acquisition of Cam Jurgens will hopefully bring some stability via a true center. Ioane will also be able to move back to his natural position, where he can continue a strong start to his NFL career without the burden of running the operation at the line of scrimmage. – Nikhil Mehta Baltimore is turning over a new leaf in close games After the win, Kyle Hamilton and Zay Flowers both acknowledged that the Ravens have a history of losing these tight matchups. But Jesse Minter’s “be at your best when the best is needed mantra” may have taken root in the locker room. His team did not play their best football for the first three quarters, but the defense kept them in the game and the offense mounted two impressive scoring drives to close it out. That would have been impressive with Lamar Jackson and Trey Hendrickson on the field; without them, it’s a tremendous accomplishment. – Nikhil Mehta
author: Frank Platko

title: Josh Allen, Buffalo Bills win OT ‘MNF’ thriller against Los Angeles Rams
summary: Halfway through Monday Night Football, it appeared as though the primetime audience got a bit of a dud in Week 5. The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams were too in their heads, trying to play a game of keep-away due to MVP quarterbacks Josh Allen and Matthew Stafford. After Ray Davis’ opening kick return […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 12: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball against the Los Angeles Rams during the fourth quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Halfway through Monday Night Football, it appeared as though the primetime audience got a bit of a dud in Week 5. The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams were too in their heads, trying to play a game of keep-away due to MVP quarterbacks Josh Allen and Matthew Stafford. After Ray Davis’ opening kick return of 70 yards, what unfolded early was downright ugly football. That’s quite a feat given how little time Buffalo’s offense had the ball. Right down to the arm punt to end the first half, things felt eerily similar to last Sunday. It seemed at that moment as though Josh Allen was broken. Most people knew that if Buffalo was to win in Los Angeles, they’d have to put their spikes in and sprint to the finish on offense. Yet, at halftime it looked like the Bills were still in the sort of funk that allowed them to throw away a game to the New England Patriots in Week 4. To be fair, Allen lacks the sort of riches Stafford has catching passes on a routine basis. That doesn’t excuse the arm punts, which have officially re-entered “trend” territory. But just as was true of two fumbles by running back James Cook III, Allen’s interception didn’t cost the Bills a win. That’s a trend Bills Mafia can rally around, if necessary. There is much work to be done, however. That’s true of the entire roster. In that moment, Allen should have run for yards, or checked the ball down, or even out of bounds — anything other than heaving it into traffic. Live another down, run more clock, and make it that much harder on Stafford and company looking for quick points. Though, again, it ultimately didn’t do the team harm. At the half, it was a bit stunning to see the Bills were ahead. How many people do you think went to bed? They’re in for quite a surprise when they wake up with the sun. But who could blame a person? Everything just felt off, yet familiar to what plagued them in last week’s loss. Then something clicked at halftime. Both teams came out firing, perhaps throwing a bit too much caution to the wind in key moments. Yet as I’ve already stated: No turnover decided the game. Instead, we can look back at a pair of bold points I made pre-game . The Bills would probably need to convert a two-point conversion (and against a team near-equally woeful converting them), and they had to capitalize on special teams mistakes against a woeful Rams unit. That first point proved a challenge once again, as Brady and the offense played it cute with so much goofy pre-snap motion that it led to a false start. There’s too much thinking outside the box with their two-point offense. With Allen, the move should always be to run the ball or get him on the move and looking for Kincaid. Well, they missed the first try, then made up for it later with a still-glitchy but successful try with a pass from Allen to Kincaid. More of that, with less glitch is a good idea. Brady’s reaction was all you needed to see in understanding how big a moment it was to convert that two-point try. As to the special teams point, it’s a full course meal. Ray Davis was shot out of a cannon early as a kick returner. Had he not been caught from behind by a defensive lineman playing kicker, Davis was scoring on the first play. It wasn’t ideal settling for a field goal after that return, but they proved to be important points. Special teams would once again play a huge role late in overtime following Cook’s second fumble. Rousseau once again coming up huge in the crunch, leaping to deflect the Rams’ game-winning field goal attempt. Out of nowhere, the Bills had new life and no one was more relieved than Cook. (The Bills are 2-0 this season when Cook fumbles twice in a game.) The football world knows what happens when you keep giving Josh Allen chances. If you were to try defending the idea of QB wins as a stat, all you’d need do now is play the tape of the Bills’ final drive in overtime. Allen took complete control of the game, running through, around, and over any defender in his way. One man (and, yes, an offensive line) against 11 defenders. Understanding the moment, once Allen got into Bass’ comfortable field goal range, head coach Joe Brady wasn’t leaving anything to foolish chance in order to create a more ideal scenario. Brady’s hunch proved correct, and Bass walked off a hero who’d been given the keys to trust. This is the type of win that could properly fuel the team. There’s a lot of season left and they’re certain to face similar or worse adversity. They played a heck of a game of chess against a Super Bowl favorite. Now the Bills need to get things figured out on defense, while continuing to capitalize on every bit of good luck that comes their way. It’s unfamiliar territory, to be sure, but winning in overtime looks great on Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills.
author: Matt Byham

title: Bills at Rams Week 5 game analysis: Josh Allen dominates for first OT win
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Rams 37-34 in overtime on Monday Night Football to improve to 4-1, and Josh Allen got his first career overtime win. It’s a signature win that could pay dividends for the team down the stretch. Here are my notes by half, overtime, and final thoughts. 1st Half 2nd […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 12: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates a touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the fourth quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Rams 37-34 in overtime on Monday Night Football to improve to 4-1, and Josh Allen got his first career overtime win. It’s a signature win that could pay dividends for the team down the stretch. Here are my notes by half, overtime, and final thoughts. 1st Half Ray Davis, All-Pro kickoff returner. Awesome start. Scoring a TD on the 1st drive would be huge in this game. Josh Allen keeps refusing to take those short routes. Eats a sack after refusing to throw to the open receiver on the flat. Drive stalls, FG, 3-0 Bills. Despite what Joe Brady said, Noah Igbinosun is out there opposite Christian Benford, not Maxwell Hairston. He’s deserved the nod, but it’s not nice to see a 1st-round pick benched after one poor game. The Rams simply have too much talent for the Bills’ secondary to deal with. The quick game is easy for Matthew Stafford and his receivers right now. (383 passing yards, 3 TDs) Kyren Williams and their run game isn’t an easy task as well, especially with how scared they are about their WRs. Bills’ defense keeps failing to get out of the field on 4th downs. It wasn’t an easy one, but still. Getting stops there could be huge for them. A lot of space for Puka Nacua behind the Bills’ LBs in the cover 3 defense. Thankfully Stafford misses the throw. We’ll need those. (17 receptions, 138 yards, 1 TD) Oh, missed FGs are also welcome. Still 3-0 Bills. Good next drive. Josh looks healthy , moving well, even running defenders over. Great. James Cook’s also looking good. Fast and physical. (23 carries, 108 yards, 2 TDs) Aaron Donald schools O’Cyrus Torrence and sacks Josh. Gotta protect the franchise better. He has taken way too many hits recently. Josh misses Dawson Knox high in the back of the endzone. Eli Manning points out he looked scared of the DB there, and if you’re gonna miss those kinds of throws, you miss them high to avoid INTs. Another missed opportunity after a very good drive, another FG. 6-0 Bills. Too much Knox and too little Dalton Kincaid in the passing game so far. Bills’ D continues to play too many soft zones . Stafford, Puka, and Davante Adams are killing them. Also, bad tackling after the catch is costing stops. Rams at the goal line, as soon as Stafford sees Adams 1-on-1 with CJ Gardner-Johnson, it’s a wrap. TD Rams, and Adams has some words for CJGJ, who was loud on a previous play where Adams couldn’t score on IGB. Damar Hamlin is the option to replace Dee Alford again today, but he’s not lining up as the nickel CB. Cole Bishop is playing there in the nickel package. Still not ideal, mainly on passing downs. I’d like to see Benford there a bit. Two consecutive successful screen plays in a row, to set up a James Cook TD run. First a WR screen to Khalil Shakir, on what looked like an RPO play. Then a nice RB screen to Ty Johnson, with that orbit pre-snap motion with Shakir going the other way. Creative ways to move the chains in a game our WRs haven’t been able to beat their matchups so far. 13-7 Bills. Hairston’s getting snaps outside now. Allowed a 1st-down completion. DeWayne Carter with the sack. Great to see the big guy making plays. Oh, unfortunate penalty on CJGJ here. Literally separated the TE from the ball. I believe the hit was perfectly timed, just unfortunate there was a bit of helmet-to-helmet. This defense needs those big plays so bad, so far Jim Leonhard’s unit is clearly a bend but don’t break type, allowing a lot of yardage. Kaleb Elarms-Orr almost with the pick. Terrel Bernard with the pressure on Stafford on a delayed blitz, giving the rookie an opportunity. Gotta make those plays. Bills get the ball back for a 2 min drive but run out the clock on the first two downs, then burn a timeout on 3rd and 1 with 37 seconds left. Brady is totally going the Sean McDermott way today. Long drives on both sides, fewer possessions overall. After a penalty making it 3rd and 6, Josh arm punts. I’m fine with those, and I’ll tell you one thing: it pisses me off the way WRs allow those to happen. Fight for the ball, justify the QB’s trust in those kinds of situations. Josh’s pass also could’ve been better, but there was time for Keon Coleman to go for it. Stafford almost pulls out a miracle pass to close the half. Inches away from a big-time TD. How can the Bills’ coverage allow that there? IGB got lucky. Despite looking really ugly, conceding just seven points to this Rams offense in the 1st half is definitely mission accomplished by this defense. Probably more lucky than competent, but still. 2nd Half Another forced 4th down. A penalty makes it 4th and 6, and they still can’t get out of the field, my goodness. Bishop’s being exploited in coverage as the nickel. 4th-and-6 conversion and PI in the endzone on him. TD Blake Corum. 14-13 Rams after the extra point. Weak penalties are killing the Bills’ O right now. Josh’s in bad situations, forcing passes as nobody’s getting open. Looks like last season’s passing offense. They need healthy DJ Moore badly. (7 completions through three quarters) Good defensive drive. Desperately needed. My gosh, James Cook. Another fumble. Luckily Knox recovered it. Josh’s making things happen on the move but questionable penalties again. PI on Keon, Bills inside the 10. 2nd week in a row Josh is struggling to find open receivers on his rollouts to the right. Defenses figured those plays out, it’s time for Brady to design some different routes there. Skyler Bell with an opportunity to make a play for Josh there, drops it in the endzone. Pass a little behind, not the easiest catch. After a false start and then a defensive holding, Cook loses yards, but Josh finds Keon on a nice route combo that freed him in the endzone. Well-designed play. Can’t say the same about the 2-point try. What are they doing there? False start and missed kick after it. Bills lead 19-14, but 2-point conversions continue to be an issue. Corum breaking tackles for a big gain after the catch, CJGJ seems hurt. Goal-line fade to Puka, over IGB, TD Rams. 2-point conversion not good! TJ Sanders flashes here. 20-19 Rams. Run game is looking good early in the 4th again. Cook with 2 runs, and then 2 play-action plays. Josh scrambles for a big play, followed by a great screen to Ray Davis, who again takes advantage of his opportunity. Bills at the goal line. Tush push stopped from the 3-yard line, with a defensive penalty. Next play, TD Josh Allen, another tush push. 2-point conversion is good! It looked bad at first, but Josh extends it a bit and Kincaid gets open. 27-20 Bills. We need one more stop here by the D, and the offense must close this one. Bernard and Benford are shaken up on this drive. The LB is quickly back. Rams keep moving the ball easily downfield. People are holding Deone Walker and it doesn’t matter, he still makes the play vs. the run. TD Rams on 3rd down. Middle-of-the-field route behind the Bills LBs, and the safety is nowhere to be found in the deep middle zone. Way too easy for Stafford. Josh’s looking like Josh. Makes defender miss for a 1st down. Great catch by Shakir on a deep in route. Had to survive the hit in the middle of the field to guarantee the 1st down. We need more of this from him. Silly fouls smh. 2nd and 16 becomes a 1st and goal. That’s Josh, you really think he looked healthy last week? Awesome scramble, not afraid of contact. Bills in command of this game. (10 carries, 121 yards, 1 TD) Superman is back. Nate Landman with another stop, tackling Cook. We don’t have anything like that at LB. TD Bills, James Cook. He broke some tackles to get into the endzone. Rams still have 1 timeout left, and 1:39 is more than enough for them to score against our defense. Can this D close this…

title: Joe Brady’s overtime field goal decision was a mistake even if it worked
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Rams on an overtime field goal from Tyler Bass. That’s great. But the decision to take the kick with two minutes left was a mistake, and head coach Joe Brady needs to know that. There are two big reasons it was a mistake, so let’s get cracking. Two […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 12: Head coach Joe Brady of the Buffalo Bills looks on against the Los Angeles Rams during the second quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills beat the Los Angeles Rams on an overtime field goal from Tyler Bass. That’s great. But the decision to take the kick with two minutes left was a mistake, and head coach Joe Brady needs to know that. There are two big reasons it was a mistake, so let’s get cracking. Two minutes was enough time for the Rams to score after a miss It all boils down to this; you add another negative possibility by kicking it with two minutes left. The Bills could have run it down to 30 seconds and kicked the same field goal attempt. In that case, you either win or tie and a loss isn’t on the table without a field goal block return (which could happen at the 2-minute mark, too). A couple of tush pushes and you run out the clock and don’t really have a ton of fumble concern. You don’t even need to hand it off. A miss with two minutes and you know the Rams can drive it and score and you lose. They did it at the end of regulation. Do you open yourself to another fumble? Sure. A false start could add five yards. But it mitigates the chance of a loss. And a tie is much better than a loss. Tyler Bass already missed from closer in the game Bass missed an extra point from 38 yards in the third quarter, but now we are trusting him to make a 44-yard field goal AND if he misses, the Rams have a chance to drive and score and win the game. This was no gimme. This is why running down the clock was the right call. Some more notes on the game management The Bills still employ a game management specialist. Marc Lubick has been in that role for three seasons. The Rams absolutely bombed their game management. They probably should have gone for two at the end of regulation. The Bills had only stopped them on one play all game, it felt like. The Rams should not have settled for the long field goal in overtime for the same reason. Second and 10 at the Bills 35, they hit Puka Nacua for 5 yards. A weak run to the right gains nothing to set up a 47-yard field goal. Again, not a solid special teams year and he’s missed kicks that long already in the game. I have criticized a Bills head coach for an overtime decision before. In 2017, Sean McDermott punted in overtime when the Bills needed a win to keep their playoff hopes alive. With a third-string QB slinging it in a blizzard. The Bills ended up getting a stop and driving the length of the field for a win, but it was the wrong decision. And we were critical of McDermott’s game management for most of his career AND if bit them in the butt in 13 seconds and other moments later. That’s why we bring it up even when they win. I am glad it went in. I am glad they won. Let’s do better next time.

title: Horns up, horns down for Buffalo Bills vs. Los Angeles Rams
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams played a tough, back-and-forth game this evening, and ultimately, it was the Bills who prevailed, winning 37-34 in an instant-classic overtime battle. Before the season began, there were plenty of folks who had this one circled as a potential preview for Super Bowl LXI. Well, if this were […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 12: James Cook III #4 of the Buffalo Bills scores a 17 yard touchdown against Kamren Kinchens #5 of the Los Angeles Rams during the second quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams played a tough, back-and-forth game this evening, and ultimately, it was the Bills who prevailed, winning 37-34 in an instant-classic overtime battle. Before the season began, there were plenty of folks who had this one circled as a potential preview for Super Bowl LXI. Well, if this were a Super Bowl preview, then at least we can assume that we’ll have an entertaining game come February. Hopefully, though, if there is a rematch between these clubs, the game doesn’t do this much to my heart rate. After Buffalo led 13-7 at the half, the teams traded the lead multiple times throughout the night. There were seven lead changes in regulation alone to go with two ties. Buffalo took a 34-27 lead with 99 seconds to go, and that proved to be too much time for their defense to stop the Rams’ offense, who needed just 94 of those seconds to march down the field to tie the game. In overtime, there were more twists and turns, but in the end, it’s the Bills winning an overtime game for the first time in Josh Allen’s career, ending one of the weirder statistics to follow Buffalo’s QB1 throughout his career. There are plenty of accolades—and plenty of jeers—to go around tonight, and sometimes, those belong to the same person. Here are our horns up and horns down from tonight’s wild Buffalo win. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Up: James Cook III Cook came out on fire, and while Buffalo’s passing game didn’t do much in the first half, the running game carried the load for the offense. Cook, in particular, was excellent in the early going. He carried nine times for 55 yards and a score in the first half, adding one catch for seven yards receiving, as well. He picked up tough yards between the tackles and was able to shake some defenders on the edges, running hard throughout the game. On a night where quarterback Josh Allen and the passing game weren’t effective or efficient, Cook was a welcome boon to the offense. He’s an elite-level talent, but I will add one caveat: He needs to protect the football. Despite his big runs, I find myself holding my breath with each Cook carry, and he fumbled again tonight in the third quarter. The recovery was initially given to the Rams, but eventually overturned to a Buffalo recovery. Cook is too good a player for us to need to worry about ball security, but he continues to put the ball on the turf. The reason Buffalo needs to keep feeding him the ball, though, is just how dynamic he is. Cook’s second touchdown of the night gave the Bills a 34-27 lead with just 99 seconds left in the game. Cook totaled 111 yards and two touchdowns on 25 carries. He caught just that one pass for seven yards. Horns Down: James Cook III Just an absolute killer fumble in overtime to bring what most likely would have been a scoring drive to an end. After a long gain from Khalil Shakir, who narrowly missed scoring a touchdown and was just tripped up by a shoelace on the play prior, Cook just needed to gain some yardage and set up second down. Instead, he fumbled for the second time, Aaron Donald recovered, and the Rams were in business. All’s well that ends well, perhaps, but Cook needs to work on ball security, and that’s an understatement. Horns Up: Tyler Bass Once again, Buffalo’s kicker was effective. He nailed both first-half field goals, hitting from 49 yards on Buffalo’s first drive and from 23 yards on the Bills’ second possession. He also hit an extra point following James Cook’s 17-yard touchdown run in the second quarter. Bass also was effective on kickoffs, hitting each one high and deep within the landing zone, which allowed for Buffalo’s top-notch coverage unit to do what it does. Of course, after initially writing about how well Bass performed in the first half, his first PAT in the second half was wide right after a false start penalty knocked him back five yards. Bass continues to be excellent on field goals and iffy on extra-points, but he did drill an extra point after Cook’s touchdown to give the Bills a seven-point lead in the fourth quarter. Then, at the two-minute warning in overtime, Bass delivered a victory for the Bills with a 45-yard field goal to win it. Horns Up: Greg Rousseau Groot made the play of the game for the Bills, and it wasn’t on defense. Faced with a game-winning field goal attempt in overtime, Harrison Mevis lined up for a makeable 47-yard try. Rousseau knifed through the left side of the line, put those big limbs up, and blocked the kick. It was the second miss for the Thicker Kicker, and it gave Buffalo life. Rousseau had just one tackle and one QB hit on the night, but his big blocked kick was the play of the game. Horns Up: DeWayne Carter The third-year player notched his first career sack in the first half, continuing a strong streak of play this season. Carter isn’t the only defensive lineman to take a step forward under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, but he might be the one who has taken the most surprising leap. In the first half, Carter had two tackles and the aforementioned sack. He added one more tackle in the second half, but he was disruptive in the backfield, knifing his way past blockers and eating space at the point of attack. He’s been a welcome addition to the front-seven rotation after missing last season with an Achilles tear. Horns Down: Cole Bishop The third-year safety was a step slow too often today, as he just found himself close to making plays, but not close enough to actually make the plays. On the Rams’ first drive of the second half, for example, he was a step slow coming out of his break to take away tight end Tyler Higbee on a fourth down, allowing the big tight end enough space to make a catch to extend the drive. Later in that same drive, Bishop was in man coverage against Higbee, and he was burned so badly that he essentially tackled Higbee while the ball was in flight to avoid giving up a touchdown. That pass interference penalty only delayed the inevitable, as Blake Corum plunged forward for a one-yard score and a 14-13 Rams lead. Bishop is a tremendous athlete, but he struggled to pick up the nuances of former head coach Sean McDermott’s defense as a rookie, and after settling in and looking very good last season, we’ve seen some of those hesitant, rookie-year moments this season as he learns a new scheme with Jim Leonhard. Horns Down: First-Half Josh Allen Antsy in the pocket. Not accurate on throws that went beyond the line of scrimmage. Holding the ball, patting it, and staring down receivers. It was an ugly half overall for QB1, whose first-half numbers were buoyed by a 40-yard gain on a screen pass to running back Ty Johnson. Otherwise, Allen threw a bad interception on what was essentially an arm punt (Johnson was open early in the route, but Allen didn’t see him as he was evading pressure), and he nearly threw another interception on a third-and-21 when he started down Skyler Bell before forcing it to the rookie in double-coverage. Allen was able to make some gains with his legs, where he rushed three times for 21 yards. He completed just 4-of-7 passes for 60 yards and the aforementioned interception. Overall, though, it was an ugly first-half performance. Horns Up: Second-Half Josh Allen Well, good thing for the Bills (and my fantasy team) that the first-half wasn’t the whole game. Allen looked much better in the second half, hitting Keon Coleman on a seven-yard touchdown in the third quarter before plunging ahead for a one-yard rushing touchdown in the fourth quarter. Allen even completed a pass on the two-point try, hitting tight end Dalton Kincaid in a jump-ball…

title: Buffalo Bills at Los Angeles Rams, Week 5 ‘MNF’ fan discussion
summary: The Buffalo Bills are in Inglewood, CA this evening to take on the Los Angeles Rams while closing out the action in Week 5 with Monday Night Football. In what felt like a game that would never arrive, it’s finally time, Rumblers. Quarterback Josh Allen and the Bills must have put their Week 4 dud […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 08: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills watches his throw in the third quarter of a game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on December 08, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are in Inglewood, CA this evening to take on the Los Angeles Rams while closing out the action in Week 5 with Monday Night Football. In what felt like a game that would never arrive, it’s finally time, Rumblers. Quarterback Josh Allen and the Bills must have put their Week 4 dud in the past if they hope to win what could become another shootout with the Rams at SoFi Stadium. Those that claim things state that SoFi is “Rams House,” but that shouldn’t cause head coach Joe Brady and company to shudder. Buffalo has a similar base of firepower to play match-set-point with Los Angeles this evening, and you can bet the last two NFL MVPs in Allen and Matthew Stafford will have their say about what’s in store for the evening’s winner and loser. Each team brings a defense to the field that might best be termed an “incomplete” after the first month. They both give up yards and points. Buffalo will have to adjust plans if the injury bug continues to plague its defensive backfield. That could mean significant starting snaps at nickel cornerback for safety Damar Hamlin or someone else — perhaps newly called-up cornerback Anthony Kendall. Despite the challenges that await the Bills this evening, there aren’t many other teams as well-poised to take down the mighty Rams en route to their dream matchup as a true home team in Super Bowl LXI. Tonight serves as a litmus test, Bills Mafia. A loss doesn’t doom either team’s season, but could become a key point of reference during playoff season. Will Buffalo improve to 4-1 and maintain its lead in the AFC East, or will Los Angeles hand them another crushing early season blow in their playoff bid? We’ll find out in due time. With that, here’s your open thread for all of tonight’s action during Bills at Rams for Monday Night Football . As always, be kind to one another — and in all things… Go Bills!

full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Anthony Kendall #30 of the Buffalo Bills breaks up a pass during a preseason game against the Carolina Panthers at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have signed cornerback Anthony Kendall to their 53-man active roster ahead of their clash with the Los Angeles Rams for Monday Night Football in Week 5. To make room for Kendall, Buffalo made a corresponding move to release veteran outside linebacker Mike Danna. Kendall was most recently a member of Buffalo’s practice squad after spending training camp with the team this past summer. Sean Murphy’s detailed scouting report in August laid out an unlikely path to Kendall seeing live snap in the regular season, or rostered with the team, if all things went as planned. Injuries to the Bills’ group have called to action a once-unlikely backup plan. Kendall entered the NFL with the Tennessee Titans back in the 2023 NFL Draft. The former Division III players is a 5’10”, 188-pound corner who hasn’t played in a regular-season game or otherwise since his rookie year, and even then most of his snaps came on special teams. Kendall isn’t an elite athlete, but he did clock a 4.53-second 40-yard dash, a 4.44-second 20-yard shuttle, and a 7.02-second three-cone drill. The numbers that stand out the most, however, were his 39.5” vertical, 10’9” broad jump, and 19 reps of 225 pounds on the bench press . Sean Murphy astutely pointed out Kendall’s Relative Athletic Score (RAS) of 8.31, stating that “he clearly has potential based on his athleticism alone.” What Kendall’s signing actually means for the cornerback depth chart remains to be seen later tonight, or if it’s a move to bolster needs on special teams. It’s important to note that the Bills did not place anyone on Injured Reserve, which is good news regarding long-term plans. Additionally, on Friday Buffalo only ruled out two starters, that being wide receiver Joshua Palmer and defensive tackle Ed Oliver. However, there are some unknowns in the defensive backfield. Starting nickel cornerback Dee Alford is listed as questionable for tonight, and top cornerback Christian Benford has been dealing with a toe injury that initially had him in a walking boot. Benford’s injury sidelined him in Week 4, but head coach Joe Brady informed the media that the team’s CB1 will play. We have made the following roster moves: – Signed CB Anthony Kendall from the practice squad – Released OLB Mike Danna pic.twitter.com/eYSk1aAKOE — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) October 12, 2026

Additionally, we have elevated DL Phidarian Mathis and WR Trent Sherfield Sr. from the practice squad. — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) October 12, 2026 Mathis, 28, re-signed with Buffalo in the offseason after joining the team partway through the 2025 season. Last year, he totaled 13 tackles in six games. The veteran appeared in all three of Buffalo’s preseason games this season, totaling five tackles and a sack. Thanks to an alcohol-related incident stemming from his time with the New York Jets last season, Mathis was hit with a three-game suspension to begin this season. After his suspension period ended, Mathis was released from Buffalo’s roster, but re-signed to the team’s practice squad almost immediately thereafter. He’ll be making his 2026 season debut tonight if he’s active. Sherfield Sr., 30, also spent the offseason with Buffalo in what is his second stint with the club. The veteran caught all seven of his targets during the preseason for 76 yards in three exhibition games. He has been with Buffalo’s practice squad since he was released at the end of the preseason. Ed Oliver and Joshua Palmer were ruled out on Friday, and with T.J. Sanders (knee/appendectomy) and DJ Moore (shoulder) also dealing with injuries, it makes sense to supplement those positional groups. With tonight’s game set to kick off at 8:15 p.m. EDT, each team’s inactive list will be official as of 6:45 p.m. EDT. The Bills also announced that they released veteran outside linebacker Mike Danna in order to make room for cornerback Anthony Kendall on the 53-man roster.

title: NFL predictions: 4 bold takes for Bills-Rams ‘MNF’ matchup in Week 5
summary: A wild slate of NFL action comes to an end this evening with the Buffalo Bills set to face the Los Angeles Rams in front of a national audience for Week 5 of Monday Night Football. Despite the 3-1 record, a lot of folks are down on the Bills at the moment, which also includes […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 08: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills rushes for a touchdown in the fourth quarter of a game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on December 08, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images A wild slate of NFL action comes to an end this evening with the Buffalo Bills set to face the Los Angeles Rams in front of a national audience for Week 5 of Monday Night Football . Despite the 3-1 record, a lot of folks are down on the Bills at the moment, which also includes a bit of concern about quarterback Josh Allen. Buffalo is a routine playoff contender and frequent Super Bowl favorite because of Josh Allen. Without him, the Bills resemble a lot of those teams from the drought era. It’s natural to show some concern, as much of it has to do with fans’ understanding about Allen’s importance to the team. Yes, it’s a team and there’s plenty of room for others to make their mark. What’s said above of Allen might well stick to running back James Cook III, for example. So perhaps Week 5 will serve as a get-right game for Buffalo, if you believe they need one. “Crazy talk,” you say? The Rams aren’t too dissimilar from the Bills as a team with plenty of firepower on offense led by an NFL MVP quarterback, but also a group that struggles to stop opponents on defense. They’re a .500 squad that’s lost to the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos, while defeating the New York Giants and Philadelphia Eagles. The Bills are marching into SoFi Stadium to take on a beatable team in Los Angeles that’s propped up by a lot of hype. There are a few things that need to happen if Buffalo’s going to exit Week 5 4-1, and for sure it has to look different than the game plan in Week 4. Below are what I believe are some (admittedly safer) bold takes to consider. What that means, in this case? We’re not going to stand by predicting a pick-six for Damar Hamlin, or that rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell will catch the game’s first touchdown pass, which will also be recorded as the first reception of his career. You also won’t find anything laying claim to a defensive stalemate between these teams. Instead, we’re rolling with bold but realistic takes that could be key toward getting the Bills a win and back near the head of the NFL class. Some bold takes call for a stiff drink, and Skarekrow has the perfect recipe if that’s your plan. But we like to think you’ll save the cocktail for the victory dance. Buffalo Bills convert a 2-point attempt It’s one of several pink elephants in the room, Buffalo’s continued struggle converting two-point tries. Ask anyone tuned in to the Bills and they’d say the preferred move is to always kick for one simply because the alternative leaves them chasing points. For whatever reason, Allen and the offense just don’t have the right chemistry while going for two in most situations. That’s interesting because Allen has been great, historically, in goal-to-go scenarios — which is exactly what he’s faced with during a two-point try. The go-to should first and foremost be Allen using his legs to get the points, but there’s a pair of pass catchers who make sense as the focal points in these situations. It’s all about height and hands, which is what the Bills have in tight end Dalton Kincaid and wide receiver Keon Coleman. Additionally, and this should happen elsewhere on the field, head coach Joe Brady would be wise to utilized both running backs Ty Johnson and Cook. Each of them are major threats as receivers, while both are severely under-utilized. Any defense will be stressed having to account for Coleman and Kincaid in the paint, while Cook and Johnson operate out in the flat near the goal line, and all before spying Allen as a rusher. It’s time to stop trying to get cute in unconventional situations. Use the guys who stand to help you the most. I have a sneaky feeling Buffalo will be forced into a two-point situation against the Rams, and they’re going to convert it. Bills capitalize off Rams’ ST woes The Rams field the worst-ranked special teams unit in the NFL. It’s a menagerie of awful, highlighted by a place kicker who struggles to convert points much beyond a distance of 40 yards. There’s truth to the idea that settling for field goals often leads to misery, but every point counts. As we discussed above, the Bills are almost always better off kicking for one instead of trying for two due mainly to their own deficiencies. Conversely, the Rams may be far better off going for the first down instead of a long field goal simply because the numbers don’t favor converting the kick. That could benefit Buffalo on Monday night, if they’re assignment sound and ready to tackle. That idea extends to the Bills’ coverage and return units. Specifically, if Buffalo can force a turnover or two on special teams, it could ignite the spark needed to build a lead the Rams must constantly chase. Josh Allen rushes for two TDs vs. Rams You might not believe it, but Allen is on pace to rush for 30 touchdowns this season. As a quarterback. Stop and consider how difficult it is for a full-time running back to hit 30 touchdowns in a season, then stroll back to Allen’s opportunity. Mind-boggling stuff, to be clear. Allen doesn’t come across as a records chaser, but you can be certain more than a few people in the building have taken note of the potential feat. Admittedly, there’s no nudging necessary in asking Allen to use his legs (and feet) to claim six. He’s a natural at it, and Allen’s role as a rusher is a key part of what I like to say renders him a fire-breathing unicorn. Almost no one wants to tackle Allen (other than Christian Wilkins), and that’s precisely why he’s so consistently good at picking up anywhere between a yard and 80 on any play. Los Angeles has probably tried to prepare for Allen’s rushing threat, but it’s difficult for most teams to replicate regardless of who mans the role in practice. The oddsmakers at FanDuel Sportsbook tend to agree here, currently listing Josh Allen with the second-best odds (+500) to score 2+ touchdowns . This means a score via rushing or receiving. Book it: the bold take here is that Allen’s set to vulture a pair of touchdowns away from Cook this evening. Greg Rousseau gets back in the sacks column This one isn’t all that bold, at least beyond the idea that Rousseau is building a bit of a legendary season as a sack artist. I’ve also featured Rousseau in this space often in 2026, and that’s because of how much I enjoy watching him blossom as a 3-4 edge rusher. He spent many seasons as a guy limited by scheme, doing decent work that was lost in the shuffle. On to the meat… You know who isn’t all that similar to Josh Allen? Matthew Stafford. Okay, the guy is a really talented quarterback, and he’s also the defending NFL MVP. But have you seen him rush the football? Right. Stafford is not much of a scrambler, and isn’t even all that great avoiding pressure as a pocket passer. Rousseau should get back to his newly featured quarterback-hunting ways in Week 5, perhaps notching a pair of sacks and maybe a turnover-worthy play or two in pursuing Stafford. Buffalo must make Stafford uncomfortable in the pocket to throw off his rhythm, and fortunately the defense has improved in that department under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. FanDuel Sportsbook lists Greg Rousseau with the second-best odds at recording a sack (+136) . So maybe it’s not too bold to say he doubles the effort. title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Chris Cole
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: ATHENS, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 26: Chris Cole #9 of the Georgia Bulldogs runs a fumble recovery back for a touchdown during a game between the Georgia Bulldogs and the Oklahoma Sooners at Sanford Stadium on September 26, 2026 in Athens, Georgia. (Photo by Steve Limentani/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Georgia Bulldogs linebacker Chris Cole Bio Cole (6’3”, 235 lbs.) was the top rated player in the entire state of Virginia, choosing to attend Georgia instead of other offers like Miami, Penn State, and Tennessee. Despite going to Georgia, Cole managed to see the field as a true freshman, even earning a SEC All-Freshman nod. He saw the field even more as a sophomore, notching 59 tackles, seven for loss, 4.5 sacks, and a couple pass breakups. So far this season, he has grown even more and become an explosive game changer for the Bulldogs’ defense. He already has 22 tackles, five for loss, 1.5 sacks, and two fumble recoveries including an 85-yard scoop and score. Strengths/Weaknesses Cole is often considered one of the best cover linebackers in the Draft. He has elite speed for the position and the versatility to line up at off-ball linebacker, nickel, and even edge defender. His athleticism allows him to be a true sideline to sideline player against the pass and the run. His strong hands allow him to reroute receivers and tight ends while giving him the ability to finish tackles efficiently. While he has produced as a pass rusher, his technique leaves quite a bit to be desired if he’s truly going to be used as a blitzer at the next level. Cole also struggles against linemen who meet him at the second level on running plays. He’s not a thumper in the run game, leaving him to occasionally get washed out by the bigger, stronger blockers. Projection Chris Cole is a dynamic cover linebacker with the size and speed that NFL teams look for at the next level. His coverage ability and alignment versatility add to the pros side of the chart for Cole. He doesn’t have the bona fides against the run, especially against downhill plays where he needs to use his strength instead of his speed. Devin Lloyd has been an absolute steal for the Panthers (despite paying him gobs of money), and Bobby Okereke has been a solid find as well. After those two, however, the cupboards are pretty bare after injuries to depth players and the release of Trevin Wallace. Adding another quality cover linebacker would help the Panthers run their desired zone scheme under Ejiro Evero. Even if the defensive coordinator changes next season, Cole is a versatile piece that any DC would love to have on their team. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Chris Cole is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
