title: After slow growth, Cowboys defense struggles vs lowly Bucs
summary: The Dallas Cowboys defense let up their second lowest point total of the season while simultaneously having one of their worst games. Let’s take a look at how they performed this week. Team stats allowed Against the Buccaneers, the Cowboys defense allowed three touchdowns and one field goal. 17 of the 24 points allowed came […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys defense let up their second lowest point total of the season while simultaneously having one of their worst games. Let’s take a look at how they performed this week. Team stats allowed Against the Buccaneers, the Cowboys defense allowed three touchdowns and one field goal. 17 of the 24 points allowed came in the third quarter. Tampa Bay ran for 241 yards on 39 attempts, good for an average of 6.2 yards on the day. Two of the three touchdowns scored would come from the rushing attack. The Buccaneers would end the day with 24 first downs, a 53.8% conversion rate on third down, and a 60% touchdown rate in the redzone. The Cowboys defense struggled getting off the field, allowing Tampa Bay to hold the ball for nearly 40 minutes. Individual stat leaders on defense Dee Winters finished with a team high ten tackles, six of which were solo. Otito Ogbonnia led the team in tackles for loss with two. Rookie Malachi Lawrence found his first NFL sack on the day. Advanced analytics The highest graded players on the day per Pro Football Focus were Markquese Bell (81.2), Malik Hooker (75.9), and Malachi Lawrence (74.4). The lowest graded players were DaRon Bland (29.6), Shavon Revel (36.9), and Kenny Clark (41.7). The Buccaneers cashed in on explosive plays, generating seven on Thursday night. Two of the biggest explosives on the day, Bucky Irving’s 72-yard run and Tez Johnson’s 64-yard reception, led to touchdowns in the third quarter. How’d the rookies look? Caleb Downs finished the game with four tackles, but also missed two on the night. Injuries are forcing him to sit back and play deep safety, which is an unfortunate waste of his talent. Once the Cowboys’ secondary begins to get healthy, expect to see Downs back to his normal role at nickel. His impact in run support around the line of scrimmage has been missed. Jaishawn Barham recorded seven tackles and one miss. He also had another goal line stand this week, sparking life into a team hanging on by a thread. The rookie linebacker continues to be an important piece in the middle of the defense. Malachi Lawrence was the best of the Cowboys rookie class on Thursday. He recorded his first sack of the season, while also adding three pressures and a pass defended on the night. As Dallas’ most productive pass rusher, Lawrence should continue to see his role increase as the season continues. LT Overton had 23 snaps this week, generating one pressure and recording one tackle. He flashes on tape, but hasn’t had a huge impact on the box score. He’s a potential bright spot down the road when he sees an increase in snaps. Final grade: F Christian Parker and his defense entered Thursday Night Football with a massive opportunity for a get right game. They started their night on defense by allowing a seven point Tampa Bay drive that consumed nearly an entire quarter. After that they buckled down they forced three punts before the half was over. Things were looking up on defense. But then the third quarter began. On the first play of the second half, Bucky Irving broke free on a run that seemed to take an eternity to cross the line of scrimmage, finally taken down by Caleb Downs after a 72-yard scamper. The very next play resulted in a Tampa Bay touchdown. Two plays, 86 yards, seven points. The next drive, coming after a Ryan Flournoy tipped ball interception, blew open on a Tez Johnson 64-yard catch and run. DaRon Bland tripped over his own feet, allowing Johnson to run free deep into Cowboys territory. After three back-to-back run plays, the Buccaneers would go on to score another touchdown. The final points in the third quarter would come from a field goal after a KaVontae Turpin special teams fumble. A commendable effort by the defense on a drive that started at the Dallas 37. Those two explosive plays by Irving and Johnson, however, changed everything. In addition to the explosives, Dallas finished the game with 12 missed tackles. Could this be a result of schedule exhaustion? Traveling to Rio to get beat up by a physical Ravens offense, returning to face off against a winless-but-tough Texans team, and then playing again just four days later surely played a role. But the Cowboys were still a clear favorite for a reason. And to allow an undrafted rookie free agent quarterback to not only survive, but to thrive, is a travesty. In no world should Jalon Daniels finish with a 76% completion rating and a 40 point higher quarterback rating than Dak Prescott. And that’s no insult to the Buccaneers quarterback – this just isn’t a league that normally allows players in his position to play as well as he played. Daniels even attempted to give the game away late, throwing a short pass into the arms of DaRon Bland. But the veteran corner rejected the potential game-tying gift, dropping the interception and leaving Cowboys fans across the globe screaming in agony. The Cowboys didn’t pressure the quarterback enough. The secondary constantly made mistakes, including a 22-yard gain on 3rd-and-21. And the 12 missed tackles contributed to the massive Buccaneers day on the ground. Allowing 24 points is one of the few positives on the day. With an offense as good as Dallas has, there won’t be many games this team loses when holding opponents to that total or less. It should have been enough to win this game (my score prediction was 34-24), but the offense had a surprisingly tough night as well. When considering the winless opponent, their undrafted rookie quarterback starting just his second game, and the struggles Tampa Bay has had in pass protection, this should have been a game the Cowboys defense would use to right the ship. Instead they surrendered an unconscionable amount of yards on the ground and allowed the rookie quarterback to live free of pressure for most of the night. For these reasons, this defense gets their first F of the season. There is hope for better days brought by the return of injured players on defense and the insertion of Joey Porter Jr. into the lineup. We may also see some changes, with Brian Schottenheimer vowing to shake things up . Next week, Dallas travels to Lambeau Field to take on Jordan Love and the Packers on Sunday Night Football . We’ll see if the Christian Parker’s defense can begin to right the ship against Green Bay’s 28th ranked scoring offense.
author: Dyllan Rivers

title: Struggling Jake Ferguson keeps dropping the ball for the Cowboys
summary: Since stepping into the starting role in 2023, tight end Jake Ferguson has cemented himself as a key component of the Dallas Cowboys’ offense. His quick emergence allowed the team to transition away from Dalton Schultz to Ferguson at a much lower price. The young tight end quickly earned the trust of Dak Prescott, establishing […]
full_text: Since stepping into the starting role in 2023, tight end Jake Ferguson has cemented himself as a key component of the Dallas Cowboys’ offense. His quick emergence allowed the team to transition away from Dalton Schultz to Ferguson at a much lower price. The young tight end quickly earned the trust of Dak Prescott, establishing himself as a reliable safety valve and a vibrant source of energy for the offense. Through his first four years in the league, he put together two Pro Bowl seasons as he found ways to find soft spots in coverage and make the most of every reception with impressive toughness and the occasional hurdle of defenders. Having a seam-stretching tight end who commanded attention helped make a dynamic Cowboys offense even more dynamic. Fans loved him. Last July, Ferguson signed a four-year, $52 million extension with the team, putting him under team control through the 2029 season. While his athleticism and locker room energy made him a guy the team wanted to hold on to, a pattern of costly mistakes is starting to raise questions about his overall consistency and long-term effectiveness. In past seasons, the veteran tight end has shown good hands, making contested catches look effortless, but recently his focus has wavered at critical moments. Through five games this year, he has a drop rate of 9.5%, which is a high percentage for a player targeted on short-to-intermediate routes. Obviously, the most devastating example came on Thursday night when the ball was thrown right at his grill. Not only did he not secure the catch, but the ball deflected off his face and stayed in the air forever until a Buccaneers defender could safely get under it. A potential comeback drive turned into a costly game-ending mistake. Even more alarming than the periodic drop is Ferguson’s ongoing battle with ball security after the catch. Over the last three years, he’s put the ball on the turf a staggering eight times, leading all tight ends in that span. That’s a rate of once every 19.6 times he touches the ball. For perspective, that is like a running back who touches the ball 20 times a game who fumbles once every game. That’s atrocious. His fumbling woes have caused opposing defensive coordinators to openly admit to going after him. Ferguson has a bad habit of carrying the ball away from his frame, making him vulnerable to aggressive defenders who deliberately swipe at the ball. And it’s worked. He had a costly fumble on a shovel pass against the Baltimore Ravens a couple of weeks ago that erased a promising scoring drive. We can argue until we are blue in the face about whether that should’ve been ruled incomplete, but either way, Ferguson isn’t doing a good job securing the ball. These things are harmful to the team, but some might be willing to give him a little leniency if he were a strong blocker. He’s not. His chip blocks are ineffective, and he routinely misses his blocking assignments in the running game. There are more and more instances of Ferguson being tossed aside as a blocker. It’s not good. The Cowboys invested a second-round pick in Luke Schoonmaker in 2023, but he has not worked out as planned. The team reupped on Ferguson, but now, suddenly, he has created a bit of concern as well. The front office also wisely extended Brevyn Spann-Ford, who is the team’s gritty blocker and special teams contributor, but one can’t help wondering if we could see a change in responsibilities as the season moves forward. If Ferguson can’t clean up some of his problems and start being more of a net positive than a liability, the Cowboys might have some tough decisions ahead. Jake Ferguson's hands have turned into a liability for the Cowboys. pic.twitter.com/4eEDmsaYSr — Dan Rogers (@DannyPhantom24) October 11, 2026
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys’ coaching staff isn’t providing answers to team’s problems
summary: At some point, a bad loss stops being an isolated incident and starts becoming a reflection of the people responsible for preventing it, going all the way up to the front office. Yet, since the Cowboys are structured and operated the way they are that’s a story for another day. For now, the focus should […]
full_text: RIO DE JANEIRO, BRAZIL - SEPTEMBER 27: Head coach Brian Schottenheimer of the Dallas Cowboys watches play during the first quarter of the game against the Baltimore Ravens at Maracana Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. (Photo by Wagner Meier/Getty Images) | Getty Images At some point, a bad loss stops being an isolated incident and starts becoming a reflection of the people responsible for preventing it, going all the way up to the front office. Yet, since the Cowboys are structured and operated the way they are that’s a story for another day. For now, the focus should be on the field with the people who are making decisions in real-time. Thursday night’s 24-16 defeat to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was another reminder that the problems plaguing this team extend far beyond one player, one position group or one unfortunate bounce of the football. Dallas lost at home to an 0-4 team starting an undrafted rookie quarterback in his second NFL start. Tampa Bay left AT&T Stadium with its first win of the season after outgaining Dallas in yardage, controlling possession for more than 39 minutes and winning the turnover battle 3-0. The Cowboys once again struggled to stop the run, failed to sustain their offense, surrendered a costly special-teams turnover and watched their final realistic opportunity disappear when Jake Ferguson couldn’t secure a pass that became the game-sealing interception. Individual mistakes played a role, but they cannot explain away the broader failure. Dallas looked unprepared to handle Tampa’s pressure, unable to stop its rushing attack and incapable of consistently executing in any phase of the game. When those problems appear simultaneously, the scrutiny has to extend beyond the players making mistakes and toward the coaches responsible for preparing them. Brian Schottenheimer, Christian Parker, Klayton Adams and Nick Sorensen all have different responsibilities, but Thursday exposed shortcomings across their respective units. Five games into the season, the Cowboys have given fans little reason to believe this staff can turn a talented roster into a consistently competitive team. Brian Schottenheimer keeps coming up short Again… I recognize Schotty has to speak. A lot. Part of the job. This is just so tone deaf at best imo. On some level I admire the tunnel vision required to do the job. But these are empty words and sound like corporate buzz speak when you are coaching like he is right now. https://t.co/mTnow5xPzd — RJ Ochoa (@rjochoa) October 9, 2026 Schottenheimer’s responsibility extends beyond calling plays. As head coach, he sets the team’s standards, oversees its preparation and ultimately answers for the product Dallas puts on the field. As offensive play-caller, he also has a direct hand in an offense that struggles at inopportune times. Dallas opened Thursday’s game with a promising touchdown drive, but managed only three additional points before its final touchdown with 5:26 remaining in the fourth quarter. Tampa’s pressure disrupted Dak Prescott, and the Cowboys never found a consistent counter until the game was nearly out of reach. When Dallas can establish its preferred rhythm, the offense has enough talent to score against anyone. When an opponent disrupts that rhythm, however, the Cowboys too often look as though they are waiting for the original plan to start working again rather than finding a different way to attack. Every play-caller has bad games, but the better ones recognize when an opponent has taken away the first option and respond before an entire half slips away. Schottenheimer’s offense failed to do that against Tampa, and Dallas finished with three turnovers while leaving too much of the burden on Prescott to manufacture a comeback. The struggles were not limited to the play calls themselves. TE Jake Ferguson’s blocking has been inconsistent, and his three-catch, 19-yard performance against Tampa ended with a drop that became an interception when Dallas was trying to mount a late comeback. Not every tipped interception is the receiver’s fault, but Ferguson needed to secure a catchable pass in that situation. Combined with his ongoing difficulties as a blocker, the play highlighted another weakness the offense has not adequately addressed. Ferguson has shown he can contribute as a receiver, but a tight end who struggles to finish blocks and cannot consistently deliver in critical moments puts his offense in difficult situations. The coaching staff must find a way to improve his execution or reconsider how heavily it relies on him. Continuing to use the same personnel in the same ways without addressing the results is not a meaningful adjustment. Schottenheimer cannot catch passes or prevent every turnover, but he can put his players in better positions to succeed. His offense needs a more adaptable approach, and his team needs greater discipline in the situations that decide close games. Until those improvements become visible, it is fair to question whether he is the right person to lead this operation. Christian Parker’s defense has no identity If Schottenheimer’s offense failed to adjust, Christian Parker’s defense failed to stop the most obvious threat in front of it. Tampa Bay ran for 241 yards, with Bucky Irving accounting for 165 on 21 carries. Irving broke off a 72-yard run to open the second half, setting up a touchdown on the next play, and later added a one-yard scoring run. The Buccaneers finished with 419 total yards while controlling the game through their ground attack. Meanwhile, quarterback Jalon Daniels completed 19 of 25 passes for 189 yards and a touchdown. He played efficiently without needing to take over the game, largely because Tampa could rely on its running game to move the chains and keep Dallas’ offense on the sideline. That is an increasingly troubling reflection on Parker’s defense. Dallas entered the season expecting a new identity under a new coordinator, but the unit has struggled to stop the run, generate consistent pressure and create turnovers. Through five games, the Cowboys have yet to record an interception, although Daron Bland just tried his best to secure one. In fairness, maybe Parker deserves some time to establish his system, and injuries have complicated his personnel decisions. Joey Porter Jr., acquired to strengthen the secondary, was unavailable Thursday because of an illness. Those circumstances deserve consideration, but they do not explain away the fundamental breakdowns against Tampa. Quinnen Williams has missed 9 tackles thus far this season, per PFF, 4 more than the next closest interior defensive linemen Donovan Ezeiruaku is tied for the 2nd-most missed tackles among EDGEs at 5 and Malachi Lawrence is tied for the 4th-most at 4. Dee Winters is tied for… — John Owning (@JohnOwning) October 9, 2026 A defense should still be able to maintain gap discipline, tackle effectively and prevent an opponent from repeatedly exploiting the same weakness. The Buccaneers did all the things Dallas needed to prevent, and the Cowboys had no effective answer. The performance also raised legitimate questions about the team’s preparation and effort, particularly on defense. Effort cannot be measured simply by looking at the final score, and a poor performance does not automatically mean players were unmotivated. But repeated failures to finish tackles, control the line of scrimmage and respond when Tampa seized momentum are difficult to overlook. These are fundamental responsibilities that should not disappear because an opponent has a favorable matchup or the game is being played on a short week. Parker’s challenge is not simply to install a scheme; it is to establish a dependable standard of execution. The issue is not that he has failed to rebuild the defense in five games, but that his unit has yet to demonstrate a reliable foundation on which that rebuild can succeed. Nick Sorensen’s special teams are another problem Special teams should…

title: Empty promises and defensive meltdowns plague Cowboys
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have descended into a deeply unsettling territory where their ongoing performances have become a recurring nightmare. For three straight weeks, we have gone into a game with this level of excitement only to realize that this team isn’t very good. They get us every time. How can we be such suckers! The […]
full_text: Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys have descended into a deeply unsettling territory where their ongoing performances have become a recurring nightmare. For three straight weeks, we have gone into a game with this level of excitement only to realize that this team isn’t very good. They get us every time. How can we be such suckers! The reason we fall for it is because they do have talent. Yes, more of that talent is on the offensive side of the ball, but there is no excuse for this team to be playing as poorly as they are. No excuse. The loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was especially frustrating because the offense, supposedly the dependable side of this team, never found a comfortable rhythm. To be fair, the Bucs have a good defense, but there was still an expectation that Dallas would move the ball and create enough offense to control the game. Instead, the Tampa defense brought pressure, put Dak Prescott in tough spots, and forced the Cowboys into uncomfortable situations. Prescott had escaped a few dangerous throws in previous games when deflections fell harmlessly away, but this time, his luck ran out. The bigger concern was that Brian Schottenheimer and the offense didn’t have an effective counterpunch. CeeDee Lamb was completely neutralized. Tyler Smith returned but could not spark the running game, and even the later success involving George Pickens and Ryan Flournoy didn’t come easily, as both of them had to make incredible catches in traffic. Sadly, this team cannot survive if they experience any type of lingering offensive drought. That is because of the real problem with this football team. The major problem. The Cowboys’ defense. There is no nice way to articulate it. This unit is outright terrible right now. The tackling has become sloppy and the coverage breakdowns have become straight-up embarrassing. Even when this team is hustling around looking as if they’re going to make a huge play, their grabby hands will come up empty and shifts into a big play for the opposing offense. And this is happening all the time. It’s hard to explain why this is happening. It’s about as puzzling as why DaRon Bland can’t stay upright and is always tripping over the ground, allowing a receiver to graze in wide-open spaces. And that is what the secondary does. Receivers are left unattended, assignments are missed, and communication disappears at the worst possible time. The most aggravating part is that they are showing no sign of improving. After the big play to Zay Flowers late in the game against the Baltimore Ravens that only took six seconds and cost them the game, you would expect such a thing to sting to the point where they would be like, never again! Instead, two games later, the Cowboys’ defense surrendered a completely inexcusable 3rd-and-21 conversion when they ever-so-desperately needed a stop. And Tampa made it look easy. That makes it even more annoying. Opponents arrive with a plan, and the Cowboys spend the afternoon reacting to it. That seems like a pretty good indicator that a team is being outcoached. We know things are bad, but where do the Cowboys go from here? That is difficult to answer because the offense still has enough talent to make noise. Prescott, Lamb, Pickens, a capable offensive line, and a functional rushing attack should form one of the league’s better groups. And they are on most days. Expecting the offense to produce at a high level isn’t unreasonable. It is the minimum requirement if the Cowboys want to remain relevant. The problem is that there is almost no margin for error because of what is happening on the other side of the ball. Dallas cannot casually take a few possessions off while the offense searches for answers, because the defense is not equipped to keep the game within reach. Every possession carries extra weight, and every stalled drive feels like the beginning of the end. The defense must find a way to be better. Asking for a takeaway almost seems absurd. A takeaway? How about they just get a stop? Make tackles. Stay disciplined. Communicate assignments. Get the correct calls in. Get off the field on third down. If they could somehow just do some of the basic things, it would feel transformational. The schedule will not wait, either. Tougher opponents and better quarterbacks are coming, and even modest progress may not be enough by then. There are reasons for some hope. Joey Porter Jr. should help. Quinnen Williams is still a great player. And rookie defenders such as Caleb Downs, Jaishawn Barham, and Malachi Lawrence offer potential. The supply cabinet is not empty. They have some tools. That’s what makes the current performance hard to excuse. Christian Parker and his staff must turn this talent into a defense that understands its responsibilities and executes them. The question is whether meaningful change can happen quickly enough. A late-season rise to mediocrity seems like the ceiling for this group, but it will likely be too little, too late. And while Parker’s failures have been on full display, Schottenheimer’s leadership deserves scrutiny as well. We’re not talking about the trivial stuff. No one should be overly bothered by the failed two-point attempt or trotting Brandon Aubrey out there for a long field goal only for it to get blocked. Criticize the execution, not the decision. The real concern with Schottenheimer is that he appears to believe this team is better than it has shown. His calm demeanor can keep him composed in a difficult post-game interview, but it also screams complacency when the same problems continue to happen. That was one of the most frustrating traits of the Mike McCarthy era. The belief that Dallas was basically fine and only needed minor adjustments. It was often good enough to win regular-season games, but never good enough to accomplish anything significant. Schottenheimer preaches accountability, yet the Cowboys keep repeating unaccountable football. At some point, there needs to be a sense of urgency. Nobody is asking him to throw furniture, but a little visible frustration would at least suggest the alarm is sounding inside the facility. Right now, the Cowboys look too comfortable with problems that should make everyone uncomfortable. And that’s not a good sign. That leaves the Cowboys in an awkward place. It is hard to imagine this team making serious noise this season, but there should be urgency in identifying how they can improve and who the people are that are going to help them achieve that noise one day. Which young players can become dependable contributors? Who needs to be replaced? The Cowboys brought in plenty of new faces, and the remaining schedule should provide a clear evaluation period. The positive is that there is enough talent to build around, but they are pressed for time. The Dak Prescott window is entering its final stages, so patience is not a luxury the organization can afford. The Cowboys have also borrowed more from future cap resources than they typically do. Fans want the front office to go all out. Well, they got it, but aggressive moves carry consequences when the wins do not follow. That makes this season particularly disappointing. The division remains up for grabs, and nobody has taken firm control of the NFC, yet the Cowboys cannot take advantage. The road only gets tougher from here. For fans, all we can do is search for progress, guard our optimism, and prepare for more turbulent waters.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys news: Dallas still firmly in division race thanks to other NFC East teams
summary: Things got a little better on Sunday morning for the Cowboys as the Eagles fell to the Jaguars thanks to late-game heroics from Jacksonville. Then, the Giants and Commanders game ended in a tie due to poor clock management from Washington. While a Commanders win would be preferable, it was a good Sunday for the […]
full_text: Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images | DeFodi Images via Getty Images Things got a little better on Sunday morning for the Cowboys as the Eagles fell to the Jaguars thanks to late-game heroics from Jacksonville. Then, the Giants and Commanders game ended in a tie due to poor clock management from Washington. While a Commanders win would be preferable, it was a good Sunday for the Cowboys, all things considered. To win the division, though, Dallas will have to start stringing together back-to-back wins. Back-to-back wins have been rare in the Schottenheimer era. All in all, we can enjoy a Sunday without the disappointment of Cowboys football. Updated NFC East Standings: Wild NFL Sunday Benefits Cowboys After Week 5- Randy Gurzi, Sports Illustrated Although Thursday night was an upsetting game for Cowboys fans, there is a silver lining after Sunday’s action. The rest of the NFC East is doing the Cowboys favors by giving them an opportunity to climb back into the division. 2. Philadelphia Eagles (2-3) Right now, the Philadelphia Eagles have the tiebreaker over the Cowboys because they are 1-0 in the NFC East, compared to 1-1 for Dallas. They should be 3-2, however, after taking a lead against the Jacksonville Jaguars with eight seconds to play. NFC East Is For Losers: Cowboys Joined By Incompetence Across Division – Adam Schultz, Yahoo Sports The division is still wide open thanks to help from other teams. However, to take advantage of the lack of success from other teams, they will need to string together wins. A task they have only done once in the Schottenheimer era. Add it up, and incredibly, all four NFC East teams played this weekend … and they combined for zero wins! The division remains there for the taking, but … Why can’t the Cowboys win back-to-back games? That is one question we are all asking in the aftermath of the 24-16 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday night. Cowboys’ possession battle woes, ruinous defensive penalties among maddening Week 5 stats- Todd Brock, Cowboys Wire It has been well documented that the Cowboys are the only team without a defensive interception this season. And in the moment they could have changed that and flipped the outcome of the Thursday Night Football game, they failed. 0: Interceptions by defense… on the year DaRon Bland’s blatant drop in the fourth quarter likely would have given the Cowboys a go-ahead touchdown with under four minutes to play and might have sealed a Week 5 win, but it also would have snapped a rather ugly streak of futility. Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . 5 Coaches Who Could Take the Cowboys to the Next Level- Cody Warren, Inside The Star During a long week, it may be a good time to think about what if. Granted, Schottenheimer absolutely has time to turn the ship around, but if it doesn’t happen Jerry and the organization needs to think about what’s next. 1. Kirby Smart Has Earned the Top Spot Smart’s two National Championships at the University of Georgia put him first on my list, but what happened between those two titles is interesting. Georgia lost eight defenders to the 2022 NFL Draft, including five first round picks. The next team won another championship while allowing 16.0 points per game . Christian Parker turning Matt Eberflus into a sympathetic figure is rock bottom- Jerry Trotta, The Landry Hat No fan expected the Cowboys to go from worst to first defensively simply by hiring Christian Parker and getting an exciting new rookie safety. However, possibly regressing after a horrific 2025 defensive campaign seemed equally unlikely. Former Cowboys wide receiver Jesse Holley echoed a similar sentiment , tweeting that “Parker is actually doing much less with much more, making his job performance worse than Matt Eberflus.” Being a prisoner of the moment is natural after an embarrassing primetime loss. This isn’t that. There’s real credence to the idea that Parker has been worse than Eberflus.
author: Aidan Davis

title: Broncos’ stats and analysis vs. Chargers
summary: By most accounts the Denver Broncos should have won this game in a blowout, and yet, this team managed to need another fourth quarter comeback from Bo Nix to get a win after being down 17-10 in the fourth quarter. The Los Angeles Chargers were starting an offensive line with almost no experience and they […]
full_text: By most accounts the Denver Broncos should have won this game in a blowout, and yet, this team managed to need another fourth quarter comeback from Bo Nix to get a win after being down 17-10 in the fourth quarter. The Los Angeles Chargers were starting an offensive line with almost no experience and they were missing their best WR on offense in Ladd McConkey. The Charger starting offensive line was Jake Slaughter, Travis Burke, Alex Harkey, Logan Taylor, and Cole Strange. Harkey had never taken an NFL snap on offense. Slaughter is a rookie who has started all five games so far. Burke and Taylor are both rookies who were making their first career starts. Strange is a journeyman veteran on his fourth team in five NFL seasons, but he did enter the game with 48 starts. This OL was facing the defense that led the NFL in sacks in both 2024 and 2025. The Bronco defense should have been making life miserable for Justin Herbert, but that didn’t really happen in the fourth quarter. The Bronco defense did have five sacks and six QBhits (remember a hit is not sack, and a sack is not a QBhit), but all but one of those happened in the fourth quarter. The one that didn’t was Nik Bonitto’s sack on the last play of the first quarter. Nik had a great game on paper with 3 TFL, 2 QBhits, 2 sacks, and 4 tackles (3 solo), but he didn’t seem to have that big of an influence on the game and he really should have dominated against a team starting two backup OTs. Three TFL is a career high for him. His season high was 16 in 2024. While he got 3 in this game, he only has four on the season. The Bronco defense gave up another long run. This time was similar to the others in that the opposing RB broke a bunch of tackles on route to the endzone. The Bronco defense joins the Colts and the Raiders as the only defenses who have allowed three runs of 30+ this season. Those would be the 30 yard run by Kyren Williams, the 42 yard TD run by Kimani Vidal Sassoon, and the 60 yard TD run by Kenneth Walker. At the time of writing, prior to the Monday night game, the Bronco run defense is 25th in YPC allowed at 4.7. The Jaguars are the best allowing 2.9 and the Panthers are the worst at 5.4. What’s more troubling is the third down conversion percentage allowed. The Broncos were one of the best teams in the league over the last two seasons at stopping conversion on 3rd down. They currently stand at 26th – allowing conversion on 45.2 percent. The Cowboys are the worst at 52.6 percent and the Vikings are the best at 22.2 percent (this helps explain their 5-0 start). The Denver defense has allowed 33 third down conversions so far this season. Only the Lions have allowed more at 36. The Bears have allowed 13. Will Lutz was extremely reliable last season even hitting 4 of 6 from 50 or longer. He is currently 3 of 6 from 40 or longer with two of those misses coming from 40-49 yards. Currently NFL kickers are 75 for 91 from that distance (81.5 percent). Lutz only missed two from that distance all last year and he now has two misses from that range. While Lutz has been having a bad season so far, Jeremy Crawshaw has been having a great season. He has gotten 50 percent of his punts downed inside the 20 (12 of 24), and 8 of 24 have been downed inside the 10. Using my system that rewards punts downed inside the 10 with increasingly more value as you get to the one, Crawshaw is currently 5th with 34 points. A punt downed at the 10 gets one point, while a punt downed at the 1 gets 10 points. Notice how the Bengal’s punter has five downed inside the ten, but four of them were downed at the 8. He only gets 14 points, while the Steeler’s punter, who also has five, has 35 points, because he has one downed at the four, one at the two, and one at the one. Every team has at least one, but the Viking punter only has one and it was downed at the 10. This stat is a punter stat, but it is also a punt coverage team stat. The Bronco punt coverage team has been really good so far this year. I don’t know how many of Crawshaw’s inside the 10 punts were “coffin corner” punts where he angled them out of bounds. I know he is good at that and has done it as least four times this season that I can remember. Only six on Crawshaw’s 24 punts have been returned and those are only averaging 7.7 yards per return. That’s currently tied for the second least YPR in the NFL. Only the Packers punt coverage team has been better (7.4 yards per PR). 25 percent return rate is one of the lowest in the NFL. Michael Dickson of the Seahawks has the lowest at 15 percent, while Rigoberto Sanchez of the Colts has had 69 percent of his returned.
author: Joe Mahoney

title: Denver Broncos news: ‘Finding a way to win’ is still winning, no matter how ugly
summary: Following an ugly but effective 23-17 win over the Chargers on Sunday, quarterback Bo Nix was the first to admit it wasn’t “his best.” “The game, the feel and the results of drives told me that it wasn’t necessarily pretty, but we just found a way to win,” Nix said, adding the offense as a […]
full_text: Following an ugly but effective 23-17 win over the Chargers on Sunday, quarterback Bo Nix was the first to admit it wasn’t “his best.” “The game, the feel and the results of drives told me that it wasn’t necessarily pretty, but we just found a way to win,” Nix said, adding the offense as a whole was OK. “At the end of the day, we’ve got to score more points, and that’s something that we’re going to continue to work on.” The problem, as Nix sees it, is consistency. “Right now, there’s just a little subtle piece of overall offensive execution that we’re still working towards, because at times, it’s there and we’re really good,” he said. “At times, for whatever reason, the drive stalls.” “I don’t think we win the game without those turnovers,” Nix said, noting the offense should have been able to get touchdowns instead of field goals out of the short fields. So we need to clean that up.” Bo NIX If it weren’t for the defense, which practically gift-wrapped 13 points for the offense, it would have been a much messier day and not a win. “I don’t think we win the game without those turnovers,” Nix said, noting the offense should have been able to get touchdowns out of those short fields instead of having to settle for field goals. “So we need to clean that up.” Head coach Sean Payton thinks a big part of the answer is better protection up front. “I think it’s important from a protection standpoint, that early in games we provide that clean pocket so that clock doesn’t get juiced up a little bit,” Payton added. Of course, Nix’s footwork bears some responsibility for the offense’s struggles too. Payton thinks the QB is “settling down a little bit,” but the coach reiterated his complaint from last week that the entire team, especially the offense, needs to be good at the details. “I think after four weeks there’s a handful of things that collectively — and you know, it starts with me — where it’s like, all right, let’s focus on these details,” Payton said. “And I think the byproduct helps the [quarterback].” “[Bo Nix]'s really, really, right now, struggling with just his feet in the pocket.” @danorlovsky7 breaks down what's going wrong for the Broncos' QB recently 😬 (Via @PatMcAfeeShow ) pic.twitter.com/SNpUUl0A0q — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) October 12, 2026 No matter Nix’s struggles this season, Payton has let him know he’s guy the coach wants in control. “I said to him ‘man, you’re the guy we want here. Let’s go. You’ve done a ton of things well.’ But I think a lot goes into that,” Payton noted. “I want him to make sure that we can let it rip.” For Nix that means trusting what he sees. “You’ve got to sort of earn that right,” Nix added. “When you do the preparation, you earn the right to react so that you can let it rip.” The main problem with that is Nix and the offense “earn the right” one series and then lose it the next. “I’ll say it again, you’re always looking for small steps [of improvement.] Sean Payton “There were times I felt like I was really good when the play was there,” Nix said. “There’s other times I feel like there’s still some things that I could either see or process better. …It’s just the layers and layers of being a quarterback and processing. Nothing’s ever going to be easy,” Payton reiterated that he coaches for small steps of improvement — and as coach he’s accountable for that too — particularly when it comes to calling protections so the offense can convert a few more (or any!) third downs. “I’ll say it again, you’re always looking for small steps,” Payton added. “The strength of that front, the edges can be a problem, and then they do a pretty good job with some zone pressures.” Nix joked it would be great if the defense lined up exactly like they wanted because “you’d probably have a lot of touchdowns and a lot of points.” But that’s not going to happen. “The important thing is we’re sitting here talking about a win,” Nix added. “That’s really, really important.”

(Photo by Will Lester/MediaNews Group/Inland Valley Daily Bulletin via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Late last week I was curious and looked up some pass rush statistics on the Denver Broncos, because I just felt like they just hadn’t been getting the job done through the first four games. And that hunch proved correct . They were near the bottom in pressure percentages, sacks, and QB hurry percentage despite being among the league leaders in blitz percentage. So Vance Joseph was trying to create pressure and still wasn’t able to get it done. After their second half domination of Justin Herbert and the Los Angeles Chargers, they still rank poorly overall, but they showed out with a five sack effort moving them back into the Top 10 in sacks. My hope is that we’ll see that pressure and hurry percentage increase, because as it stands they are dead last in QB hurries even after yesterday’s game. This is a trend I hope continues this week. title: Denver Broncos Stock Up, Stock Down: Week 5 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers
summary: Well, it wasn’t pretty, but the Broncos perfected winning ugly last season, and they are continuing that this season with a 23-17 comeback victory over their divisional rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers. The struggles on offense continued throughout this one, but they did show some life late while the Broncos’ defense dominated for the most […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos looks on prior to the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, it wasn’t pretty, but the Broncos perfected winning ugly last season, and they are continuing that this season with a 23-17 comeback victory over their divisional rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers. The struggles on offense continued throughout this one, but they did show some life late while the Broncos’ defense dominated for the most part, outside of a handful of rather bad plays. It wasn’t a perfect game by the Broncos by any means, but at the end of the day, they got the win and improved to 3-2 on the year. Still, there are some things the Broncos need to improve on, and improve on quickly, if they want to continue having success this season. Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos’ 53-man roster and tell you which Broncos players’ stock is going up, down, or remains unchanged. After an ugly win vs. the Chargers on Sunday, we have a good mix of stock-ups and stock-downs today. Quarterback Bo Nix – Stock down: His early-season struggles continued on Sunday. He looked unconfident, lost, and simply did not play well. We have seen Nix go through stretches like this, but he eventually bounces back and improves as the season goes on. Still, this might be one of his worst stretches. I have faith that he will bounce back, because we have seen Nix play MUCH better than this, but it did not look good on Sunday vs. a banged-up 0-4 Chargers team. Next up, a difficult Seattle Seahawks defense on a short week. Jarrett Stidham – Unchanged: Veteran backup quarterback. Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged: Emergency third-string quarterback. Running Back JK Dobbins – Stock up slightly: I am going slightly because, for most of this game, he was not very good. Lacked explosiveness and, at most, was getting three yards and a cloud of dust. He had just 27 yards through 3 quarters on Sunday, but had 41 yards on 6 carries in the 4th quarter when the Broncos went on a 13-0 run. That fourth quarter was the first time we saw 2025 JK Dobbins, and the Broncos and this offense need to see that version of Dobbins a lot more moving forward. RJ Harvey – Stock down: After seeing heavy usage the last few games, we barely saw the Broncos’ explosive runner on Sunday. He played just 37% of the snaps and had just 3 carries for 7 yards and 1 target for 0 catches. Do I think this will continue? Probably not. However, this was the first game with Sean Payton calling plays this season, and we saw an increased workload for Dobbins and less work for Harvey, Tyler Badie – Unchanged: He did not see the touches he was getting previously, but his role remained the same. He is a third-down pass-blocking back who occasionally gets some touches in the run and pass game. Adam Prentice – Unchanged: Played just 6 snaps on offense but did see his first carry of the season. Wide Receiver Jaylen Waddle – Stock down: The Broncos’ big offseason addition started to show some frustration on the field on Sunday, and well, it’s warranted. He was supposed to change this offense, but once again, he was an afterthought during the game, finishing with 5 targets and 2 catches for 19 yards. He did have a costly drop late in the game, and it was simply another disappointing effort for the Broncos’ explosive pass catcher. We need Nix and Waddle to improve their chemistry on the field, and do it quickly. Courtland Sutton – Stock up slightly: Like Dobbins, Sutton was invisible for most of the game. However, in the 4th quarter, he showed some life and caught his first touchdown of the season. His stat line is nothing to write home about, but we need to get Sutton going and, hopefully, these signs of life lead to more consistency moving forward. Marvin Mims Jr. – Stock up: His play as a wide receiver was lackluster, but he showed life as a returner for the first time this season and had a 27-yard punt return to set the Broncos up in good field position. Troy Franklin – Stock up: With Pat Bryant going on the short-term IR, Franklin saw added snaps on Sunday, but it did not amount to much. Still, it appears Franklin will have a larger role in the offense until Bryant returns from an ankle injury. Lil’Jordan Humphrey – Unchanged: He was added to the roster after Bryant was added to the IR and saw 14 snaps with the offense vs. the Chargers. LJH saw 2 targets and turned that into 1 catch for 8 yards. Tight End Evan Engram – Unchanged: Engram has been outsnapping Adam Trautman the past few weeks with Davis Webb calling plays, but with Payton back calling plays, both saw 30 snaps on Sunday. With that said, Engram led the team in receiving with 4 catches for 55 yards, including a 34-yard reception early on that led to the Broncos’ first-quarter touchdown. We’ll see how this trend continues moving forward. Adam Trautman – Unchanged: His role is what it is, and Sean Payton favors him, so he’ll keep playing. Nate Adkins – Unchanged: Adkins played 31% of the snaps, and his role as the third tight end/blocking specialist remains unchanged. Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: Red-shirt rookie year for the Broncos ‘ 7th-round tight end. Offensive Line Garett Bolles – Unchanged : The Broncos OL has struggled a bit this season, but Bolles remains solid as Nix’s blindside blocker. Ben Powers – Stock down: I am no offensive line expert, but the Broncos have had a lot of pressure come through the middle of the line. I am not sure if it all lands on Powers, but the pressure is happening. Luke Wattenberg – Stock down: His snaps continue to be off target from time to time, and the pressure is coming through the middle of the line. Quinn Meinerz – Unchanged: All-Pro caliber guard. Mike McGlinchey – Stock down: Penalties and inconsistent blocking have been a trend this season for the Broncos veteran right tackle. Alex Palczewski – Stock up: Saw 8 snaps on offense on Sunday in heavy packages, and with the Broncos leaning on the run game more, he could see more snaps moving forward. You could also make the case that he should see time at left guard or even right tackle. Matt Peart – Unchanged: Saw 6 snaps on special teams. Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: Saw 6 snaps on special teams. Kage Casey – Unchanged: Redshirt rookie year and is probably locked in the weight room. Defensive Line Zach Allen – Stock up: Sack, forced fumble, and continues to be one of the best overall players on the Broncos this season. DJ Jones – Stock up: Showed some life as a pass rusher and sacked Justin Herbert Malcolm Roach – Unchanged: Played solid from what I saw. He has been consistent all season, but I hoped we would see a little more pass rush from him. Eyioma Uwazurike – Unchanged: Played 45% of the snaps vs. the Chargers and had a big TFL late in the game. Sai’vion Jones – Unchanged: He was active ahead of Jordan Jackson and played 30% of the snaps but did not register a tackle. Jordan Jackson – Stock down: Was inactive on Sunday as the Broncos decided to go with Jones instead of him. Tyler Onyedim – Unchanged: Redshirt rookie year continues. Hopefully, we can see him get some playing time this season. Edge rusher Nik Bonitto – Stock up: Bonitto finally showed some life on Sunday and totaled 2 sacks vs. the Chargers’ banged-up OL and Justin Herbert. We need more of these types of performances from Bonitto moving forward. Jonah Elliss – Unchanged: He pressured Herbert a few times, but overall, I still want more from Elliss. Que Robinson – Stock up: His play is not perfect, but he has made more impact plays this season than Jonah Elliss. He changed the entire momentum on Sunday when he stonewalled Justin Herbert on a 4th-and-1 QB sneak. That turnover on downs led to a 13-0 run by the Broncos, who would go on to win the game. Dondrea Tillman – Stock up: He’s in a reserve role but made a few impact plays…

title: Sean Payton expresses faith in Bo Nix despite early season struggles
summary: Ugly wins are still wins. That’s precisely what the Denver Broncos achieved beating the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. Had it not been for a ferocious fourth quarter effort by the defense, the Broncos may very well have lost the game to a beat-up, hapless, and winless Chargers squad. Broncos Country will be content with […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Inglewood, California, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) talks to a referee against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first half at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: William Liang-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Ugly wins are still wins. That’s precisely what the Denver Broncos achieved beating the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. Had it not been for a ferocious fourth quarter effort by the defense, the Broncos may very well have lost the game to a beat-up, hapless, and winless Chargers squad. Broncos Country will be content with the victory. 3-2 at this juncture is much better than 2-3. However, the struggles on the offense and quarterback Bo Nix still linger. That’s still a huge cause for concern with no clear solution in sight. Despite a change in play calling, the offense still failed to operate at a high level. Their only saving grace was being able to score several times on short fields off turnovers forced by the defense throughout the game. Was that enough to win? Yes, but it certainly isn’t good enough to beat the best teams in the NFL and be contenders moving foward. Another game, another sluggish performance by Bo Nix. The third-year signal caller went 16-of-27 for 123 yards and 1 touchdown with one lost fumble. The Broncos converted just one third down out of twelve attempts the entire game and averaged just a little over four yards per pass. After the game, Head Coach Sean Payton talked about Nix’s performance and what he and his teammates can do to help set him up for success. “I would say this. I think the one area, I think obviously there’s a lot been said about his feet. I think he’s settling that down. I think it’s important from a protection standpoint, that early in games we provide that clean pocket so that clock doesn’t get juiced up a little bit,” stated Payton. “I think after four weeks there’s a handful of things that collectively — and you know, it starts with me — where it’s like, all right, let’s focus on these details. And I think the byproduct helps the quarterback. Obviously, the hardest thing to do in this league is play that position if you’re not rushing the ball,” added Payton. Against the Chargers, the Broncos made it a priority to run the football. In prior games with Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb calling the plays, the run-to-pass ratio was drastically different. In this matchup with Payton dialing up calls, they toted the rock 29 times and gained 106 yards. Even though that’s under four yards per carry, Denver’s emphasis on the ground game helped them control the pace of the game. They decisively won time of possession battle which proved to be big factor in their road victory against a division rival. Even with less of a burden on Nix’s shoulders, the aerial attack failed to take off. There were missed plays down the field and meat left on the bone. On one particular occasion, Jaylen Waddle looked visibly frustrated with how the offense was performing and showed his frustration on the field, as well as on the sidelines. With nearly a third of the season over, the Broncos’ offense appears, especially the play of Nix, to have regressed in all facets compared to seasons prior. Nevertheless, Payton was steadfast in his commitment to Nix after the game. Even though things haven’t gone as planned thus far, he remains optimistic his hand-picked quarterback from the 2024 NFL Draft can revert back to prior playing form. “Like I said to him ‘man, you’re the guy we want here. Let’s go. You’ve done a ton of things well.’ But I think there’s a lot that goes into that. In that old TBS series The Bear , where they say, ‘just let it rip.’ I want him to make sure that we can let it rip.”

title: Broncos Will Lutz cause for concern?
summary: While most of Broncos Country has been wringing their hands over the offensive play of the 2026 Denver Broncos, there has been another area of growing concern in Denver. What is up with Will Lutz? Lutz joined the Broncos as one of the handful of Saints players that followed coach Sean Payton over from the […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Wil Lutz #3 of the Denver Broncos looks during the game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images While most of Broncos Country has been wringing their hands over the offensive play of the 2026 Denver Broncos, there has been another area of growing concern in Denver. What is up with Will Lutz? Lutz joined the Broncos as one of the handful of Saints players that followed coach Sean Payton over from the New Orleans Saints in 2023. While in New Orleans, he was 195 of 169 field goals attempted clocking in at 84.6%. His time in Denver has been an improvement, making 97 of his 111 attempts for an 87.4% success rate. However, this season he has not continued on that trajectory, making 8 of 11, for a much diminished 72.7% make rate. Against the Rams, Lutz missed a 43-yarder in the 1st quarter. His 58-yard attempt against the 49ers in the 4th quarter was no good. Then, on Sunday against the Chargers, his 42-yard attempt could not find the uprights. While it’s still relatively early in the season, things are not trending well for a franchise that has high expectations for kickers. Denver has had a wealth of clutch kickers over the years. While in Denver, ring of fame kicker Jason Elam averaged 80.6% of his kicks. Matt Prater hit 82.9% of his kicks. Brandon McManus was solid for 81.4% of his kicks. While those numbers are less than the 87% Lutz mustered last season, these guys were also known for crushing the big kick when it mattered most. Jason Elam tied the NFL record at the time with a kick 0f 63-yards and McManus set the record at the time of 64-yards. Matt Prater didn’t set a record for kicking in Denver, but turned in a killer 61-yard field goal in 2021. Will Lutz’s career longest field goal was 60-yards back in 2022 and with Denver, hasn’t hit one longer than 57-yards. Simply put, if you don’t have the leg to make those big time kicks, you need to at least be consistent. If these first 5 games are any indication, concern over Will Lutz leg is becoming more and more justified. Is it a momentary blip on an otherwise solid career or is it a sign of yet another unforeseen challenge these Denver Broncos will have to overcome this season? More importantly, if it does continue at this rate, will Sean Payton have the wherewithal to make appropriate adjustments? Broncos Country will have to wait and see.

title: Discussion: What changes do the Detroit Lions need to make after their bye week?
summary: The Detroit Lions bye week is upon us after five weeks of up-and-down football. The team enters the break on a high after trouncing the Arizona Cardinals 45-21 on Sunday, but there is still room for improvement across the roster and coaching staff. The bye week is an opportunity to get healthy and get reinforcements, […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on during the fourth quarter against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions bye week is upon us after five weeks of up-and-down football. The team enters the break on a high after trouncing the Arizona Cardinals 45-21 on Sunday, but there is still room for improvement across the roster and coaching staff. The bye week is an opportunity to get healthy and get reinforcements, and the Lions will surely benefit from the return of Brian Branch and Cade Mays to the lineup, among others. However, the bye is also a time to reflect on what has and has not worked early in the season. An NFL season is a marathon and not a sprint, so any lessons they can take from their early slate of games can be used to improve down the stretch. What aspect of the Lions is in need of a change after the bye? Today’s Question of the Day is: What changes do you want to see from the Detroit Lions after their bye week? My answer: I want to see the offense be more efficient and effective in the first quarter. There is no shortage of improvements that Detroit needs to make. Their secondary needs to maintain the level of play they had versus the Cardinals. The linebackers need to improve in coverage, especially against tight ends. The team in general needs to clean up their execution and reduce their number of false starts, holds, delay of games, and illegal formation. One avenue that I think the Lions can and should improve upon is their first quarter scoring. Through five weeks, the Lions have scored an absurd 164 points, all without a defensive or special teams touchdown. Surprisingly, only 10 of those points have come in the first quarter. They scored a touchdown on their second drive versus the New Orleans Saints in Week 1. They were shut out against the Buffalo Bills and New York Jets in Weeks 2 and 3. They mustered a lone field goal against the Carolina Panthers in Week 4. Against the Cardinals in Week 5, they started with back-to-back-to-back three-and-outs. It is a testament to how good this offense can be that they are scoring this many points despite essentially punting away the first quarter. In contrast, the Lions have scored 57 points in the second quarter, 45 points in the third quarter, and 52 points in the fourth quarter and overtime—that is a staggering difference. What is causing the slow starts? Are crowds hyped up early in the game and causing poor communication? That is perhaps an answer for the Buffalo game, but Detroit has also had two home games, one of which featured their only first quarter touchdown. I would not say that travel is the cause. Neither would I say that chemistry or offensive scheme is the issue. Despite some shuffling of the offensive line, the blocking up front has been largely effective and cohesive, especially compared to 2025. As for play calling, Drew Petzing can clearly get the offense operating at an elite level, but for some reason it takes a quarter for things to start rolling. I think the recurring trend is a negative play causing the offense to stall: Versus the Saints, two of their first quarter drives ended in punts after suffering some type of loss: a loss of three on third-and-1 killed the first drive and the second was hampered by a holding penalty on first down. Versus the Bills, the Lions gave up two sacks and a botched snap on the first two drives. Versus the Jets, Jared Goff was again sacked twice over the opening pair of drives. Versus the Panthers, their first two drives stalled due to holding penalties on first down, though they managed to end the first drive with a field goal. Versus the Cardinals, Goff was sacked on each of the first three drives en route to a three-and-out. There is a very clear trend: if the Lions offense falls behind the sticks due to a negative play, whether self-inflicted or not, they sputter. Penalties should be correctable, but the Lions are being particularly hurt by sacks allowed. Across their five games this season, the Lions have only scored 10 points on a drive in which Goff was sacked: a field goal versus the Saints in the fourth quarter and a touchdown versus the Bills in the dying minutes of the game. Simply put, getting sacked early in the game is killing drives. The despite the sacks allowed, I think blame is not solely on the starting offensive line or Goff. There is a myriad of reasons why the sacks have been happening. Backup Larry Borom was on ice skates versus the Bills. Opponents have been springing well-timed blitzes. Routes have been slow to develop or simply smothered by good coverage. If the Lions offense can clean up their procedural mistakes and minimize these early-game stumbles, imagine how much more threatening this team could be. Though the defense played well versus Arizona, there is still a legitimate question about how effective they will be against better competition. One way to help out the defense is to keep them off the field for as long as possible. Another way to help out is to simply score early and score often. I think that the Lions offense has the ceiling to do both. What do you want to see the Lions clean up during the bye? Join the conversation. Join the conversation! title: 27 kick, punt returner options for the Detroit Lions to replace Tom Kennedy
summary: The Detroit Lions will be on a hunt for special teams reinforcements. Returner Tom Kennedy suffered a knee injury against the Arizona Cardinals that will sideline him for the entire 2026 season. It is a brutal blow to both player and team. For Kennedy, he had been a mainstay on the Lions’ practice squad since […]
full_text: Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) returns a punt against the Arizona Cardinals during a game at State Farm Stadium in Glendale on Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions will be on a hunt for special teams reinforcements. Returner Tom Kennedy suffered a knee injury against the Arizona Cardinals that will sideline him for the entire 2026 season . It is a brutal blow to both player and team. For Kennedy, he had been a mainstay on the Lions’ practice squad since 2019 (back in the Matt Patricia days), but 2026 was his best opportunity to establish a permanent roster spot for himself. After a solid start to the season as a kickoff and punt return, he now heads to the Injured Reserve. As for the Lions, they now have to do some scouting for his replacement. Kennedy had 15 returns thus far in 2026, and Detroit will need someone to replace that productivity. Will their new returner come from the active 53-man roster? Will they elevate someone from the practice squad? Or will they search for external options in the form of free agents or practice squaders? Let us examine some of the tires that Detroit could kick in the coming days. Internal Active roster: Tay Martin: limited punt return experience (two in college, zero in the UFL or NFL), no kickoff returns Amon-Ra St. Brown: has experience as a punt returner in college (19 returns for 107) and is the Lions’ emergency punt return option (he had two punt returns versus the Cardinals after Kennedy’s injury) Isaac TeSlaa: zero kickoff or punt return experience at any level Jameson Williams: zero punt returns in college or NFL, but had a role as a kickoff returner in 2021 at Alabama (10 returns for 352 yards and two touchdowns) Jahmyr Gibbs: zero punt returns in college or NFL, but was a frequent kickoff returner at Georgia Tech and Alabama (44 returns for 1052 yards and one touchdown) Jacob Saylors: one of Detroit’s current kickoff returners (13 returns for 338 yards), but zero experience returning punts at any level Sione Vaki: limited experience as a kickoff returner in college (one return) and NFL (four returns), no experience as a punt returner Khalil Dorsey: has 16 career kickoff returns, though none since 2024 Of these internal options, St. Brown has the most experience returning punts and has shown the ability to do damage (he had a 31-yard return against the Cardinals). However, given his importance to the offense, do the Lions want to risk him on special teams? Dan Campbell himself said he does not want St. Brown back there for most of the game. The same can be said about Gibbs and Williams at kick returner: sure, they could be electric returners, but trotting them out on what is typically a violent-yet-unimportant play might be ill-advised. As for Vaki and Dorsey, they might have more value on special teams as blockers and tacklers than returners. Lions practice squad: Lucky Jackson: one punt return in college, but had 13 punt returns for 153 yards in the UFL in 2026. Also had one kickoff return in the UFL for 23 yards Lawrence Keys: recorded 18 punt returns for 229 yards and 39 kickoff returns for 942 yards across two UFL seasons Dominic Lovett: one punt return in college; was involved in kick return competition in training camp this year Jabari Small: two preseason kickoff returns with the Lions in 2025 and 2026, zero punt returns The name that stands out the most on this list is Keys, who not only has significant experience returning both kickoffs and punts, but also has recent experience returning kickoffs and punts. It is worth remembering that the UFL pioneered the dynamic kickoff that the NFL eventually adopted and adapted. Keys has played in that format before, whereas players like Gibbs or Williams (with college experience) have not. External Free agents: Jabrill Peppers: 87 punt returns and 34 kickoff returns since being drafted in 2017. However, he has not had a return since 2023 Tyreek Hill: has been an electric player since being drafted in 2016 (13,681 all-purpose yards and five return touchdowns), but has been marred by injury and legal issues Raheem Mostert: significant kickoff return experience (76 returns for 1,846 yards), but no punt returns and is currently 34 years old Taysom Hill: multifaceted weapon on offense and special teams and has crossover with Dan Campbell from their time with the New Orleans Saints, but is currently 36 years old and has just six kickoff returns since 2019 Tyler Lockett: formerly an elite returner (three-time All-Pro with 130 punt returns and 112 kickoff returns from 2015 to 2018), but has not returned a kick since 2022 and is currently 34 years old Caullin Lacy: 2026 undrafted rookie who was waived with an injury settlement by the New York Jets. Recorded 86 punt returns and 34 kickoff returns in college Cedrick Wilson: Wilson shined as a receiver in preseason with the Lions but suffered a knee injury and ended up on Injured Reserve. However, he was released with an injury settlement on August 26, meaning that he would be eligible to re-sign after the settlement period plus three weeks elapses. Wilson has 37 career punt returns and three kickoff returns, but he did not see any action there in preseason. While I think it would be worth checking on the injury status of Lacy and Wilson, none of the other players stand out. Experience is unquestionably important, but age is a factor working against most of these names. Most of the younger and/or experienced returners are signed to active or practice squad rosters—the ones that are leftover are available for a reason. Practice squads: A.J. Henning (MIA): 79 punt returns and 33 kickoff returns in college with Michigan (2020-2022) and Northwestern (2023-2024) Gage Larvadain (BAL): 24 punt returns for 167 yards with the Cleveland Browns in 2025 as an undrafted rookie James Proche (CLE): veteran punt returner with 68 career punt returns for 591 yards Trebor Peña (JAX): 2026 undrafted rookie, recorded 63 punt returns and 37 kickoff returns over a six-year college career Kolbe Katsis (DEN): 2026 undrafted rookie, recorded three punt returns for 39 yards (including a 28-yarder) and four kickoff returns for 107 yards after being elevated for Denver’s Week 3 game Deven Thompkins (LV): undersized (5-foot-8 and 155 pounds) but has 91 combined punt and kickoff returns since 2022 Dylan Drummond (ATL): former undrafted rookie with the Lions in 2023. Limited professional experience (four kickoff returns in 2025) but had 21 punt returns and 18 kickoff returns in college at Eastern Michigan Xavier Smith (SF): Smith was the Rams’ starting returner from 2024 to 2026 but was waived on October 2. Though he has ample experience as a returner (43 punt returns and 19 kickoff returns), he garnered some infamy for muffing two punts in the Rams’ 2025 NFC Championship loss, one of which set up the Seattle Seahawks deep in Rams territory and wound up costing Los Angeles the game Practice squad poaching could be an option for the Lions, especially since the injury to Kennedy will open up a roster spot. There is a mix of veterans and youngsters for Detroit to contemplate, and there is no necessarily right approach. Out of these players, I would pay the most attention to Thompkins and Katsis. Thompkins has enough professional experience that he could slot in instantly without missing a beat. As for Katsis, he did have a muffed punt offset by a penalty, but Broncos special teams coordinator Darren Rizzi—a veteran coordinator who overlapped with Dan Campbell in Miami and New Orleans— remained optimistic about Katsis’ potential as a returner . Verdict The Lions have many avenues to explore, but I think the likeliest option is to promote internally. I do not want to risk injuring a player like St. Brown or Gibbs on special teams despite the potential upside. Therefore, given the lack of alternatives on the active roster, I think the best choice is to sign someone from the practice squad. That person is…

title: Detroit Lions expected to lose WR/RET Tom Kennedy to season-ending injury
summary: Detroit Lions wide receiver/returner Tom Kennedy’s 2026 season is almost certainly over, as NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reports that the Lions returner is expected to undergo surgery to repair an MCL injury suffered in Week 5: “Tom Kennedy suffered a significant MCL injury that is expected to require surgery and will end his season […] Dan […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 04: Tom Kennedy #85 of the Detroit Lions runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Ford Field on December 4, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Detroit Lions wide receiver/returner Tom Kennedy’s 2026 season is almost certainly over, as NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reports that the Lions returner is expected to undergo surgery to repair an MCL injury suffered in Week 5: “Tom Kennedy suffered a significant MCL injury that is expected to require surgery and will end his season […] Dan Campbell was hopeful Kennedy’s absence would be shorter but further testing revealed the extent of the damage.” In the first half of the Lions game against the Arizona Cardinals, Kennedy returned a punt and was awkwardly tackled, pinning his right knee under the Cardinals player. He was originally listed as questionable to return, but after halftime, he was declared out, as the early test did not look great, according to Lions coach Dan Campbell . “It doesn’t look good, as far as anything short-term,” Campbell said. “We’ll know a lot more tomorrow. I think it could be a sprain somewhere in there–a pretty good sprain.” Those follow-up tests Monday morning led to the diagnosis Garafolo reported and the speculation that he won’t play again this season. Kennedy was the Lions’ primary punt and kick returner, and there is no clear answer for who will replace him in those roles. Starting wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown took over emergency punt return duties, but the Lions won’t want to subject him to the extra punishment that comes with the role and will likely need a different option. On kick returns, cornerback Khalil Dorsey was the emergency option to line up opposite Jacob Saylors, and his speed and experience could keep him in play as a replacement. Dorsey does not have NFL experience as a punt returner, so he likely is not in the running for that position. With the Lions headed into a bye week, and Kennedy’s injury being season-ending, they can take their time before placing him on injured reserve and finding a replacement. Stay tuned to Pride of Detroit for updates on this situation as it unfolds.
