title: Detroit Lions Week 5 snap counts: Keith Abney adds range to Secondary
summary: The Detroit Lions got back to their winning ways in Arizona, handily defeating the Cardinals 45-21. The Lions got off to a slow start, falling behind 7-0 in the first quarter, but they responded with 24 consecutive points in the second quarter, along with five consecutive three-and-outs forced by the defense. The Lions scored another […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Keith Abney II #6 of the Detroit Lions intercepts a pass during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions got back to their winning ways in Arizona, handily defeating the Cardinals 45-21. The Lions got off to a slow start, falling behind 7-0 in the first quarter, but they responded with 24 consecutive points in the second quarter, along with five consecutive three-and-outs forced by the defense. The Lions scored another touchdown on their first offensive possession of the second half, and it was pretty much a wrap from there. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 63 (95%) Josh Dobbs: 3 (5%) Goff was once again terrific. His efficiency was impressive, registering a 125.8 passer rating (he averages 111.3 for the season, third-best in the NFL), and his 271 passing yards vault him to the top of the NFL passing yards list (save for the results of Monday Night Football). Here’s coach Dan Campbell on Goff’s performance: “Goff is just Goff. He’s as good as they come. I’ve just been so impressed with the way he’s played these five games here. I thought he’s just gotten better every year, and here we are five in, and he’s even better than last year. He’s the real deal.” Dobbs got in the game for the final drive, after the Lions pulled their starters, but he didn’t attempt a pass and simply handed the ball off to Sione Vaki three times to run the clock. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 46 (70%) Sione Vaki: 23 (35%) — 21 special teams snaps (66%) Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 21 (66%) With the Cardinals’ run defense checking in fourth in DVOA, most analysts didn’t anticipate the Lions working hard to establish their rushing attack. While it wasn’t perfect early, the offensive line leaned on the Cardinals’ front, and Gibbs gashed them for chunk yards, amassing 151 rushing yards on 25 carries, while Vaki added another 11, and Goff earned a yard on a goal-line QB sneak for a score. Gibbs also caught five receptions for 56 receiving yards, and probably could have had more had the Lions not started scaling his touches back late in the game. Both Gibbs and Vaki were also very solid in their pass-protection roles as well. Long developing plays like this do not work unless you have great blocking. The OL does a great job and just watch Vaki. pic.twitter.com/yJvglhYdwr — Talking Grit: Detroit Lions Podcast (@talkinggritpod) October 12, 2026 Wide receiver Jameson Williams: 59 (89%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: 57 (86%) Isaac TeSlaa: 26 (39%) Tay Martin: 3 (5%) — 21 (66%) Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 4 (12%) — INJURED St. Brown fumbled twice in this game (the Lions recovered both), once on offense and once on his first punt return after taking over for an injured Kennedy, but Goff never lost his trust in the All-Pro, who led the team with 11 targets and six receptions. Williams caught only two of his four targets, but both went for long touchdowns and helped open things up for the rest of the offense. Martin was once again stellar on special teams. He recovered St. Brown’s fumble and downed a Jack Fox punt inside the five-yard line. The unfortunate news from this group came via injury, as Kennedy looks like he’ll miss some time, according to Campbell: “It doesn’t look good. As far as anything short-term, we’ll know a lot more tomorrow. I think it could be a sprain somewhere in there – a pretty good sprain. Neither one of them (Kennedy and LB Devin White) are going to be around here for a while so I hate that. Both players have done a really good job for us. “‘TK’ I really thought he really hit it. We challenged him on hitting some of these returns. His first was outstanding, and I thought his second one – he caught it, put his foot in the ground, and he took it to heart. I hate it for him that (it) happened. I don’t think it’s long-term — I think it is something where we’ll miss him for a little bit. We will see.” Tight end Sam LaPorta: 59 (89%) Brock Wright: 44 (67%) — 11 (34%) Tyler Conklin: 8 (12%) Jackson Meeks: DNP ( INACTIVE ) When the Lions were stuck in an offensive rut in the first quarter, LaPorta pulled them out, converting a tough fourth-down on the Lions’ first scoring drive and then scoring a touchdown on the next drive to help them gain momentum. Among the reserves, Wright saw his snaps increase as the Lions deployed more 12-personnel sets, while Conklin got the nod over Meeks, allowing the Lions to use more 13-personnel. Offensive line LG Christian Mahogany: 66 (100%) — 7 (21%) RT Blake Miller: 66 (100%) — 7 (22%) LT Penei Sewell: 63 (95%) C Juice Scruggs: 63 (95%) — 7 (22%) RG Tate Ratledge: 63 (95%) — 7 (22%) LT/6th OL: Larry Borom: 8 (12%) — 7 (22%) C Seth McLaughlin: 3 (5%) RG Miles Frazier: 3 (5%) LG Ben Bartch: DNP ( INJURED ) The Lions offensive line made a pass-blocking mistake on each of the Lions’ first two drives, causing them to stall, but they cleaned it up quickly and dominated the rest of the game. In the run game, they routinely moved bodies around, opening holes for Gibbs. Here’s more from Campbell: “We have a young (team). Our right tackle is young, our right guard is young, our left guard is young. So when your O-line has some youth in it, they have to continue to grow and you have to be able to trust if we get certain looks, or we get a curveball, (or) it’s 4th down. There’s a lot that goes into it, and I really feel like they’re growing. They did a heck of a job today.” On the final drive, the Lions rested Sewell, Scruggs, and Ratledge, letting Borom, McLaughlin, and Frazier fill in at left tackle, center, and right guard, respectively. Borom also saw the field in Jumbo packages as a sixth offensive lineman five times. With Aidan Hutchinson drawing doubles, McNeill is benefiting from single blocks and thriving. “We closed the pocket in and made some huge plays there. Just to get that many 3-and-outs back-to-back-to-back, and then you answer offensively — that’s the white squall. Here comes the massive wave that’s coming at you, and it felt that way a little bit, so that’s good.” Williams and Gill-Howard provide a solid complementary 1-2 punch opposite McNeill, while Onwuzurike could be in danger of losing reps to Wingo if he keeps making mistakes. In addition to creating opportunities for his teammates (like McNeill and Wonnum—who added two more sacks in this game), Hutchinson earned three more pressures and a key fourth-down stop, sacking Jacoby Brissett. title: Lions report card, grades: Secondary takes huge strides vs. Cardinals
summary: The Detroit Lions got back on track on Sunday afternoon with their most complete win of the season over the Arizona Cardinals. Here are my grades for each position in their convincing victory. Quarterback: A Jared Goff wasn’t electric against the Cardinals, but he also played pretty close to mistake-free football. He finished the game […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Roger McCreary #21 of the Detroit Lions breaks up a pass intended for Reggie Virgil #82 of the Arizona Cardinals during the second quarter of an NFL football game at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions got back on track on Sunday afternoon with their most complete win of the season over the Arizona Cardinals. Here are my grades for each position in their convincing victory. Quarterback: A Jared Goff wasn’t electric against the Cardinals, but he also played pretty close to mistake-free football. He finished the game with 271 yards, a season-high 9.0 yards per attempt, three passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown. He still has yet to turn the ball over this season, and has produced 13 total touchdowns. Hard to disagree with Dan Campbell here: “Goff is just Goff. He’s as good as they come. I’ve just been so impressed with the way he’s played these five games here. I thought he’s just gotten better every year, and here we are five in, and he’s even better than last year. He’s the real deal.” Running backs: A Jahmyr Gibbs was phenomenal again on Sunday. NextGenStats credited him with 10 missed tackles forced against the Cardinals, and it honestly felt like more. No one was getting him down on the first attempt. His 93 yards after contract was second most of any running back in Week 5, and his +2.0 rushing yards over expected per rush was sixth-best of the week. Perhaps most impressively, Gibbs (and Sione Vaki) were excellent in pass protection, which helped the Lions hit on some big plays. Long developing plays like this do not work unless you have great blocking. The OL does a great job and just watch Vaki. pic.twitter.com/yJvglhYdwr — Talking Grit: Detroit Lions Podcast (@talkinggritpod) October 12, 2026 Tight ends: A+ When the Lions offense looked like they were stuck in a rut, it was Sam LaPorta who pulled them out with an impressive fourth-down catch that kept their first touchdown drive alive. Then, when Detroit was behind the sticks on a third-and-11 on the next drive, his individual effort to turn it into a fourth-and-1 was impressive. And, of course, on the very next play he did this. There goes Sam pic.twitter.com/jWOW1mJVFT — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 11, 2026 LaPorta finished the game by catching all five of his targets for 88 yards and a score. I thought this was also quietly one of Brock Wright’s best games as a blocker, and the PFF grades seems to back that up (79.5 pass blocking, 57.1 run blocking). Wide receivers: B- It’s odd to see that on such a dominant day on offense, the Lions’ receivers caught just eight collective passes for 116 yards and two touchdowns. Jameson Williams was obviously hugely impactful with his two touchdown catches (on two total catches), but it was a down game from Amon-Ra St. Brown. He had at least one drop, fumbled the ball twice, and just wasn’t that impactful until later in the game. That said, screen passes to St. Brown were highly effective because he’s such a smart, patient player who knows how to follow his blocks. Offensive line: B The Lions’ offensive line still has some problems clocking blitzes and adjusting properly—which gives me quite a bit of concern for the upcoming Vikings game—but they settled into this game very nicely. After allowing a sack on each of the first three drives of the game, Goff was spotless the rest of the way. The run game was a bit inconsistent, and I feel like Gibbs bailed them out quite a bit, but against a very good Cardinals run defense, they battled and wore them down. There was definitely more good than bad with the offensive line, but there is still clearly room for improvement, as well. Defensive line: B Oddly, this felt like a bit of a down game for the defensive front, despite Detroit tallying five sacks against Jacoby Brissett. Detroit produced their lowest pressure rate of the season (27.8%) and second-fewest amount of pressures overall (15). Considering they faced 53 passing plays, they need to be better than that. However, Detroit’s run defense was phenomenal on the day. They stuffed a career-high 27.8% of rushes in this game, and produced the best EPA/rush mark of the season (-0.24). Or, in more traditional stats, 56 rushing yards and 3.1 yards per carry are stellar numbers that are actually inflated by a very late Brissett scramble for 18 yards. Without that run, Arizona managed just 38 yards on 17 carries (2.2 YPC). Linebackers: B+ The linebackers deserve a lot of the credit for that improved run defense, including a much more familiar-looking Jack Campbell. The Lions’ All-Pro linebacker tallied 11 tackles, including four defensive stops. Most impressive, though, was this unit’s coverage against the Cardinals. It certainly wasn’t perfect, but when lined up in man-coverage against a pair of very talented Cardinals tight ends, Detroit held their own. Both Campbell and Malcolm Rodriguez were forcing Trey McBride and Elijah Higgins to make seriously contested catches, which was a relieving sight after how much Detroit has struggled against tight ends this year. Secondary: B Well, well, well. It seems the Lions’ cornerbacks can actually cover. Roger McCreary posted a franchise-best six pass breakups against the Cardinals on a whopping 18 targets. D.J. Reed may have even been better. Although he managed just one pass breakup, he also allowed just 30 yards in seven targets. Both players were absolute forces in the run game, as well. Reed produced three tackles for loss, and both players ranked in the top 15 in run defense grades for cornerbacks this week (Reed: 74.7, 14th; McCreary: 79.6, fifth). Keith Abney seemed to provide some stability at safety, even if he didn’t make too many plays (was only targeted three times). But there are still too many blown coverages by this unit. It was a step in the right direction, but Detroit’s defensive backs need to continue to improve if they want to compete against better offenses. Special teams: A Just a stellar day from Dave Fipp’s crew. Detroit’s punt return game averaged 17.3 yards per return, with three of their four plays going for at least 10 yards. Kick return was solid with a 27.3 average on four Jacob Saylors attempts. And the coverage teams were outstanding, as well. Throw in another perfect day from Jake Bates, a late pinning by Jack Fox, and it’s hard to complain about literally anything from this group outside of St. Brown’s fumble. Coaching: A- It sure sounds like Dan Campbell and company really lit into the Lions player this week at practice , and it was nice to see them respond to it on the field—albeit about a quarter late. The slow starts are certainly concerning, but hard to pinpoint on what exactly is going wrong. But Detroit made some very logical coaching decision throughout the week that made sense. The move to more man coverage was something that I was calling for given the front-four’s success at generating pressure on their own. The numbers could update in the morning, but TruMedia had the Lions in man coverage on 31 percent of their snaps against the Cardinals. That was the fifth-highest man rate among teams that played this week. The Lions were at 15.6 percent from Weeks 1-4. — Colton Pouncy (@colton_pouncy) October 12, 2026 They also deserve credit for putting Abney’s rangy athleticism at the safety position, and benching Christian Izien’s too-inconsistent play. Throw in some great passing design plays, and Dan Campbell’s invaluable aggression (three fourth-down touchdowns), and I thought this was a much-needed, well-coached game.

title: Detroit Lions vs. Arizona Cardinals post-game reaction: Is Detroit fixed?
summary: The Detroit Lions are heading into the bye week after an emphatic win over the Arizona Cardinals. It was a convincing win, not just because they ended up winning by 24 points, but because literally every phase of the game shined on Sunday. The offense scored on seven straight drives. The defense held Arizona scoreless […]
full_text: Arizona Cardinals receiver Michael Wilson (14) just misses catching a pass while being defended by Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4) at State Farm Stadium in Glendale on Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions are heading into the bye week after an emphatic win over the Arizona Cardinals. It was a convincing win, not just because they ended up winning by 24 points, but because literally every phase of the game shined on Sunday. The offense scored on seven straight drives. The defense held Arizona scoreless on seven straight drives—including five consecutive three-and-outs. The return and coverage teams were outstanding on special teams. So on this week’s PODcast, we celebrated a little. It’s been a while since we’ve seen a complete game from the Lions, and it’s nice to bask in that glory for a minute. It’s much better than the alternative of heading into the bye week 2-3, craving for some heads on a platter. Then we dig into the nitty gritty of the game. What changes did the Lions make to find some success on defense? How did the Lions’ cornerbacks—specifically Roger McCreary and D.J. Reed—suddenly look like top-tier coverage defenders? And what successes were offensive coordinator Drew Petzing able to find? We also look at the bigger picture of this team. While this was a good game, how will they look when they face a tougher Packers offense next game? What will Detroit do with the secondary when Brian Branch returns? And what the heck’s the deal with these slow starts on offense? We tackle it all on this week’s PODcast, which you can listen to on any podcasting platform you enjoy by searching “Pride of Detroit.” We’ve also made it easy for you by embedding this week’s episode below: You can always catch the video version of the PODcast—the live version with bonus content—over on our YouTube channel and Twitch pages .

title: Injury updates: Detroit Lions lose 2 players to potential significant injuries
summary: The Detroit Lions got off to a slow and tough start against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. Not only did they fall behind 7-0 in a hurry, but two Lions players also went to the locker room with injuries. While Detroit managed to rebound on the field in a big way, it wasn’t great news […]
full_text: Detroit Lions punt returner Tom Kennedy (85) celebrates a run against Arizona Cardinals during the first half at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions got off to a slow and tough start against the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. Not only did they fall behind 7-0 in a hurry, but two Lions players also went to the locker room with injuries. While Detroit managed to rebound on the field in a big way, it wasn’t great news for the two injured players. First was linebacker Devin White. It wasn’t clear how White, who was active for the first time since Week 2, suffered his injury, but he was listed as questionable to return with a forearm. The FOX broadcast showed him taking a cart to the locker room. Unfortunately, coach Dan Campbell confirmed after the game that White suffered a broken forearm that will likely necessitate surgery. “I think Devin’s probably going to need surgery. It’s a broken forearm; it’s unfortunate. I hate it because he was doing some good things for us in this game,” Campbell said. In White’s absence, the Lions split LB3 snaps between Malcolm Rodriguez (23 snaps) and Trevor Nowaske (9). Shortly thereafter, Lions punt returner Tom Kennedy suffered a knee injury on a return in which his foot was caught in the ground and his body was bent awkwardly. Kennedy was initially able to walk to the sidelines and was treated in the blue tent. However, eventually, he was carted to the locker room. The Lions officially listed him as questionable to return with a knee injury before downgrading him to out in the second half. Campbell said they’ll know more about his condition on Monday after more tests, but the expectation is he will miss significant time, too. “It doesn’t look good, as far as anything short-term,” Campbell said. “We’ll know a lot more tomorrow. I think it could be a sprain somewhere in there – a pretty good sprain. Neither one of them are going to be around here for a while so I hate that.” He later added, regarding Kennedy, “I don’t think it’s long, long-term — I think it is something where we’ll miss him for a little bit. We will see.” On the subsequent punt, Amon-Ra St. Brown was the returner for Detroit, and fumbled the ball, but the Lions recovered. He’s unlikely to serve as Detroit’s full-time punt returner, so we’ll have to wait and see how Detroit responds. In kick return, it was cornerback Khalil Dorsey who took Kennedy’s spot.

title: Discussion: How much better do you feel about the Lions after their blowout win over Cardinals?
summary: After the first quarter of the Detroit Lions’ Week 5 matchup against the Arizona Cardinals, we were staring into the abyss. Detroit was outgained 84 yards to -9 after the first 15 minutes, and it looked like we were headed for some major changes. I won’t lie. I even considered if this was the beginning […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta (87) makes a catch defended by Arizona Cardinals linebacker Mack Wilson Sr. (1) during the fourth quarter at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Matt Kartozian-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After the first quarter of the Detroit Lions’ Week 5 matchup against the Arizona Cardinals, we were staring into the abyss. Detroit was outgained 84 yards to -9 after the first 15 minutes, and it looked like we were headed for some major changes. I won’t lie. I even considered if this was the beginning of the end for the entire regime. But the rest of the game told a completely different story. The Lions offense scored on their next seven possessions, including six touchdowns. The Lions defense forced five consecutive three-and-outs and seven scoreless drives in a row. It was a complete and utter beatdown for the remaining 45 minutes, and it’s the best the Lions have looked all year by a country mile. But how much does it mean? How many of Detroit’s problems seem solved vs. how much was this just beating up on a bad Cardinals team? Today’s Question of the Day is: How are you feeling about the Lions after their blowout win over the Cardinals? My answer: I would say a little to a lot better. It’s impossible to know whether Detroit’s defensive success will carry over to future games. I find it hard to believe that they are suddenly going to be a top-half-of-the-league defense all of a sudden. Certainly, they won’t find as much success against teams with deeper wide receiver rooms and better quarterbacks. They’ll have a much bigger test out of the bye with a Green Bay Packers team that isn’t afraid to air it out deep. However, I’m not going to discount the possibility the Lions may have figured some things out. The entire defense looked far more comfortable in more man-heavy coverage looks. The back-end settled down considerably with rookie Keith Abney manning one of the safety spots. And say what you will about how bad the Cardinals are, there isn’t a single team so far that has held them to five straight three-and-outs. Hell, the undefeated 49ers defense only held them to two three-and-outs all game. In terms of Detroit’s run defense, they held the Cardinals to their lowest success rate (22.2%), second-lowest EPA/run (-0.24), and highest stuffed rate (27.8%) of the season—even after playing the Seahawks and 49ers defense. Arizona hadn’t been sacked more than twice in a game, and the Lions got to Jacoby Brissett five times. Point being, even as bad as the Cardinals are, Detroit beat them more handily than just about anyone this year, and that counts for something. I haven’t even touched on the offense, which managed to brush off a dreadful start to put together their most complete game of the year, as well. Not only did offensive coordinator Drew Petzing find some solutions in the passing game, but Detroit penetrated what had been a pretty successful run defense from the Cardinals all year. The Lions’ +0.10 EPA/rush, six rushes of 10+ yards, and +1.38 rushing yards over expected per attempt were all season highs allowed by Arizona this season. So, yes, the Lions played a crappy Cardinals team. But they played them better—or at least as well—as some of the best teams in the NFL. Going into the bye week, I couldn’t have really asked for more from one single game. So I’ll say I’m feeling a lot better. What about you?
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Packers’ next opponent hires Mike Pettine, former Green Bay coordinator
summary: The struggling Dallas Cowboys have hired former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Mike Pettine to help right the ship. The Cowboys’ defense is allowing 27.2 points per game this season and has allowed a passer rating of 120.5 against, the worst mark in the NFL through five weeks of NFL action. First-time defensive coordinator Christian […]
full_text: (Photo by Jeff Haynes /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) The struggling Dallas Cowboys have hired former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Mike Pettine to help right the ship. The Cowboys’ defense is allowing 27.2 points per game this season and has allowed a passer rating of 120.5 against, the worst mark in the NFL through five weeks of NFL action. First-time defensive coordinator Christian Parker, who got his start in the NFL as a defensive quality control coach with the Packers in 2019, was originally hired by Pettine, who was retained in Green Bay’s head coach transition from Mike McCarthy to Matt LaFleur. Since leaving Green Bay in 2021, when Parker was hired by the Denver Broncos, he has spent most of his time in the Vic Fangio tree, spending the 2021-2023 seasons with Denver and the 2024-2025 seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles. Notably, Pettine’s defense, which is more man-coverage-heavy than the Fangio tree, is a bit different from Parker’s background. The Cowboys have some extra time to practice this week, as the team is coming off a Thursday Night Football loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. We’ll see if that extra rest and the addition of Pettine can help Dallas when they make the trip to Green Bay for their upcoming Sunday Night Football matchup.

title: Packers have no league updates on Josh Jacobs’ situation
summary: Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur stated on Monday that the team has not received any updates regarding running back Josh Jacobs’ status. Jacobs pleaded no contest to charges of battery and criminal damage to property, stemming from an incident that involved his then-girlfriend. At the moment, the NFL has Jacobs on the commissioner […]
full_text: (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur stated on Monday that the team has not received any updates regarding running back Josh Jacobs’ status. Jacobs pleaded no contest to charges of battery and criminal damage to property, stemming from an incident that involved his then-girlfriend. At the moment, the NFL has Jacobs on the commissioner exempt list, with no timetable for his return, as the league investigates the incident and attempts to receive evidence from the case — including video from Jacobs’ garage. That video is currently being discussed as potentially being permanently sealed, a decision that will ultimately come down to the Hobart-Lawrence police department. Beyond the Jacobs of it all, LaFleur also noted that edge defender Micah Parsons will not practice this week, as he has not been cleared by the medical staff. Apparently, the issue right now is making sure that Parsons’ legs are equally as strong as each other, to avoid a future injury. LaFleur also stated on Monday that he believes that defensive lineman Jordon Riley, who tore his Achilles last season, is “pretty close” to returning to the team and that defensive lineman Anthony Campbell will “get rolling this week.” The defensive line depth is becoming an increasing concern for Green Bay — not because of the unit’s performance so far this year, but because the team has had two players poached at the position and has had two major injuries to Warren Brinson and Javon Hargrave. Brinson is currently on the injured reserve, while Hargrave tore his Achilles and is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season. Riley is currently on the physically unable to perform list, while Campbell missed last week’s action due to injury. Right now, there are only four healthy players at the position on the Packers’ 53-man roster, and the team usually goes into games with five players (or more) on the interior defensive line.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers By The Numbers: Stats from the Week 5 win over the Bears
summary: As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports. Today we’re looking at the 31-7 victory over the Chicago Bears in Week 5. Offense Last week we saw a drastic decrease in the Packers usage of 11 personnel (1 RB, […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) passes the ball against the Chicago Bears on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Packers won the game, 31-7. Tork Mason/Green Bay Press-Gazette | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports . Today we’re looking at the 31-7 victory over the Chicago Bears in Week 5. Offense Last week we saw a drastic decrease in the Packers usage of 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR), and a big uptick in their usage of 13 personnel (1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR). Their usage of 11 jumped a bit from last week, but this feels more like the area they want to live in if given the opportunity. Here was the Packers personnel usage this week: The running game was still churning out negative numbers no matter which personnel grouping they were in, but their passing game was positive EPA in every grouping they trotted out. It’s worth noting that most running offenses post a negative EPA per Play. The Packers posted a rush EPA per Play of -0.09 in both 11 & 12 personnel, which would put them 20th in the league. They posted a 50% Success Rate when running out of 12 personnel, which is a very good rate. In terms of Success Rate, their 12 and 13 personnel packages were doing work in the passing game. They posted a 70% success rate in 12 and 50% in 13. I don’t need to tell you all, but Jordan Love was chucking the ball. He averaged 2.54 seconds to throw. He was still operating off a quick release (his average time to throw in 2025 was 2.89 seconds), but 2.54 seconds is something that can resemble a functional offense. (For reference on that time to throw, Aaron Rodgers had the fastest time to throw in 2025 and he averaged 2.59 seconds to throw. So it could be better, but, based on how the first few weeks went, I’ll take 2.54 seconds.) OH MY GOSH 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/qyqGYPEsIB — Green Bay Packers (@packers) October 11, 2026 Loved turned in an absolutely absurd game when throwing deep. Look at those numbers, man. They’re beautiful. He was also very good against the blitz. When blitzed, Love was 8/10 for 130 yards (+0.6 EPA per Play). When not blitzed, he was 17/21 for 237 yards (+0.43 EPA per Play). He was absolutely shredding this week, man. Their run/pass ratio on the game looked a lot like last season. For the game, they were passing 55.9% of the time, but that’s in part due to taking the air out of the ball in the 4th quarter. They came out relatively conservative (52.6% pass rate in the 1st quarter), cranked up the rate in the 2nd quarter (77.8%), kept their foot on the gas in the 3rd quarter (75%), then throttled down the pass rate in the 4th quarter (26.7%). Even then, they didn’t truly let off the gas until midway through the 4th. They opened the 4th with a 66.7% pass rate and didn’t go run-heavy until there was 8:26 left in the game, holding a 31-7 lead (it’s worth noting that they broke a 23 yard run after winding down the game). That’s how I’d like to see them operate. Set some stuff up in the 1st, attack in the middle quarters, then finish the game off. Zero complaints with the run/pass mix this week. Let’s talk receivers because, buddy, they were putting on a show. Christian Watson caught 6 of his 8 targets for 143 yards and 2 TDS (+1.29 EPA per Reception). Matthew Golden caught 6 of his 7 targets for 123 yards (+1.08 EPA per Reception). We also saw Tucker Kraft show up, catching all 5 of his targets for 64 yards (+0.62 EPA per Reception), with 38 yards after the catch. Defense You know who else showed up? My guy Dani Dennis-Sutton. 😤 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/4X3w0n5gFg — Green Bay Packers (@packers) October 11, 2026 He posted a 25% pressure rate, with a 50% pressure rate on stunts (34.8% above the NFL average). When he’s been on the field he has looked like a monster. In terms of personnel, the Packers primarily lived in Nickel in this game (85.3% Nickel, 13.2% Base, 1.5% Dime). That makes sense given the Bears approach in this game. Here is their personnel breakdown: The Packers dialed down their blitz rate significantly in this game, choosing instead to drop back into coverage. After being pretty blitz-heavy through the first 4 weeks, the Packers only blitzed on 14.9% of dropbacks this week, 15.2% below NFL average. Despite that, they generated pressure on 40.4% of dropbacks, +0.58% above NFL average. That pressure rate was more due to forcing the QB to hold the ball than anything else. Their quick pressure rate of 17% was 2.9% below NFL average. For the QBs, Tyson Bagent averaged 2.67 seconds to throw while Case Keenum averaged 2.92 seconds to throw. full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Zaire Franklin #44 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates after a play during the third quarter of the NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears talked a big game heading into their Week 5 matchup with the Green Bay Packers. That didn’t exactly work out well for them when the two teams actually played their game on Sunday afternoon. The Packers dropped bomb after bomb on the Bears’ defense as Jordan Love connected with Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, and Tucker Kraft in an impressive aerial display. When the dust cleared, the Packers emerged with a 31-7 win, pulling even with the Bears on record at 3-2 and earning an important early-season head-to-head win. After the game, a few Packers players made it clear that they didn’t appreciate the comments that they heard the Bears making during the offseason and during this week. And so they went out and did something about it — they worked on themselves during the week and attacked their opponent’s greatest weakness, the secondary. Love finished the day with the most passing yards by any Packers quarterback against the Bears in a Lambeau Field game, 369, and both Watson and Golden had more than 120 receiving yards. The defense cleaned up with five turnovers. And all in all, the team avoided the self-inflicted mistakes that have cost them wins this year. The two teams will meet again on Christmas Day. But for now, the Packers can be the ones to talk for a while — if they want to. title: Value of Things: In the Rearview Mirror
summary: These are happier times at least for the time being. Even our model for this particular piece changes as we slide over to great, good, and bad in lieu of good, bad, and ugly. The Texans defeated the Titans 26-3 in a game that felt competitive for all of one quarter. Furthermore, you were 7.5 […]
full_text: These are happier times at least for the time being. Even our model for this particular piece changes as we slide over to great, good, and bad in lieu of good, bad, and ugly. The Texans defeated the Titans 26-3 in a game that felt competitive for all of one quarter. Furthermore, you were 7.5 point favorites on the road which is practically a double digit line for an 0-4 football team. That probably tells you everything you need to know about the Tennessee Titans. They will be in a race with the Miami Dolphins for the first overall pick. So, this win feels good in the same way you feel good when you pass a first grade spelling test. You feel more relieved. At any rate, it was an infamous get right game in a lot of respects and that is particularly true on the defensive end. They generated multiple times for the first time on the season and also managed four sacks on the afternoon. It will help the bottom line as the aggregate now says that the Texans are a solid defense. Obviously, two of their games would say otherwise, but let’s take a look at the numbers from the game. The Key Numbers Total Yards: Texans 63/328, Titans 58/187 Rushing Yards: Texans 27/79, Titans 18/57 Passing Yards: Texans 36/249, Titans 40/130 Third Downs: Texans 6/12, Titans 4/11 Fourth Downs: Texans 0/0, Titans 0/2 Sacks: Texans 4, Titans 2 Turnovers: Texans 0, Titans 2 Penalties: Texans 11/95, Titans 7/83 Time of Possession: Texans 34:29, Titans 25:31 Of course, we will get into this in more detail throughout the week as the biggest news occurred away from the field on Sunday. This is the kind of game we could have predicted from the Texans. The Titans just aren’t good at football. They haven’t been good at football since they let Mike Vrabel walk for reasons. They are likely fighting for the number one overall pick with the Miami Dolphins. So, you do nothing but hold serve in this one. The Great Will Anderson is good at football. I’ve said that three weeks in a row now. He added three sacks in this one and he is making his quest to be the Defensive Player of the Year. He probably will have to put up a few more games like today to get into that conversation, but he is at the point where he is stacking great efforts back to back. Cam Ward wiggled out of three or four sacks on the afternoon or this could have been a historic effort from a defense we thought would be historic coming into the season. Yes, DeMeco Ryans was calling plays this time around, but we need to hold off before anointing this defense as back. This was a historically bad offense on the other side of the field. Still, they did what they were supposed to do. They smothered a weaker opponent and never let them get hope outside of an opening field goal. Those guys are paid to play football too, so you can’t simply just show up and have it happen. These guys clearly put in some work and it could be the first building block to getting back into the season. The Good C.J. Stroud now has his own section, so this one goes to Woody Marks. The numbers show he caught four balls for 23 yards and rushed 15 times for 62 yards. More importantly, it looks like he might be taking over as the featured back after David Montgomery’s groin injury. Sometimes, performance dictates a change and sometimes fate knocks you across the dome and you are forced to make a change. Four yards a carry won’t make anyone forget Arian Foster, but it is credible and credible is that the Texans are hoping for. You can acquire all of the wide receivers in the world, but if you don’t have a credible running game it really doesn’t matter. The Bad Nothing can be truly ugly in a 26-3 game, but we focus on things in victory we wouldn’t overlook in defeat. This team commits too many stupid penalties. One of them cost you a Woody Marks touchdown. These are things that slide by in a 26-3 win over a terrible football team. They don’t slide by when you are facing a team like the Glitter Kitties. It would be one thing if this were a one time thing, but this is a weekly occurrence. It is safe to say it has cost you at least one football game if not two. We would feel far differently at 2-3 or 3-2 than we currently do at 1-4. Focus on Stroud The stat sheet will say that Stroud was 26 for 34 with a 107.5 quarterback rating. That obviously raises both the completion percentage for the season but also the overall quarterback rating for the season. More importantly, this game was a sign that the team is slowly turning over the keys to the kingdom to Stroud. Naturally, that might not be a complete vote of confidence. It could be the total lack of a consistent running game, but adding a Marvin Harrison Jr. doubles down on that thought as they try to give him as many weapons (and one he is familiar with) as they possibly can. That tells me two things. First, they definitely have made up their mind about the future of the quarterback position as not only has he played well, but they are giving him more and more responsibility for this offense. Secondly, they brought in a familiar target because they want him to be happy. That recognizes that he had reason not to be.David Mulaghetta is not above shopping for new homes for his clients. A 2-15 or 3-14 season could have made Stroud and company think twice about committing to the Texans. Now, they see that they went out and got a buddy. Will that work? It remains to be seen, but it is a clear signal of where this offense is going.

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Colts’ performances from Week 5 loss at Pittsburgh
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (2-3) fell to the Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) on Sunday afternoon, 34-22, and the Horseshoe was simply outcoached, outplayed, and out-willed in a tough road environment where they haven’t won since 2008—with that franchise losing streak only continuing. Without dwelling on this latest loss, let’s take a look at some of the individual […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (2-3) fell to the Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) on Sunday afternoon, 34-22, and the Horseshoe was simply outcoached, outplayed, and out-willed in a tough road environment where they haven’t won since 2008—with that franchise losing streak only continuing. Without dwelling on this latest loss, let’s take a look at some of the individual highlights and lowlights: Horsepower PK Spencer Shrader: The Colts returning kicker has been arguably their best player through 5 games, and made all 5 of his field goal attempts in Pittsburgh, tying a Horseshoe franchise single-game record. In inclement weather conditions, these weren’t easy kicks either by any means, as Shrader’s makes included longs of 57 and 56 yards. You hate to kick 5 field goals in any game instead of scoring touchdowns offensively, but he’s been a huge special teams asset and most notably, from long distance as of late. TE Tyler Warren: Colts head coach Shane Steichen finally was able to get Warren unleashed a bit, who led the Indianapolis offense with a team-high 7 receptions for 83 total receiving yards, as well as a 1-yard fullback touchdown run on 4th and goal near midway through the second quarter. CB Sauce Gardner: This could’ve been one of the big bragging points for Colts fans—had Indianapolis actually been road warriors and won on Sunday. Steelers wideout DK Metcalf inexplicably pretended to not know who Gardner was prior to the game when speaking to the media , and Gardner limited the former to just 1 reception on 2 targets for 9 total receiving yards when matched up opposite one another in coverage. Gardner clearly had a rough outing in London, but bounced back in Pittsburgh in a big way. Unfortunately, the Colts couldn’t make enough plays to land the W. Horseplay Run Blocking : The Colts are a ‘run-first’ team with star running back Jonathan Taylor rushing to set up the pass, but Pittsburgh kept both running backs in check holding Taylor to a paltry 3.0 ypc avg. on 15 carries and rookie backup Seth McGowan to 3.2 ypc avg. on 5 carries as a change-of-pace. The Colts had a very challenging time consistently running the football effectively, as the Pittsburgh front seven was clearly committed to shutting down #28 first and foremost as their top priority in tough weather conditions. Colts Defense: Whether it was Aaron Rodgers initially starting a perfect 10 for 10 in pass attempts, throwing for 3 passing touchdowns to 0 interceptions, or Steelers running back Jaylen Warren making NFL history on the ground and through the air , it was collectively a miserable showing by the Colts already much maligned defense. There was hardly any edge pressure yet again, as the Colts had just one sack, and the Indianapolis run defense was gashed, allowing a whopping 6.7 ypc avg. to Warren on 15 carries—with his 50-yard, 3rd quarter touchdown run clearly boosting that number. The Colts struggling linebackers can’t cover middle of the field in pass coverage, the Indy pass pressure isn’t nearly consistent enough, and the Colts corners give up too easy of short throws with provided cushion. To me, it’s both a coaching and personnel issue for the Colts defensively, and it’s a fair question of whether they have the horses and juice right now to actually get it solved in-season. I don’t want to hear anymore about a lack of effort or ‘want to’ regarding tackling. We’re already 5 games in. If it hasn’t happened already, when will it?

title: Colts Monday Morning Awards: Week 5 @ Steelers
summary: After splitting the first four games of the regular season, the Indianapolis Colts got yet another reminder of the horrific performances that have been left at Arcisure Stadium in a 34-22 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. The Colts controlled the pace of play and scored on six of their nine true drives, but were forced […]
full_text: After splitting the first four games of the regular season, the Indianapolis Colts got yet another reminder of the horrific performances that have been left at Arcisure Stadium in a 34-22 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. The Colts controlled the pace of play and scored on six of their nine true drives, but were forced to settle for field goals as the offense could not capitalize inside the red zone and twice with goal-to-go. MVP of the Game: Spencer Shrader At this point, is there an argument for anyone other than Jonathan Taylor or Spencer Shrader who have been the Colts’ most valuable player this season? It’s getting much harder to dismiss, since Shrader is actually the league-leading scorer this season after collecting 58 points through five games. Shrader made all five of his field goal attempts Sunday, connecting from 57, 56, 22, 40 and 28 yards. Despite kicking on a wet field in windy conditions and one of the more difficult road environments in the league, Shrader was automatic from distance. His first 57-yarder gave Indianapolis its only lead and tied Steelers kicker Chris Boswell for the second-longest field goal ever made at Acrisure Stadium. Shrader has made all of his NFL-best 16 field goals through Week 5, including six from beyond 50 yards. Spencer Shrader has been PERFECT on field goals through five games this season. 🔹 16/16 Field Goals Made (100%) 🔹 6/6 from 50+ Yards 🔹 Longest: 58 Yards 🔹 58 Total Points Scored Is Shrader the best kicker in the NFL right now? — SleeperColts (@SleeperColts) October 12, 2026 Dud of the Game: Rushing Attack For the second consecutive season, running back Jonathan Taylor finished with 45 rushing yards against the Steelers. One of his 15 carries actually broke loose for 20 of those yards, so do the math. His other 14 carries produced just 25 combined yards. Pittsburgh made it difficult for Taylor to find any daylight, stuffing him three times near the goal line while constantly meeting him near the line of scrimmage. The offensive line deserves its share of the blame as Tanor Bortolini and Matt Goncalves particularly struggled against Pittsburgh’s Cameron Heyward and Yahya Black. Pittsburgh’s front-seven finished with four tackles for loss, three QB hits and a sack. When Taylor is restricted, the Colts lose their biggest offensive advantage. Daniel Jones completed 24 of 44 passes Sunday, and although he avoided turnovers, the offense could not capitalize starting with excellent field position or inside the red zone. Worst Play of the Game: Bryce Boettcher missed tackle results in 80-yard touchdown Indianapolis held a mere 3-0 lead for exactly one snap and it’s not the first brutal sequence where the defense was simply not prepared for the game speed their opponent was ready to strike with. Aaron Rodgers recognized the instant pressure and tossed a quick swing route to Jaylen Warren. Pittsburgh’s running back burst past the diving reach of rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher, who was left chasing the play as Jaylen Warren dashed down the sideline for an 80-yard touchdown to claim a 7-3 lead that Pittsburgh never relinquished. It was the ninth passing TD of 80-plus yards in the career of Rodgers, coincidentally tying fellow future NFL Hall of Famer Ben Roethlisberger for the most in NFL history. It was the fourth-longest offensive play of the NFL season through Week 5, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Sure, it was Warren longest catch this season, but it wasn’t even his longest play this season as he owns two of the top four longest plays in terms of total distance. Warren finished with 188 scrimmage yards, leading the game in both rushing and receiving. Mistakes are part of the learning curve, but the larger issue is that the Colts continue to give up explosive plays that require little effort from the opposing offense and demand an awful lot of chasing from behind. What was even more frustrating than a rookie mistake was DK Metcalf clearing a runway downfield by taking out both Charvarius Ward and Cam Bynum by himself as the lead blocker. One simple swing pass cannot result in a touchdown because the stampede failed to finish the play. Jaylen Warren was the engine of Pittsburgh’s offense against Indianapolis. 15 CAR, 101 RUSH YDS, 6 REC, 87 REC YDS, 2 TOTAL TD Warren helped Pittsburgh move to 3-2 and stay right in the thick of the AFC North race. pic.twitter.com/PJ6Zrma88E https://t.co/MPEVHWyg0p — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) October 11, 2026 Best Play of the Game: DeForest Buckner sack terminates drive After relying on another field goal from Shrader, the Colts needed a defensive stop late in the third quarter. DeForest Buckner used a wraparound stunt to sack Rodgers on third down and terminate Pittsburgh’s drive. Rodgers had less than three seconds before surrendering himself to Buckner inside his own 10-yard-line. It was sack No. 75 for the 11-year veteran, who has logged a tackle for loss in each of the last four games. Buckner finishing the sack was the type of disruptive interior pressure Indianapolis needs far more often. The Colts rank dead last with a 24% pressure rate, which is the only team with a sub-30% pressure rate, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Here comes Buck ‼️ 📺CBS pic.twitter.com/7g2K87xWwJ — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 11, 2026 Best Position Group: Special Teams Shrader did his part to ensure the special teams had another effective outing. He’s just the second player ever in NFL history to connect on at least 34 field goals through his first 14 games, joining Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker. That’s how stellar Shrader has been to start his young career. Over the last three weeks, Shrader has accounted for 59% of the Colts total scoring, so Indianapolis cannot keep asking its kicker to finish drives that its own offense should be driving into the end zone. Shrader wasn’t out there kicking alone to help the special teams. Anthony Gould returned two kickoffs for 81 combined return yards, including a career-long 54-yard return that helped set up the offense inside Steelers territory. Rookie Seth McGowan also returned a trio of kickoffs for 84 total return yards, with two of his returns leading to scoring drives. Unsung Hero: Tyler Warren Tyler Warren was another one of the bright spots delivering his best game of the season. He hauled in a season-high seven catches for 83 receiving yards, while adding a crucial rushing touchdown. His one-yard plunge into the end zone came while facing fourth-and-goal in the second quarter brought Indianapolis back within one point. Tyler Warren lines up like a fullback and gets the rushing touchdown @INDvsPIT on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ESC43z7DtA — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 The 2025 first round draft pick has become a reliable target for Jones. Warren’s four-game streak with at least five catches is the longest current streak among NFL tight ends. Through five games, Warren has 30 catches for 213 receiving yards and three total touchdowns. Rookie of the Week: AJ Haulcy A.J. Haulcy collected a career-high six combined tackles and forced a pass breakup. The third-round safety has been the most encouraging young player on a defense that needs to find some answers. Through five games, Haulcy has 21 combined tackles, while allowing a mere 25% completion rate on 16 targets, according to Pro Football Reference. Haulcy is getting opportunities and showing signs that he can become a meaningful part of the secondary. The same cannot be said for every member of the rookie class just yet. Haulcy benefited from claiming his starting job and has played 251 total defensive snaps, double the combined amount of snaps that rookie linebackers C.J. Allen and Bryce Boettcher have played through their first five games. Shrader is an immaculate kicker, better than anyone outside of the building could have anticipated. The Colts wasted multiple scoring opportunities from close range, couldn’t establish Taylor and…
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Colts have more questions than answers
summary: When watching games, I generally only have three or four things that I think are relevant enough to mention and I know that sometimes those overlap with what colleagues have written, or members have posted. My list is longer this week, containing at least nine bullet points that I’d like to bring up and discuss. […]
full_text: When watching games, I generally only have three or four things that I think are relevant enough to mention and I know that sometimes those overlap with what colleagues have written, or members have posted. My list is longer this week, containing at least nine bullet points that I’d like to bring up and discuss. So, in no particular order, here are a bunch of things that caught my attention vs the Steelers. John Madden famously said that “If you have two QBs, you have none.” Well, what if you have five LBs in a system that only uses two? If Davis-Gaither, Carlies, Ajiake, Boettcher, and Allen are all finding their way on the field, just answer me why? Sure, they are all basically new to the system, but are you trying to get the right guy for each situation? I’ll be honest, I was in favor of moving on from Franklin. I did sort of think we would retain Pratt to have a veteran presence. In short, it is a bad unit, that lacks the instincts of good NFL LBs. The LB woes lead right into the next observation/gripe in that you can’t win if you do not tackle. Old timers will tell you the basics of the game are blocking and tackling and it holds water. The tone was set on Warren’s (theirs) 80 yard reception. A missed tackle by Boettcher and no interest in taking on Metcalf, let alone the ball carrier in the secondary, saw him nearly untouched. Bad angles, arm grabs and trying to bump someone down is just too common of an occurrence. In my humble opinion, tackling is nearly 100% effort, and it looks we are gave about 50%. If blocking and tackling are the basics, I thought we pass blocked well, but what is wrong with the run blocking? JT is obviously a great RB, so why hasn’t he gained 100 yards in game, since London last year? There has been some mention made of playing from under center more, but those attempts did not go well either on Sunday. I am going to speak the blasphemous, by saying that JT’s “patience” that he is famous for, sometimes needs to be changed to hitting the hole that has the best chance of being there, and hitting it quickly. My note of the pass blocking being sufficient, brings to light another concern. We had a cleaner pocket, but still many passes were from retreat mode, rather than stepping into the throw. I know it is necessary sometimes and you can’t be a great QB if you do not have that backfoot throw in your arsenal. Still, you are going to complete far more of the ones that you set, then drive to your target. If you don’t have the confidence to do that, maybe you should sit until you do. I’m not suggesting a QB controversy, but more asking DJ to take a look in the mirror and ask himself if he is ready. I haven’t seen snap counts, but I think we were heavy in TE usage most of the game. We did manage to get it to Mo twice and Ogletree once, but if you are going to have them out there, they need to be targeted more, otherwise just bring Tenuta in. You are running a lot of short routes anyway, so make defenses be aware of their existence. They have proven capable of making the catch when thrown to. If they simply have to be there in order to have any protection at all, then you have a different problem. The D wasn’t good and I will point to a lack of confidence in Lou that I have written about in the past, and agree with Andrew Aziz’ call for his removal as DC. I will just ask you this, are you confident that you will make a team punt when you back them up with a hold on first down? You should be able to stop a team from gaining 20 yards in three downs. Hell, the game is about stopping them from gaining 10. I have little to no confidence that even when our opponent is well behind the sticks, that we can make them give up possession. We’ve picked off one pass and recovered one fumble over five games. My last three concerns are Shane related. If you are consistently settling for FGs, then your play calling is not aggressive enough. Not necessarily going for it instead of taking the points, but not putting receivers past the sticks on 3rd down. I thought he displayed a sort of killer instincts at the beginning of last year, but that appears to have been the exception, rather than an improved philosophy. There is no aggression in his play calling and he is too happy trying to call plays that keep them in FG range, rather than extending drives. Speaking of aggression, Burkes needs to be on the field far more often. He has shown the ability to get behind a CB. If he beats a couple of them, the Safety has to honor it. I want to see if he has that ability to go up and get it. He’s got some strength and vertical jump, so he needs the same kind of targets that Pierce got as a rookie. Remember, he got 12 starts and 78 targets as a rookie and even though we thought he ran a ton of empty fly routes, he did stretch the field. My last Shane rant goes to our last gasp yesterday. Down two scores with just over six minutes in the game, you get a decent gain on first down and you huddle? Jones has been in the league and under center for long enough to run this requirement for anyone who plays the position. Shane needed to relinquish control at that point and needs to do it for some series during the game as well. We all saw Rivers command an offense and a team of strangers, with a tryout and two practices. He did this with no mobility and limited arm strength. Shane needs to give Jones the same freedom. You might ask why I appear to be giving Ballard a pass. My thought is that he has made his bed and nothing he does for the remainder of this year, will affect his job. If the coaches that he chose can’t get enough out of the players he chose, he will be looking for work. It does bring to my mind a thought, which my wife says is dangerous, but if player development is as difficult as it appears to be, maybe you need to use all of your draft picks on established players? The biggest benefit of a rookie is his control and contract. Why not trade your unknown for a known commodity? I read a nice piece on The Feed, from Natural Born Buddha called “Some Thoughts”. I found it hard to disagree with much of what he shared and even though we overlap a little, there are some different views on similar observations. Give it a read, I think you will enjoy it.
author: Clydesdales

title: Finish a few more drives and the Colts’ story might be different
summary: The Indianapolis Colts had a bad day in Pittsburgh. That’s the simplest way to sum it all up. It wasn’t a beat down, but it was rough. The team can’t say it didn’t have some opportunities to walk away with a win though. That’s the most frustrating thing about it. If the Colts had finished […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: Spencer Shrader #3 of the Indianapolis Colts kicks a field goal during the first quarter of a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts had a bad day in Pittsburgh. That’s the simplest way to sum it all up. It wasn’t a beat down, but it was rough. The team can’t say it didn’t have some opportunities to walk away with a win though. That’s the most frustrating thing about it. If the Colts had finished more drives by coming away with touchdowns instead of field goals, they might be singing a different tune today. Let’s give Spencer Shrader some credit in this one because without his strong, accurate leg, things would have been a lot worse. His field goals of 57 and 56 yards were enough to keep the Colts close early. His kicks from 22, 40, and 28 were enough to drive Colts fans crazy. First and goal from the 3-yard line produced a total gain of -1. The 40-yarder was tough because the Colts could have pulled back to within one or tied the game with a two-point conversion. A case to forgive that one can be made, though. There is no forgiveness for the last field goal made under the 30. Daniel Jones and Jonathan Taylor got the Colts down to the Pittsburgh 10-yard line, but three straight incompletions forfeited all momentum. A touchdown would have given the Colts the lead with less than a quarter to go. Yes, the Steelers scored a touchdown on their next possession, but a Colts touchdown might have changed things. We will never know. All we know is that the Colts made five field goals with only one touchdown and lost the game. Maybe turning two field goals into touchdowns does the trick, but then again, maybe it doesn’t. That doesn’t mean it won’t have a major impact on wins and losses going forward, though. Having someone like Spencer Shrader is a great weapon, but it would be better if he mainly kicked extra points. Use him for those 57-yarders, but too many more 22-yarders will spell disaster for the Colts.

title: Colts-Titans opening odds: A few things to tighten up
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are picking up divisional play in Week 6 against the Tennessee Titans. It’s a welcomed return home after a road trip that produced mixed results. After traveling to London and collecting a win, things went sideways in Pittsburgh. FanDuel Sportsbook is giving the Colts the edge against the winless Titans with a […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans helmet rests on the field during a training camp practice at Saint Thomas Sports Park Thursday, July 29, 2021 in Nashville, Tenn. Nas 0728 Titans Camp 003 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Indianapolis Colts are picking up divisional play in Week 6 against the Tennessee Titans. It’s a welcomed return home after a road trip that produced mixed results. After traveling to London and collecting a win, things went sideways in Pittsburgh. FanDuel Sportsbook is giving the Colts the edge against the winless Titans with a 6.5-point spread advantage. The money line is at -330 with the over/under starting at 43.5. The Colts did what they do; they lost in Pittsburgh. Unable to finish drives and giving up huge plays on defense was the story of the afternoon. After going up 3-0, they never regained the lead. Every time the Colts got close, they had to settle for 3. Luckily, Spencer Schrader was on his game, but it wasn’t enough. An 80 and 50 yard score by Jaylen Warren was too much to overcome as the Colts fell, once again, to the Steelers in Pittsburgh. The Titans and Texans were entrenched in the battle of the winless as one team would get off the schneid and the other would sink further down. Cam Ward and the Titans might really be that bad. They scored the first 3 but then allowed the Texans to rattle off the next 26. Jobs might be on the line as the season is quickly slipping down the drain. Lose again and the Titans might be eyeing a replacement for Ward in the draft with the No. 1 pick. The Colts have work to do, but the Titans might be the best remedy to what ails them. Nothing is certain, but this is a great opportunity to get to 3-3 and finish the first third of the season at .500. Finding the end zone and putting up 6 in place of 3 is a great place to start. The Colts can do it, but they have plenty to tighten up before then.

title: 3 Numbers to Know From the Jaguars’ Win Over the Eagles
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars scraped by the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5 to move to 4-1 on the season. Wahoo! Here are a few stats that stand out from the victory. 6% That was Jacksonville’s win probability with eight seconds left in the game, per NFL Pro. Jake Elliot had just knocked through a 48-yard field […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 11: LeQuint Allen Jr. of the Jacksonville Jaguars celebrates with a flag after the 2026 NFL London Games match between Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 11, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by James Fearn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars scraped by the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 5 to move to 4-1 on the season. Wahoo! Here are a few stats that stand out from the victory. 6% That was Jacksonville’s win probability with eight seconds left in the game, per NFL Pro. Jake Elliot had just knocked through a 48-yard field goal to put the Eagles up by one point. If the Jaguars had any timeouts remaining, they might’ve been able to pick up a chunk completion before stopping the clock and attempting a lengthy walk-off field goal. But the Jaguars didn’t have any timeouts, and the Eagles made sure they’d have even less time by kicking off short of the endzone to prevent a touchback. Then Ameer Abdullah happened. JAGS HUGE KICK RETURN. They're in range for one more shot at a field goal! @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XSWbKBTvW2 — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 “Man, we got the perfect call with the perfect kick,” Abdullah said. “We knew that we could hit ‘em in the alleys — that’s the one that Josh Cameron had one called back earlier in the game — so we knew that if we got the right kick, we had an opportunity. “And having a kicker like Cam Little, we knew, if we got anywhere near midfield, get down and let him handle the job.” Boy, did Little handle it. Moments don't get any bigger than this. @NFLUKIRE | @Jaguars pic.twitter.com/L0AAShGvca — NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026 It’s easy to say that the Jaguars should’ve lost this game. They were digging their own grave. Long snapper Ross Matiscik and left tackle Anton Harrison exited mid-game, which contributed to questionable coaching decisions and frustrating player mistakes. I don’t know about y’all, but I felt like ripping my hair out the entire second half. That was one of the craziest, dumbest, wildest football games these eyes have ever seen. I suppose that would be the case regardless of whether Little’s last kick went through the uprights. But since his 57-yarder did in fact win the game, it makes this one of the most dramatic victories in franchise history. Per ELIAS: This is the first game, regular season or playoffs, where each team had a go-ahead score in the final 10 seconds of regulation in the Super Bowl Era (since 1966). Eagles took a 17-16 lead with 8 seconds to play and Jaguars won it on Cam Little's 57-yard field goal. — Michael DiRocco (@ESPNdirocco) October 11, 2026 “Man, the resolve on this team is special,” Abdullah said. “I’ve never played on a team like this, that ‘it’s not over until it’s over.’ These guys fight through adversity. We started off slow, another big penalty game, we were shooting ourselves in the foot, but it seems like guys just get stronger and stronger with every rep.” “That just shows me the resolve and the toughness and just the experience that these guys have been through with being down, being up, and understanding it’s just the same.” 15 That’s how many years it’s been since an NFL team won consecutive games with 13+ penalties in each game. The Jaguars are the first team to do so since the Seahawks in Weeks 10 and 11 of the 2011 season, per NFL Pro. “Every time we went positive, we went negative,” Liam Coen described. “It was like, every time we’d have an 8-to-10-yard run, we’d have a penalty. I mean, we had 13 [penalties] again, for 100 [penalty yards]. And it felt like they were all after good plays.” “We had them in how many 3rd-and-XLs defensively and let them off the hook? So I never really felt like we were just getting flat-out outplayed. Like it just never felt that way. We were kicking ourselves in the foot—we’re 0 for 3 in the red area—and how many of those were inside the 5? Right, so you’re in scoring position, what should that game have been—I can’t say.” “To come out of it on top, it’s obviously—you always want to live in the process. You get so wrapped up in the results. But, to have one second left and the team still fighting and the team still going through it, I mean I got to be proud of that.” 8 That’s how many snaps DaVon Hamilton played at long snapper on Sunday, per PFF. 4 snaps as a field goal long snapper, 4 snaps as a punt long snapper. Hamilton is a nose tackle. He was thrust into emergency action following the aforementioned injury to Matiscik. It’s never ideal to lose a player with such a specific skill set, but Hamilton has already shown in the past that he’s up for the job. the film cut up you’ve all been waiting for every rep of DaVon Hamilton at long snapper: pic.twitter.com/Ib96qjpko6 — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) December 1, 2025 There were understandable concerns. Jacksonville became even more aggressive than usual on 4th downs, and Little missed a late extra point that probably should’ve led to overtime. But ya gotta give credit when credit is due. D-Ham stepped up big time to help steal the win on Little’s final kick. Other numbers to know: 5 : International career wins by Trevor Lawrence, breaking a tie with Tom Brady (4) for the most in NFL history. 45 : Rushing yards allowed by Jacksonville in the past two weeks (22 in Week 4, 23 in Week 5). The Jaguars are one of seven teams in the Super Bowl era to allow 25 or fewer rushing yards in consecutive games. 1 : Other teams in the Super Bowl era that did not allow an individual rusher to reach 40+ yards in their first five games of a season. That team was the 1969 Dallas Cowboys. 11 : Consecutive games Jacksonville has held its opponents to under 20 points. It’s a franchise record and the NFL’s longest active streak. 5 : Consecutive games Bhayshul Tuten has rushed for 65+ yards. He is the third Jaguar to do so, joining Fred Taylor (2003) and Maurice Jones-Drew (2011). 22 : Carries by Bhayshul Tuten on Sunday, the most of his career. He has 13+ carries in every game this season after seeing double-digit carries just once last season. 5 : Career field goals of 55+ yards for Cam Little, the most in franchise history. 1 : Banger of a post by ArtButMakeItSports .
