title: NFL Week 5 arrivals: Ravens trio channels early 2000s style ahead of 'SNF'
summary: NFL stars continue to turn game-day arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
Week 5 of the NFL season is here, and October is starting to bring a little more variety to the forecast -- and potentially to pregame fashion.

 With fall temperatures settling into parts of the country and lingering heat beginning to ease elsewhere, players have another opportunity to switch up their game-day looks. 

 California's early-October heat wave has weakened, while cooler conditions in the Northeast and a hurricane that brought heavy rain to parts of the South made for a mixed bag across the country this weekend. That leaves room for everything from lightweight fits to layered looks as players make their stadium entrances.

 Whether they're embracing the season with jackets and sweaters or sticking to their signature styles, NFL players are bringing another round of personality to the tunnel in Week 5.

 

 Monday night style 
 
 
Monday evenings in Los Angeles call for comfort wear, especially with temperatures in the mid-60s. Such was the case for the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams . But comfort wear is where players and able to showcase their creativity and style. Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald did just that with a monochromatic matching set. 
 
 
 
 

 Primetime fashion 
 
 The Baltimore Ravens turned back the clock with some early 2000s-inspired fashion ahead of their Sunday Night Football matchup against the Atlanta Falcons . Cornerbacks Chandler Rivers and Keyon Martin joined safety Keondre Jackson in rocking backwards throwback basketball jerseys, oversized shorts and nostalgic accessories. Rivers led the way in a blue Derrick Rose Memphis Tigers jersey, baggy denim shorts and wheat Timberland boots, while Martin sported Penny Hardaway's pinstriped Orlando Magic jersey and Jackson repped Carmelo Anthony and the New York Knicks . The coordinated looks brought a dose of Y2K nostalgia to the Ravens' arrival in Atlanta. 
 
 
 
 Sunday's best 
Throwback jerseys honoring New England sports legends were a theme ahead of Sunday's matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and New England Patriots . Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby arrived in a Larry Bird jersey, while Patriots safety Craig Woodson sported a Ty Law jersey as New England prepared to celebrate the 25th anniversary of its Super Bowl XXXVI championship. 
 
 Thursday night drip 
 Dallas Cowboys teammates Cooper Beebe and Brevyn Spann-Ford  showed some love to the Dallas Stars ahead of "Thursday Night Football." Beebe arrived in a Jake Oettinger jersey, while Spann-Ford repped Stars legend Mike Modano.

title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald ,  who unretired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach career top-five territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks heading into the season was 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the career list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White's.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 5 update 

 Hunter was the only player among the active leaders to record a sack this week, moving him ahead of Campbell to No. 26 all-time. Hunter now has three sacks through five games. 

 Week 4 update 

 Watt kicked off things in Week 4 on "Thursday Night Football" in an impactful way. He had one sack, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery to move his total to 4.5 sacks on the season. Other than that, there wasn't much activity with Garrett continuing to be on IR. 

 Week 3 update 

 There wasn't much movement on the list this week with only Mack (1) and Hunter (.5) recording sacks. Watt, Campbell, Hunter and Mack (in that order) now make up 25 to 28 on the all-time list. Along with Campbell, the three top active leaders -- Miller, Jordan and Garrett -- have yet to record a sack this season.  

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the career list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks (No. 2 in the NFL this season) and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded one sack apiece over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) made his  season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants after taking two years off. He finished with three tackles, one for a loss, but did not record a sack. 

 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: Removing 'a dark cloud': How the Ravens' clutch play ended a 581-game streak
summary: Baltimore became the first team to win a game down by eight or more points in the final minute in four years.
full_text:
ATLANTA -- After receiving a game ball in the locker room for his game-ending interception, Baltimore Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton wanted to provide perspective to Sunday night's 30-23 overtime win over the Atlanta Falcons . 
 
 "The last couple of years, like ever since I've been here, that's a game that we would lose," Hamilton told his teammates and coaches. "This win right here, I feel like is us." 
 
 Hamilton is referring to the frustrating reputation that the Ravens had built with years of fourth-quarter collapses and coming up short in close games. But, after an improbable comeback with backup quarterback Tyler Huntley , Baltimore believes there is a reversal of fortune happening after a clutch performance rarely seen in the NFL. 
 
 The Ravens became the first team to win a game down by eight or more points in the final minute in four years, breaking the 581-game losing streak for teams in that situation, according to ESPN Research. 
 
 "We talk about being at your best when your best is needed, and just like, [the team had] no flinch, no panic," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "That's a big step for us. And if we let it be, it can be a launch point for us to really, really get this thing rolling." 
 
 Baltimore had previously struggled in close games. From 2023 to 2025, the Ravens were 9-15 (.375) in games decided by seven points or less, which was the sixth-worst mark in the league over that span. 
 
 This season, Baltimore has won three straight games that have been determined by a one-score margin. In Week 3, Tyler Loop 's 56-yard field goal as time expired lifted the Ravens to a 34-31 win over the Dallas Cowboys in Rio. In Week 4, Malaki Starks ' leaping recovery of an onside kick sealed Baltimore's 24-18 victory over the Tennessee Titans . And, on Sunday night, Hamilton's interception of Tua Tagovailoa closed out the game in overtime. 
 
 
 
 Minter pointed out how these string of nail-biters followed a 24-17 loss to the New Orleans Saints , which featured Baltimore giving up 15 points in the fourth quarter. 
 
 "Confidence is gained by going through things and going through things together," Minter said. "And I don't know if we have the results of the last three weeks if the Saints game doesn't happen. So I think there's always ways you can take losses like that. You can learn from them and really, really try to improve and get better and look at the things that you did well and build on things." 
 
 On Sunday night, here is how the Ravens went from trailing 23-15 late in the fourth quarter to winning 30-23 in four drives: 
 
 
 In a hurry-up offense, Huntley quickly moved Baltimore 71 yards in one minute, 51 seconds, completing all six of his passes to four different receivers. The Ravens tied the game at 23 when Huntley hit Devontez Walker for a 7-yard touchdown with 40 seconds remaining and running back Derrick Henry converted a 2-point conversion with a run. 
 On the last drive of the fourth quarter, Ravens outside linebacker Tavius Robinson beat two blockers off the right edge and hit Atlanta quarterback Michael Penix Jr ., which forced him to sit out overtime with a rib injury. 
 After electing to take the ball first in overtime, Baltimore marched 68 yards on 14 plays, which is the longest touchdown drive in overtime in eight years. Huntley capped the possession by getting into the end zone on a 1-yard sneak. 
 Down 30-23, the Falcons' chance of coming back ended with Hamilton's first interception of the season. Hamilton felt Tagovailoa was trying to look him off but he just watched his eyes to make the turnover. 
 
 
 "I have said it a thousand times before, but big-time players make big-time plays in big-time games," Ravens defensive end Calais Campbell said. "And Kyle Hamilton is the best of us."  
 
 For nearly three quarters, it didn't seem like this was going to be a watershed moment for Baltimore. With Lamar Jackson out with an ankle injury, the Ravens couldn't consistently finish off drives, totaling one touchdown, three field goals and four punts on the first nine possessions. Tight end Mark Andrews watched his fumble turn into a Falcons' defensive touchdown and then failed to hold onto a 2-point conversion that would have tied the game at 17 in the third quarter. The Baltimore defense couldn't get off the field, allowing Atlanta to convert nine of its first 15 third downs (60%).  
 
 "We were able to overcome adversity," Andrews said. "In some years past, we may not have been able to do that." 
 
 This marked the first time the Ravens had come back from a deficit of eight points or more in the final minute in five years, when Baltimore beat the Indianapolis Colts , 31-25. 
 
 "That is just us getting over some sort of hump or dark cloud," Hamilton said. "I am excited for the future."

title: Bills, Josh Allen outlast Rams in overtime on MNF
summary: Using a throwback offense with downhill runs and scrambles from their star QB, the Bills escape with the win.
full_text:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. -- On a day when it seemed like the Buffalo Bills ' defense couldn't make a single play, edge defender Greg Rousseau 's special teams prowess and quarterback Josh Allen 's legs allowed the Bills to sneak out of "Monday Night Football" with a win.

 Allen and the Bills outlasted the Los Angeles Rams 37-34 in overtime using a throwback offense built around downhill runs, screen passes, scrambles and heaves to tight ends absent receivers DJ Moore and Joshua Palmer .

 Allen completed only four passes to receivers, but in a game with six lead changes the Bills emerged victorious behind James Cook's 111-yard game and Allen's 121 rushing yards.

 

 To put the Bills' game plan in perspective, the Rams targeted star receiver Puka Nacua more times than Allen threw passes. And the Rams' death-by-a-thousand-cuts offense proved efficient, with QB Matthew Stafford picking apart the depleted and maligned Bills secondary with a barrage of underneath passes.

 Injuries to cornerback Christian Benford and safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson made it even tougher to slow the Rams' passing attack late. But Allen and the Bills had possession with seven minutes left in a tie game, and the small-ball offense that benefited coach Joe Brady's bunch all evening came in handy.

 The Bills drained 5:35 off the clock and plodded into the red zone for a go-ahead score with 1:39 left. Allen's legs proved most valuable on their final possession of regulation, with scrambles of 15 and 21 yards. Of course, that soon became moot as the Rams went down the field in about 90 seconds thanks to more Stafford mastery and forced overtime.

 Both teams made calamitous mistakes in overtime, with Cook fumbling away a would-be scoring drive to start for the Bills and then Rams kicker Harrison Mevis having a would-be game-winning kick blocked by Rousseau to give the Bills another shot. Thirty-two more yards of Allen runs helped the Bills set up Tyler Bass to hit the winning kick.

 Here are the most important things to know for both teams:

 

 

 

 Buffalo Bills (4-1) 
 Trend to watch:  James Cook III  fumbled two more times, including the overtime fumble that ended a Bills scoring threat. Those were his third and fourth fumbles of the young season, coming off a 2025 campaign in which Cook fumbled six times in the regular season and once more in the playoffs.

 What to make of QB performance: Without Moore or Palmer, the Bills' passing attack was muzzled for most of the game. This wasn't much of a surprise. The same sort of thing happened in the second halves against Detroit and New England without Moore. Still, with Allen's receivers consistently unable to pop open downfield, the quarterback incorporated more scrambles into his repertoire than he has since Week 2. All this made Allen seem more human. The fact the Bills played close with this Rams team without a superhuman Allen performance is encouraging, in a sideways type of way.

 Stat to know: The Bills converted only two third downs on seven attempts. This was a significant departure from the past three weeks, in which the Bills converted more than 58% of their third-down attempts and converted at least half of their attempts in every game.

 Next game: at Las Vegas Raiders  (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET)

 
 

 

 Los Angeles Rams (2-3) 
The Rams entered the game with the NFL's second-worst special teams, according to ESPN Analytics.
 The unit continued to struggle in Monday's loss, allowing a 70-yard kick return to start the game (the fourth longest in the NFL this season), missing a 50-yard field goal in the first quarter and having the potential 48-yard game-winning field goal attempt blocked in overtime.

 The special teams woes are nothing new to a Rams team that moved on from its kicker and long-snapper in the middle of last season and later fired its special teams coordinator after a Week 16 loss.

 

 Along with the special teams miscues, the Rams could not get out of their own way.

 In the week leading up to the Rams' Week 5 loss to the Bills, coach Sean McVay emphasized that while Los Angeles escaped Philadelphia with a victory in Week 4, the Rams needed to "clean up" the penalties that could have cost them the game.

 "The things that really chapped me that I think are a reflection of an undisciplined team are the pre-snap, the procedural things," McVay said a week ago. "Those are the things that we can control with focus and concentration."

 But against the Bills, the penalties continued to be an issue. The Rams were called for 11 penalties for 84 yards, bringing their total for the season to 42, which is tied for the sixth most in the NFL. Los Angeles had four false starts on Monday, which is tied for its most in a game under McVay.

 The Rams entered this season as Super Bowl favorites, and although they've played a tough schedule through five weeks, if they cannot fix these "undisciplined" mistakes, it will be an uphill climb to get out of the NFC West. Los Angeles is now 2-3 this season in a division that features the 5-0 San Francisco 49ers (Los Angeles' Week 1 opponent) and the 3-2 Seattle Seahawks .

 Stat to know: Davante Adams had two red zone touchdowns, with catches of 4 and 5 yards. His fourth-quarter touchdown was his 62nd receiving touchdown inside the 10-yard line. He has the most in NFL history in both categories, according to ESPN Research, and his 87 receiving touchdowns in the red zone rank as the third most in league history.

 Most surprising performance: Despite the success that Rams running back Kyren Williams has had the past two weeks, Los Angeles has insisted it believes it has two RB1s on the roster between him and Blake Corum . The 2024 third-round running back out of Michigan showed why on Monday night as Corum had 19 rushing yards and a touchdown on five carries and three catches for 53 yards.

 Best quote out of the locker room:  After the game, McVay walked around the locker room, shaking each starter's hand. He told them he appreciated them and he was "sick" about the loss. He had just been at the podium talking to reporters, saying, "It's been a while since I've been this pissed after a game."

 Next game:  vs. Arizona Cardinals (Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET)

title: What are NFL overtime rules for regular and postseason play?
summary: Overtime periods can have a pivotal impact on game results. Here are key facts on regular-season and postseason overtime rules in the NFL.
full_text:
While extra football is always fun, even die-hard fans can have a hard time keeping up with the NFL's evolving overtime rules.

 From 1974 to 2010, tie games were decided with a 15-minute sudden-death period. In 2010, the NFL implemented a "modified sudden death," where a first-possession touchdown would end the game but, after a first-possession field goal, the opposing team would also get an opportunity to possess the ball. In 2017, the NFL shortened the overtime period to 10 minutes.

 The past decade has brought some bigger changes. After the Kansas City Chiefs' 42-36 overtime win over the Buffalo Bills in the 2022 AFC divisional round, NFL owners approved a rule change that ensures both teams get a chance to possess the ball during overtime of a playoff game. In 2025, NFL clubs approved a rule that aligns the postseason and regular season overtime rules by granting both teams an opportunity to possess the ball even if the first team scores a touchdown, subject to a 10-minute overtime period in the regular season. 

 Check out the NFL's current overtime rules in further detail below: 

  

 What are the NFL's regular-season overtime rules? 

 The following overtime rules come directly from the NFL's football operations site :

 
 At the end of regulation, the referee will toss a coin to determine which team will possess the ball first in overtime. The visiting team captain will call the toss. 
 No more than one 10-minute period will follow, even if the second team has not had an opportunity to possess the ball or if its initial possession has not ended. Also, if the team kicking off to start the overtime period scores a safety on the receiving team's initial possession, the team that kicked off is the winner.  
 If each team has had an opportunity to possess the ball within the 10-minute period, and if one team has more points than its opponent, it is the winner (subject to the General Rules Applicable to Overtime). If the team that possesses the ball first does not score on its initial possession, or if the score is tied after each team has had its opportunity to possess the ball, the team that scores next, by any method, is the winner. 
 Each team gets two timeouts. 
 If the score is still tied at the end of the overtime period, the result of the game will be recorded as a tie. 
 There are no instant replay coach's challenges; all reviews will be initiated by the replay official. 
 
 What are the NFL's postseason overtime rules? 

 Since playoff games cannot end in a tie, the overtime rules are slightly different. Again, these rules come directly from the NFL's football operations site :

 
 If the score is still tied at the end of an overtime period - or if the second team's initial possession has not ended - the teams will play another overtime period. Play will continue regardless of how many overtime periods are needed for a winner to be determined. 
 There will be a two-minute intermission between each overtime period. There will not be a halftime intermission after the second period. 
 The captain who lost the first overtime coin toss will either choose to possess the ball or select which goal his team will defend, unless the team that won the coin toss deferred that choice. 
 Each team will have an opportunity to possess the ball in overtime. 
 Each team gets three timeouts during a half. 
 The same timing rules that apply at the end of the second and fourth regulation periods also apply at the end of a second or fourth overtime period. 
 If there is still no winner at the end of a fourth overtime period, there will be another coin toss, and play will continue until a winner is declared. 
 
 Where can I find more NFL coverage from ESPN?  

 Fans can access stats, scores , standings , schedules  and more on the ESPN hub page .

title: Samaje Perine gives Bengals a strong jolt to end 2-game skid
summary: When the run game was struggling, the Bengals turned to Perine, whose downhill style paid dividends.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Early in Sunday's game against the Miami Dolphins , the Cincinnati Bengals realized what was going on with the run game wasn't working.

 So like they have in previous years, they decided to try something different -- yet familiar.

 Enter Samaje Perine . With Cincinnati's run game faltering again, the Bengals used a scheme that fit his strengths -- attacking the line of scrimmage and going downhill.

 And it worked. One week after getting stuffed against the Jaguars, Cincinnati was much better on the ground in a 31-24 victory. At a time in the season when the Bengals are trying to find their identity, they might have found the solution.

 "The coaches challenged the [offensive] line to create space," Perine said. "And they created a lot of space, and we just had to run."

 Perine downplayed any schematic changes Cincinnati (3-2) made to fix the ailing run game, but the numbers tell a different story.

 According to ESPN Research, 36.7% of the called runs were classified as inside zone calls. That is the third-highest rate of inside zone Cincinnati has called since ESPN started tracking that data in 2024. Conversely, the Bengals used outside zone on 10% of its rushing calls, their fourth-lowest rate in a game over the past three seasons. To be more precise, the Bengals used what could be called a "midzone" rushing scheme that attacked the middle of the line of scrimmage.

 

 And Perine was the one who benefited. Coming into Sunday, he had a combined 13 carries in the previous four games. But against the Dolphins (0-5), Perine tallied a season-high 14 carries for 68 yards and also had a receiving touchdown as the Bengals snapped a two-game losing streak.

 Bengals center Ted Karras said that the offensive line did a good job of moving Miami's defensive tackles and then blocking the linebackers, which opened up downfield rushing lanes for Perine and starter Chase Brown .

 Brown, who has been the team's entrenched starter since the 2024 season, was bottled up early in Sunday's game. In the first half, he averaged just 2.4 yards per carry while Perine was at 6.1 yards.

 As the game went on, the numbers evened out. Not only did Perine and Brown have a nearly identical split in the number of subsequent carries (seven for Perine, six for Brown), but their rushing average per attempt was nearly identical (3.6 at Perine, 3.7 for Brown).

 Moving forward, Bengals coach Zac Taylor said the offense will approach the rushing plan on a week-to-week basis for whatever is needed for the team to score. But he had a glowing endorsement of the way Cincinnati's top two running backs split backfield duties.

 "Sometimes you have two great backs that you've got trust in," Taylor said. "That's just the way it can go sometimes, and I don't think there's anything wrong with that."

 The win at Hard Rock Stadium highlighted one of the team's more unheralded players over the years.

 

 Perine, 31, is in his third stint with the Bengals. He first joined the club in 2019, Taylor's first season with Cincinnati.

 The way the game unfolded Sunday resembled Perine's second and most notable time with the club that stretched from 2020 to 2023. During the 2022 season, the Bengals ripped up their run game and implemented an approach that attacked specific gaps in the line of scrimmage.

 That favored Perine's direct style of rushing and was effective for an offense that operates primarily out of shotgun. Four years later, that suited the Bengals well.

 "He's just Mr. Reliable, and he has been my entire time here since he's been on our team," quarterback Joe Burrow said. "You can count on him to fall forward and get us an extra 2 yards."

 As the Bengals approach the bye week, they are still looking to iron out the offense and how much Burrow will be in shotgun versus under center. Finding a consistent and dependable rushing plan was a focal point for the coaching staff in recent weeks.

 Cincinnati has two weeks until its next game, at division-leading Baltimore (4-1), to figure out the best strategy to win an important AFC North matchup. As big as Sunday's win was to establish momentum heading into the bye week, Cincinnati might have found a viable ground game for the rest of the season.

title: Broncos offense searching for more big plays, ready for Bo Nix to 'let it rip'
summary: Changing playcallers wasn't an immediate fix for the Broncos' offense, which still suffers from a lack of big plays and a QB who hasn't found his rhythm.
full_text:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. -- In the moments following a tooth-grinding escape against the winless Los Angeles Chargers , Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton talked about his continued wrestling match with time.

 The Broncos hope to slightly slow quarterback Bo Nix 's internal clock between the snap and the whistle to end each play. And they feel like succeeding with that adjustment would cause everything to fall into place for Nix and the Denver offense so they can, in Payton's words, "let it rip."

 "There's a lot that's been said about his feet, I think he's settling that down," Payton said in the moments after Sunday's 23-17 victory over the 0-5 Chargers. "[But] I think it's important from a protection standpoint we provide that early in game so that clock doesn't get juiced up a little bit."

 The Broncos moved to 3-2 with the victory, but it was not a smooth operation for the offense in its first game since Payton re-assumed playcalling duties . Denver finished 1-of-12 on third down against the Chargers, gained only 224 net yards and had one play longer than 12 yards before the fourth quarter. Nix finished with the second-lowest passing yardage of his career (16-of-27 passing for 123 yards and a touchdown).

 

 Following Sunday's games, Nix is 24th in the league in QBR (43.1) and 30th in completion percentage over expectation (minus-4.1%), ahead of only Cleveland's Deshaun Watson . The Broncos find themselves near the bottom of the league in most statistical categories on offense, including scoring (29th, 18.0 points per game). Only the Arizona Cardinals have fewer plays of 20 yards or more than the Broncos' 11.

 These struggles are part of why Payton snatched playcalling duties back from offensive coordinator Davis Webb after four games. But Payton's playcalling return saw many of the same issues that prompted him to make the change. And a coach who has made his résumé on a brash, go-for-it boldness spoke of the benefit of "small steps" for the QB as the Broncos' defense once again fueled a fourth-quarter comeback win.

 "Thought guys up front settled in," Payton said. "... And when we needed it, [Nix] gave us some important ones."

 Much of the outside angst about Denver's offense has centered on the 26-year-old quarterback's play. Many former QBs, including ESPN analyst Chase Daniel, who played for Payton in New Orleans, have spoken of Nix's footwork and his penchant for moving through his progressions too quickly before Broncos receivers are into their routes enough to be targets.

 Payton has acknowledged some of that, saying that he wants "make [Nix's] job easier" with a better run-game approach and improved pass protection, especially early in games, to get the QB settled faster. That mindset was apparent Sunday, which was the first game this season in which the Broncos had more rushing attempts than pass attempts.

 Though the Broncos rushed for fewer than 4 yards per carry on their 29 attempts (106 yards for 3.7 per carry), Payton said he believes the rhythm of the run game is important in helping Nix play with a little more freedom. Nix, who had two ankle surgeries this past offseason, has run less this season, and his 5.7 air yards per attempt currently ranks last among the league's 31 qualifying quarterbacks.

 "I think after [five] weeks there's a handful of things collectively, it starts with me, where it's like 'alright, where it's let's focus on the details' and I think the by-product helps the [quarterback]," Payton said. "I think the hardest thing to do in this league is play that position if you're not rushing the ball."

 

 Payton said he and the Broncos coaches have assured Nix that he's "the guy we want here." Nix has also acknowledged that he has tried to not press when things aren't going smoothly and that he, too, wants to find the let-it-rip zone.

 "When a coach says 'let it rip,' it means play what you see, have good vision, and I think there's just, right now, there's just a little subtle piece that's overall offensive execution that we're still working toward," Nix said. "Because at times it's there and at times, for whatever reason, the drive stalls."

 When the Broncos selected Nix with the 12th overall pick in 2024, Payton said it was in large part due to Nix's "superpower" -- his ability to avoid sacks and turnovers. But Nix has fumbled four times this season, including twice on Sunday, one which he lost. Nix knows he must be more careful before truly being able to let loose.

 "Letting it rip is one of the best things that you can do as a quarterback," Nix said. "At the same time, you've got to sort of earn that right. When you do the preparation, you earn the right to react so that you can let it rip."

 Things don't get any easier this week. The Broncos have a short week before a Thursday night game against the 3-2 Seattle Seahawks , the defending Super Bowl champions. Seattle is ninth in scoring defense and has surrendered the fewest yards per play in the NFL (4.2). The Seahawks are also tied for fourth in the league in quick pressures, which will challenge Nix's ability to slow down his internal clock.

 "[Hall of Fame coach] Bill [Parcells] taught me one thing and it's on going, if you're not having the output you're looking for, you have to look at reducing the variables," Payton said. "And we're trying to do that, reduce the variables so guys can play faster."

title: Packers' Watson-Golden WR combo reminiscent of Nelson-Cobb
summary: It has been more than a decade since Green Bay had a dominant WR duo, but Watson and Golden are making their mark.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- It's time to insert Christian Watson into the conversation of best receivers in the NFL. And while you're at it, throw Matthew Golden into talk about the most improved player in the NFL.

 Together, they have a chance to be the Green Bay Packers ' most productive receiver combination since the days of Jordy Nelson and Randall Cobb more than a decade ago.

 As dominant as Davante Adams was when he led the Packers in receiving every season from 2017 to 2021, he never had a consistent running mate.

 In Sunday's much-needed 31-7 win over the Chicago Bears , Watson and Golden showed why the Packers wanted to streamline their receiver room and give quarterback  Jordan Love a few go-to guys rather than a smorgasbord of receivers, none of whom ranked among the league's best. Jayden Reed was supposed to be part of the go-to group, but the Packers lost him for the season to a neck injury in Week 2.

 

 Against the Bears, Watson (six catches for 143 yards and two touchdowns) and Golden (six catches for 123 yards) became the first pair of Packers to each record 100 yards receiving in the same game since Adams and Marquez Valdes-Scantling did in 2021 against the Minnesota Vikings .

 "We talked about it a little bit last week, how good the offense can be. It just shows right there," Love said. "Those are two guys that are dominant factors. We get flowing like this and they're making plays and we're able to take advantage of what the defense is doing. Both those guys, they're capable of doing great things. I think that's just a little bit of, show what's possible."

 What's possible is this: Watson is on pace for 1,600 yards and Golden for nearly 1,350. The Packers haven't had a pair of 1,000-yard receivers in the same season since Nelson and Cobb in 2014.

 

 "Well, we'll see," coach Matt LaFleur said. "You're only as good as your last game. They were pretty good this week."

 Or as Packers safety Xavier McKinney said when asked how tough it would be for defenses to cover Watson and Golden if they play like that: "It's different."

 McKinney should know. He has had to do it in practice all year.

 "You see the speed," McKinney said. "I'm sure the DBs on the other side, they feel that speed. And when you've got a quarterback like [Love], I've seen it now for a couple years, so I know what he's capable of doing. I've seen the throws that he's made. I know the throws that he can make consistently.

 "Then obviously you get talented guys like C-Wat, M.G., [tight end] Tuck Kraft  ... once they start to get really clicking and really going, it's going to be a scary sight to see for any team."

 Watson, who had parts of the past two seasons impacted by injuries, ranks fifth in the league in receiving yards with 474 and second in touchdowns with six (behind Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba 's seven). Golden, with 24 catches for 397 yards, has already surpassed his yardage total from last season, when he was a first-round rookie, and is five catches behind his total.

 The numbers tell only part of the story. The film shows the other. How many receivers in the league can haul in the 53-yard touchdown that Watson did in the third quarter against the Bears? He reached over Bears safety Dillon Thieneman , who was giving chase, and then made sure the catch survived the ground after Thieneman knocked him down and sent him sliding toward the back of the end zone.

 

 "Honestly, I was kind of joking around with some of the guys after, that's just one of those ones that you watch it back on tape, and you're like, 'The DB should've broken it up or it should've been incomplete,'" Watson said. "Sometimes, you just find a way. I was just tracking the ball. I wasn't thinking too much. Just go get it and came down with it."

 Golden did much the same. On his 36-yard catch in the third quarter and his 50-yarder in the fourth, Golden had to go up in the air and twist his body to make the grabs.

 

 "It's hard to stop two guys who can run all the routes and stretch the field like that," Watson said of him and Golden. "If you try to, it's going to give us other opportunities elsewhere. Obviously we've got Tucker Kraft and we've got a lot of guys who can make plays. It's just tough when you've got playmakers of the ability we have in our room and our offense, to stop it all."

 The Packers can't expect to throw it deep with as much success as they did against the Bears. There's a reason Love had more completions on passes with 20-plus air yards (six) on Sunday than he did in the first four games combined (five): They're typically low-percentage throws that teams cannot count on week in and week out.

 "You can't, but it's OK," McKinney said. "We'll get [running back  Josh Jacobs] back soon, and we'll be OK. I think that even the backs now, the guys that are playing, have done a great job of making sure they're running hard and getting the extra yards, whatever the case may be, so it can open up the pass game. But when we get [Jacobs] back, yeah, it's gonna really show."

title: Inside the NFL's wild endings and why coaches need to adapt
summary: Scoring too early and kicking the ball into the end zone can be costly, as the Cowboys learned.
full_text:
Editor's note: This story ran Friday, before the wild ending to the Eagles-Jaguars game , which became the first to feature two go-ahead field goals in the final 10 seconds of regulation in the Super Bowl era (since 1966). Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said it was a mistake to let the Jaguars return the kick with eight seconds left.  Ameer Abdullah  returned the kick 53 yards to set up  Cam Little 's 57-yard game-winning field goal. 

 The Indianapolis Colts appeared positioned for exactly the kind of finish that keeps NFL stadiums packed.

 Fourth quarter. Their ball. Down one point against the Houston Texans with 1:48 remaining. On the second play of what would be their final drive in Week 3, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones ripped a pass down the middle to receiver Laquon Treadwell for a 20-yard gain. Just like that, the Colts were cooking at the Houston 45-yard line.

 What happened next left some perplexed: The Colts began to display a sudden lack of urgency.

 They ran the ball on their next play. Next, they casually allowed the clock to tick down from 40 to 29 seconds before the following play -- that's when Houston, interestingly, called a timeout. Then, another run.

 Not until the Colts faced a third-and-6 did they make a more concerted effort to achieve a first down. Receiver Keenan Allen came up inches short after a 6-yard reception, so kicker Spencer Shrader came on and booted a 53-yard game-winning field goal with 21 seconds remaining.

 Why weren't the Colts more aggressive? And when did a 53-yard field goal become a slam dunk? The situation offered a prime example of how the traditional approach to late-game situations in the NFL has necessarily evolved at a time when more and more games are being decided late.

 In some instances, the "hurry-up" offense becomes more like "hurry up ... kinda."

 

 "That is real," Colts coach Shane Steichen said. "There's no doubt. When you have an opportunity to finish the game, you want it to be the last drive."

 Just ask the Dallas Cowboys , who can attest to it after losing a Week 3 game to the Baltimore Ravens on an inexplicable seven-second scoring drive.

 If it feels like there has been more last-minute scoring in the NFL lately, it's because there has been.

 Since the latest change to the NFL kickoff process last year, with the ball positioned at the 35-yard line after touchbacks, madness has ensued in the final moments of games. The number of drives starting in the final minute of halves culminating in a touchdown or field goal attempt skyrocketed by more than 50% relative to the 10 seasons before the changes.

 Meanwhile, the increasing strength and skill level of kickers, combined with underappreciated changes to rules governing how kicking balls -- known as K-balls -- may be manipulated by teams, has spurred a 60% increase in field goal attempts of 50 yards or longer in just five seasons. Many of those attempts are coming late in games and proving decisive.

 

 There were an NFL-record 12 field goal conversions of 60 yards or longer last season, including Jacksonville Jaguars kicker  Cam Little 's 68-yarder, the longest in NFL history.

 Subtle changes are translating into massive impacts on the game, and the trends seem unlikely to slow anytime soon.

 "Now you're seeing, I mean, chaos out there from some teams," Jaguars coach Liam Coen said. "And it's cool to watch."

 When a touchback can cost you the game 

 Of course, it's less cool if you're on the wrong side of the outcome.

 That brings us back to the Cowboys. There are a host of reasons they lost 34-31 to the Ravens on Sept. 27 in Rio de Janeiro, among them some curious coaching decisions and poor execution by players.

 

 But not to be overlooked was the role that today's kickoff rules played in the defeat. Had the Cowboys made the exact same miscues and been subject to the same circumstances just a few years ago, they likely would have held off Baltimore and pushed the game into overtime.

 One of the biggest variables in the loss was Dallas' decision to kick into the end zone after their tying field goal. With just seven seconds remaining, kicker Brandon Aubrey was instructed to aim for a touchback. But in the past three seasons, field position after touchbacks has been overhauled. After a 2024 change, teams were awarded the ball at the 30-yard line after touchbacks. (It was previously the 25-yard line.) A year later, in 2025, the rule was amended again, placing the ball at the 35.

 Ten yards of additional field position is priceless in an environment where kickers are capable of making field goals from near midfield.

 "There are so many yards at stake,"  Los Angeles Rams  coach Sean McVay said. "That's led to just so many more action plays in the kicking game in general. It's a big deal."

 Said Steichen: "You get the ball at the 35, and, shoot, someone hits an in-cut [route]. Next thing you know, they're at the plus-45 [yard line] and they kick a game-winning field goal."

 It's precisely what happened to Dallas, when quarterback Lamar Jackson hit receiver Zay Flowers for a 27-yard gain immediately after Dallas' kickoff. Baltimore called a timeout with one second remaining, allowing kicker Tyler Loop to convert a 56-yard field goal as time expired.

 Two-minute situations have been turned upside down by all of this.

 According to the Elias Sports Bureau, there were 49 game-winning drives that ended in the final two minutes of regulation in 2025, the most since 2000. Through four weeks of the 2026 season, there have already been 11 such drives. That puts this season on pace to match or exceed last year's total.

 "It used to be easy," said New York Giants coach John Harbaugh, who began coaching in the NFL when touchbacks translated to drive starts at the 20-yard line. "You kick a touchback and it's a gift. Good field position for your defense. They eliminated that because they want more returns, which I'm always for more."

 

 Adding to the issues is the complexity of today's dynamic kickoff process. Because the ball must land within the specified landing zone -- between the receiving team's goal line and the 20-yard line -- the possibility of a miss exists. When kickers are attempting to kick into the corners or hit kicks at specific angles to disadvantage kick returners, the odds of a miscue increase. The potential consequences are dire: The receiving team takes possession at its 40-yard line if a kick misses the landing zone or the ball goes out of bounds.

 The whole exercise is harder than it looks.

 "People don't get how hard it is for it to land just in the landing spot," San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said. "Not a touchback, not short and not out of bounds. It's not as easy as people think.

 "You want to kick it high in there, but you're a little amped up and [could be] a touchback and that's a big miss because it's already at the 35 now."

 Why manipulating K-balls for the kicker could be huge 

 It's a part of the game few fans concern themselves with: the origins of the footballs used on game day.

 But it's actually a huge aspect of game prep for teams, both in terms of the balls used by quarterbacks and those set aside for kicks and punts. That's why a little-discussed rule change in 2025 has seemingly played an important role in today's frenzied final minutes of games.

 The NFL years ago standardized kicking balls, putting a stop to the over-manipulation of balls by teams looking to achieve better ball flight. The balls were presented to teams by the officiating crew, fresh out of the box, 60 minutes before kickoff. Equipment managers could address the balls using water, towels and brushes, but time was limited.

 But that rule was rescinded last year. Now, teams have the freedom to address the balls to their liking throughout the week, just as they have been doing on behalf of quarterbacks for years.

 Whether it has made a tangible difference is difficult to prove. But it's hard to imagine…

title: Dolphins not worried about young roster getting discouraged by losses
summary: Miami coach Jeff Hafley doesn't believe his players will grow discouraged by the lack of results so far this season.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Five games into the 2026 season, it's been no secret the Miami Dolphins are the youngest team in the NFL. At some point, that stops being an excuse.

 The Dolphins dropped to 0-5 after Sunday's 31-24 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals , during which they cut an 18-point fourth-quarter deficit to seven points but failed to recover an onside kick to extend the game. Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis threw for 137 yards and a touchdown, with a season-high 74 rushing yards and a touchdown -- but he threw two interceptions in the first half and lost a fumble, and Cincinnati scored 10 points off those turnovers.

 Willis was critical of Miami's offensive performance after the game and insisted that the team's inexperience doesn't make up for a lack of execution or accountability.

 "All we can do is put it out the best we can, and continue to try to keep that better than it was the week before," he said. "And it is too much and too hard to keep saying, 'Oh, we're just young. Oh, we're trying to build this and build that.' At the same time, we've got to hold each other accountable because we can't keep doing this to ourselves.

 "If we're going to be in games versus good teams, we've got to be able to take advantage of it and go and win those games -- because there's no point to be in the game if you can't go and win."

 Miami's 10 active rookies played a combined 455 snaps Sunday, and that's without Caleb Douglas , Kyle Louis and Trey Moore , who are all expected to play significant roles when healthy.

 First-year coach Jeff Hafley said last week that the Dolphins have "a lot of young guys in the huddle who don't have experience playing," but added that he expects improvement every week. One third of the way through the season, Hafley said the training wheels are off for his team, and he expects everyone to produce.

 "I want to see more consistency. I want to see better execution," he said Sunday. "I want to see the same fight. I want to see the same energy. I want to see the same connection. 

 The Dolphins have played the NFL's third-hardest schedule through five weeks. Sunday's game was their first against a team that wasn't undefeated. But their past three games -- against the Chiefs, Vikings and Bengals -- have all been one-score contests in the fourth quarter.

 Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez said after last week's loss to the Minnesota Vikings that Miami still needed to learn how to win. Entering its bye week in Week 6, Willis said a focal point this week will be identifying how to start fast and how to execute in critical moments.

 "I think we just got to watch the tape and figure it out," he said. "And that's the thing that I think Coach Haf does great. He holds everybody accountable and he's honest with us. If we need to do better, we need to do better. And if we got to execute, we need to execute. We got to figure out a way to get guys on the same page because there's just a lot left out on the field that could be better than what it is.

 "We try to find a way at the end, but that's just too hard to continue to try to fight back at the end."

 The Dolphins return from the bye to face the New York Jets in Week 7 in one of the most winnable remaining games on their schedule according to ESPN Analytics.

 Hafley said the team will debrief from Sunday's game, as usual, before starting its prep for the Jets. He doesn't believe his players will grow discouraged by the lack of results, and believes the Dolphins are "building" an identity centered around physicality and effort.

 "It's just (what we have been saying since) day one. It's who we are," he said. "It's what we have to be. We got really good guys. I don't even think that's going to be an issue."

title: How Drake Maye has rebounded from bad start despite mounting Patriots injuries
summary: Has Maye found his confidence ... and his deep ball? A dominant Week 5 win over the Raiders suggests he turned things around, even as New England struggles to stay healthy.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. --  Drake Maye is rolling again and his New England Patriots teammates can't help but take notice.

 "It's just fun to see Drake smiling big on the sidelines. That confidence is obviously back," linebacker Robert Spillane said in the aftermath of Sunday's 45-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders  (3-2).

 Maye's turnaround from the first three games of the season has been dramatic. After throwing only one touchdown with six interceptions in the team's 1-2 start, and being sacked nine times, he has completed 67.6% of his passes with seven touchdowns and one interception over the past two games, while being sacked only twice.

 Maye had a season-high 96.0 Total QBR -- the third best of his career -- against the Raiders while benefitting from strong offensive line play (only two pressures in the first half) that he said allowed him to "eat a ham sandwich" in the pocket on his first scoring pass because of how much time had. Maye became the first player this season with a Total QBR of 90 or better in back-to-back games. His Total QBR over the first three games was 49.

 One thing that worked well Sunday was Maye's deep ball. He finished 6-of-9 for 182 yards and two touchdown passes on throws 15-plus yards downfield, which tied for his second-most such completions in a game in his career. In the Patriots' first four games of the season, he completed only 43.8% of those throws with one total TD.

 

 "That's our leader," receiver  DeMario "Pop" Douglas  said of the 24-year-old Maye. "How he carries himself means a lot. It's by example. I feel like for us, we need to carry ourselves that way too -- ups and downs, you still have to stay straight.

 "From those past games, anybody could have been down on themselves. Not him. He came to work, and he was still like, 'I need you. I got your back.' That's what has been taking us to the next step."

 Maye earned game balls from coach Mike Vrabel each of the past two weeks. When Vrabel presented it to him after a Week 4 road win over the Buffalo Bills , he told him that the time for taking flak from detractors was over, according to video on Patriots.com. Maye and the Patriots (3-2) look to continue the surge Sunday when they host the New York Jets (2-3).

 The shift has come despite a run of injuries ravaging the depth chart, especially at receiver, running back, fullback and along the offensive line. And Maye still sees "juice left to squeeze" with the offense, pointing out the unit has yet to produce a turnover-free game.

 He said Sunday that he took joy in watching 2026 first-round pick Caleb Lomu thrust into a challenging spot at left tackle in place of injured Will Campbell , as well as others such as Douglas (four catches, 65 yards, two TDs) and Kyle Williams (three catches, 91 yards, TD) seizing an expanded receiving role because of injuries to A.J. Brown (ankle) and Mack Hollins (calf).

 Likewise, the Patriots might need to rely more on No. 3 running back Corey Kiner and practice-squad rusher Lan Larison after losing speedy TreVeyon Henderson to an ankle injury Sunday .

 The Patriots also won Sunday despite playing with only three healthy cornerbacks, as veteran Kindle Vildor  -- who was signed to the 53-man roster from the practice squad the day before -- earned a game ball for his competitive coverage and a forced fumble.

 "I'm just proud of the guys for stepping up -- offense, defense, overall as a football team," Maye said. "We talk about 'identity' with Coach Vrabel. That's a Coach Vrabel football team.

 

 "I think one of the best things about my position is being able to spread the wealth and watch guys succeed. It's beautiful to watch."

 Summing up his two-game surge, Maye said his confidence has never wavered.

 "It's really just an example of practice execution showing up in the game," he said. "That's the biggest thing I can maybe hint at."

title: Making sense of the Giants-Commanders tie, the Texans' Marvin Harrison Jr. trade
summary: What were the Commanders doing in the final minute of OT? Why did the 1-4 Texans make an aggressive trade for Marvin Harrison Jr.? Let's try to find the logic.
full_text:
Two very different decisions -- one on the field and another off it -- had me asking the same question by Sunday afternoon on Week 5 : What are they thinking? 

 There were the Commanders, who bizarrely decided to run the clock late in overtime against the Giants in field goal range and saw the game end without ever getting a chance to attempt the game-winning kick. And there were the Texans, who won their first game of the season and celebrated by making a surprisingly aggressive move on offense, trading second- and sixth-round picks to the Cardinals for a seventh-rounder and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr ., who has underwhelmed during his pro career so far.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 I love trying to explain the inexplicable, so let's give it a shot. Why did a 1-4 Texans team -- whose playoff chances sit at 23.2% after Sunday's victory, per ESPN's Football Power Index -- trade a significant future pick to acquire a player at a position where it already has  Nico Collins ? And what on earth were the Commanders attempting to do at the end of that game?

 I'll try to answer both those questions today, starting with the decision to try to kick-start a frustrating season by trading for one of the league's most frustrating players.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 The 1-4 Texans traded for Harrison? 
 The Commanders let the clock expire? 

 
 

 

 The Texans' trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. 
 Of course, the simple explanation for why the Texans traded for Harrison starts with one simple argument. We're about two and a half years removed from Harrison entering the 2024 NFL draft as arguably the most exciting and polished wide receiver prospect of his generation. Even amid a legendary run of Ohio State wide receivers that includes the likes of Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Chris Olave , Garrett Wilson , Emeka Egbuka  and others, Harrison was seen alongside  Jeremiah Smith  as the two best pro prospects of the bunch.

 Our various draft analysts saw Harrison as  no worse than the third-best player overall  in the class of 2024. There just aren't many players with Harrison's sort of scouting reports and college pedigree to enter the league. They don't come available via trade very often, and it's even rarer to get a shot at acquiring them just after they turn 24 years old.

 The Texans have been through this under general manager Nick Caserio and don't regret their past decision. After drafting C.J. Stroud with the second pick of the 2023 draft, the Texans surprised everyone by trading two first-round picks and a second-rounder to the Cardinals to move up for edge rusher  Will Anderson Jr . with the third overall selection. It was a move that seemed overly aggressive for a team that projected to be among the worst in football the following year, but it turned out to be a masterstroke.

 

 The Texans were a playoff team with Stroud and Anderson, with the latter emerging as one of the most dominant defenders in all of football. Like Anderson, Harrison plays a premium position. And while we don't have access to Houston's scouting reports, this trade implies that it saw Harrison as a potential superstar entering the league after his run at Ohio State. Stroud, Harrison's college teammate with the Buckeyes, gave a glowing report to the organization and said that the wideout was "probably the hardest worker I've ever been around in my life."

 The difference, of course, is that in Anderson, the Texans were trading up for a player with a great college résumé who hadn't yet played at the pro level. With Harrison, the Texans are trading for a player who has been outright disappointing as a pro over a multiple-season sample. He isn't a bad player, but he has hardly been great. Since 2024, he ranks 70th out of 130 wideouts in yards per route run (1.54) and 44th in receiving yards per game (47.8). He hasn't had great quarterback play, but Harrison has been roundly outperformed by Trey McBride and Michael Wilson within the same offense.

 On one hand, Harrison's contract is extremely affordable, which is important for a Texans team that just paid Anderson and has deals for Stroud, Calen Bullock  and Kamari Lassiter to come over the next 12 months. Harrison will make just $776,000 over the remainder of 2026 and $5.6 million in 2027. Even if the Texans decide to pick up Harrison's fifth-year option in 2028, that deal projects to come in at only  $17.2 million .

 That's a total of $23.6 million over the next three years, which is just a tiny bit more than what Jakobi Meyers is making per year on his existing contract. That number rises if you factor in the surplus value of the draft picks sent to the Cardinals , which throws another $33 million onto the pile -- but even $56.6 million over the next three years would be reasonable WR2 money right now. It'll look even cheaper as the cap rises over the next two seasons.

 The Texans are obviously counting on Harrison delivering something more than solid WR2 performance and living up to his lofty predraft expectations. Will he get there? To answer that question, there were two places to look. First, I wanted to get a sense of why Harrison was struggling in Arizona to see whether a change of scenery might be likely to unlock the second-generation pro. Second, I looked back through history to find examples of highly drafted players turning things around in a second act with a new team.

 
 What went wrong in Arizona? 

 The simplest answer is the one that Texans fans would fear the most. While there are mitigating factors and potential excuses to be made, the reality is that Harrison just wasn't able to get himself open often enough to get the sort of target share or rack up the sort of receiving production his draft status suggested was coming. While anyone with access to All-22 film and a lot of free time can undoubtedly find plays where he was open and didn't get the football, that's also true for any starting receiver in football.

 

 During his time with the Cardinals, Harrison ranked last in the NFL among all wide receivers (with 50 targets or more over the past three years) in separation, averaging just 2.1 yards of separation when targeted, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Great receivers -- even ones who get plenty of attention from opposing defenses -- are typically able to create more space for themselves. The likes of Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson average over 3 yards of separation on their routes. In Arizona, McBride averaged 3.3 yards of separation on his targets during that time, while Wilson was at 2.5 yards.

 In part because of those separation issues, Harrison didn't have a lot of chances to bring in easy targets. His expected catch rate over the past three years, using the Next Gen Stats model, was only 53.7%. That's fifth lowest among wide receivers since the start of 2024. I'll get to the four below him in a minute.

 By those expectations, the good news is that Harrison has roughly delivered about what the model would project given that low expected catch rate. He has caught 53.5% of his passes so far as a pro, almost exactly in line with the model's prediction. He has generated a total of 34 receiving yards over expectation across his 202 targets, which is also essentially a match for what the model suggests. You could make a case that Harrison has done an average job with below-average opportunities and hope that his expected catch rate will rise in Houston.

 But my concern is that Harrison is not separating because he hasn't been explosive enough. The four other wideouts with lower expected catch rates are Alec Pierce , Tyquan Thornton , Marquez Valdes-Scantling  and Christian Watson . Those are all deep threats who primarily make their money with their speed and ability to get open downfield. While they're going to draw targets that don't have great chances of being caught, the huge gains those receivers provide when they do bring in the football make up for the low catch rates.

 Next Gen Stats also…

title: Can the Seahawks overcome their turnover problem? 'We're not panicking'
summary: Seattle has committed the fifth-most turnovers in the NFL so far this season -- and it cost the team a win Sunday.
full_text:
SEATTLE --  Sam Darnold and the Seattle Seahawks won Super Bowl LX despite a turnover problem that plagued them for most of the 2025 regular season. It's again an issue in 2026 -- and on Sunday, it was the difference.

 Two more Darnold interceptions and two more lost fumbles by their short-handed backfield doomed the Seahawks in a 33-29 loss to the San Francisco 49ers at Lumen Field. Three of those turnovers turned into 21 points for the 49ers, who snapped the Seahawks' nine-game home winning streak and dropped the defending champions to 3-2, two games behind San Francisco in the NFC West standings .

 The Seahawks have turned the ball over nine times in five games, which is tied for fifth most in the NFL. That includes three turnovers in their Week 3 loss to the previously winless Washington Commanders .

 

 "We need to grow quickly in terms of complementary football," coach Mike Macdonald said. "Definitely [in] taking care of the football. Way too many giveaways at this point in the season."

 For the second week in a row, Darnold was intercepted on Seattle's opening possession. He was trying to hit Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a third-down throw toward the sideline when 49ers cornerback Renardo Green picked it off. Green got him again on Seattle's first drive of the third quarter, when he jumped in front of a throw over the middle to tight end Elijah Arroyo that didn't have enough air under it.

 Darnold was sacked five times -- his most in 24 games with Seattle (including playoffs), per ESPN Research -- and did well to keep several plays alive amid a barrage of pressure.

 "There's a couple of decisions that I would like back," said Darnold, who completed 18 of 29 attempts for 195 yards and a touchdown. "The second one that I threw, just being able to kind of throw that over the top and let him go get it. I think the other one is just poor decision. Just got to continue to trust myself, trust my feet, trust what I'm seeing, which I'm doing. But just got to be better taking care of the football."

 Darnold has thrown five interceptions since he returned from a glute injury, compared to zero turnovers by Drew Lock while he filled in for most of the first two games. Darnold led all players with 20 turnovers during the 2025 regular season, though he didn't give the ball away in three playoff games despite playing through an oblique injury.

 "We're not panicking or anything like that," Macdonald said. "We're just going through what we do every day. I think if we become more efficient and more effective as an offense, that's going to help our quarterback, too. I think it's everybody. It's not just Sam. Sam knows. It's not like he wants to turn it over. We need to just play collectively more efficient. I think when that happens, then the ball doesn't become in jeopardy as much."

 As Macdonald said, it's not just a Darnold problem.  Emanuel Wilson 's fumble midway through the second quarter set up an easy 49ers touchdown. Disaster then struck in the closing seconds of the half. As the Seahawks were trying to run out the clock while backed up against their own goal line, George Holani was stripped in the end zone for another San Francisco touchdown.

 

 Wilson has been serving as the RB1 with Jadarian Price sidelined by  a chest injury , and while the Seahawks have cobbled together a serviceable run game at times, they're missing the rookie first-round pick's explosiveness. Neither Wilson nor Holani had a run longer than 9 yards Sunday as they combined for 68 yards on 24 attempts.

 The Seahawks are also missing  Zach Charbonnet 's ball security, among other things that last season's co-starter does well. Charbonnet, who has not fumbled in his first three NFL seasons, is still working his way back from February ACL surgery. Macdonald said Seattle's current plan is that he won't play Thursday night against the Denver Broncos  ( 8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video ). Price -- who lost two fumbles of his own before going on injured reserve last week -- has to miss at least two more games.

 The Seahawks' 28 turnovers last season were second most in the NFL. They overcame them thanks to the league's best scoring defense, ESPN Analytics' top-ranked special teams and an offense that was plenty explosive when it hung on to the ball.

 Special teams did its part and then some Sunday, with Jason Myers hitting all five of his field goal tries and Nehemiah Pritchett forcing a fumble on a muffed punt. Pritchett's interception was one of two takeaways for Seattle's defense, which controlled the game for three quarters -- the 49ers' only points in that span came via turnovers -- until San Francisco put together consecutive scoring drives in the fourth.

 "Without a doubt, there's frustration," wide receiver Cooper Kupp  said. "We were very aware of how good the defense is playing, the fact that up to that point we had given them two short fields that the 49ers did a great job of capitalizing on. And then you gift them seven points there at the end. We just can't do that. Offensively, we put the defense in a lot of really tough positions. They have bailed us out over and over and over again, and we just can't do that.

 "We can't put them in those spots. That's all there is to it."

 Between their franchise-record 150 penalty yards last week and seven combined turnovers in their two losses on either end of a narrow win over the Los Angeles Chargers , Macdonald's team is not playing clean football.

 

 Still, the Seahawks had a chance to tie or win this game on their final possession. It started with a 35-yard completion to Smith-Njigba, who then dropped two passes over the next three plays. One came on a quick slant in which he took a shot from a 49ers defender, causing him to miss the next snap. But his second drop came on an uncontested deep throw.

 "I have to reel those ones in and I know that," said Smith-Njigba, who caught five passes for 102 yards and a touchdown.

 This time last year, the Seahawks were also 3-2, having lost a shootout to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at home. Then they won 11 of their next 12 games to earn the NFC's No. 1 seed.

 "There was no talk of that," Darnold said. "I think a lot of guys are just pissed about not winning the game. Again, it's a whole different year. We're not in the business of comparing this year to last year. There's a lot of things that we need to get better at, plain and simple. We got to have a sense of urgency to do that."
